en: Auspiciousness.
Having paid homage to the supreme Goddess of Speech, who possesses a threefold form,
the essential meaning of the *Guru-alaṅkāra-sūtras* is here stated by means of a commentary.

In the *Alaṅkāravimarśinī* composed by Śrī Jayaratha, with the desire for auspiciousness, the author, preceded by a salutation to his own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), indicates the subject matter and the purpose in a single sentence: "Having paid homage" (*namaskṛtya*).
[He pays homage] to the Supreme Speech (*parāṃ vācam*), the presiding deity of all verbal expression, known as Parā, who is the power (*śakti*) inseparable from the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*).

Having paid homage to the Goddess— who, desiring to manifest externally in a threefold form, has her body presided over by the three modes of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī— the author, bowing down with body, speech, and mind before her for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the work he intends to compose,
states the intended meaning through a commentary on his own Alaṅkāra-sūtras; such is the application of the auspicious connection (*maṅgalānvaya*).
And thus, the expansion of the definition stated here is as follows:
"You are the very form of discernment, the wonder of ultimate reality; you alone are the essence of all things, and are called the supreme Speech."
That which is called Nāda is established within all beings in the form of the individual soul;
it is without beginning or end, subtle, and the imperishable Word.
Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the essence of speech, the imperishable syllable;
from it proceeds the evolution of the world through the manifestation of objects.
Vaikharī is the manifestation of sound; Madhyamā is the object of memory;
Paśyantī illuminates the meaning; and Sūkṣmā is Brahman alone.

In accordance with the sequence taught in such scriptures, the first transformation (*vivarta*) of the subtle, supreme power of *Śabdabrahman*—which is eternally manifest everywhere and now beginning to unfold externally—is called *Paśyantī*.
As it has been said:
"But *Paśyantī* is undivided, with its sequential order entirely withdrawn from all sides."
The light of its own nature alone is the subtle, non-departing speech within.
Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: "Undivided" means that phonemes (*varṇa*) are devoid of division by way of place of articulation (*sthāna*), cause (*kāraṇa*), and effort (*prayatna*); for that very reason, it is "withdrawn from sequence.
Likewise, it is "the internal light of its own nature," self-luminous; and indeed, it is the light that is the form of its own self (*ātman*), which bestows everything everywhere.

Or rather, it is called *paśyantī* because, like a sprout emerging from within a subtle seed, it manifests externally as a slight swelling of power (*śakti*) alone; it observes the intermediate state between the supreme (*parā*) and the middle (*madhyamā*) while remaining detached from them.
Beyond that, however—
"That which consists of internal volition and follows the sequence [of phonemes],
transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa), proceeds as the intermediate speech (madhyamā vāk)."

Thinking "I shall speak this," there arises the second transformation in the form of the *madhyamā* [speech], which consists of internal reflection and volition; it transcends the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is devoid of the manifestation of phonemes perceivable by the ear, and follows a sequential order through the process of articulating phonemes via the mind and intellect.
Indeed, the *madhyamā* is so called because it exists between the two transformations of speech known as *paśyantī* and *vaikharī*.

And immediately after that: "When the vital air has turned toward the [articulatory] places, Vaikharī speech— which assumes the form of phonemes— is produced by speakers and is dependent upon the activity of the breath."

Thus, according to its definition, the third manifestation (*vivarta*), which is manifested through the sequence of places of articulation (*sthāna*), organs of articulation (*karaṇa*), and efforts (*prayatna*), and is perceivable by the ear as a familiarity with sounds such as those of drums and lutes; consisting of words and sentences formed by a collection of the playful variations of indistinct and faltering phonemes such as *ga* and *ka*;

is called *vaikharī*. It is called *vaikharī* because it is manifested by that which is *vikhara*—that is, the specific movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) which takes (*rāti*, i.e., grasps) the specific space (*viśiṣṭaṃ khaṃ*) in the form of the mouth (*mukha*).
Alternatively, it may be called *vaikharī* because it exists in the articulated body (*vikhare śarīre*).
The suffix *-ī* is established for the sake of auspiciousness.

Thus, within this very first half-verse, through repetition, there is the application of the connection between the words and their denoted objects: namely, that the Supreme Speech (*parāṃ vācam*), in the form of the highest poetry, is the most excellent [speech] known as *dhvani*, which transcends the functions of direct denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The Goddess— so called because she is remembered by poets and listeners as possessing the respective powers (*dhātvartha*) of "playing," "conquering," "shining," "praising," "dealing," "rejoicing," "intoxication," "beauty," "sleeping," and "going" according to the rule *divu krīḍāvijigīṣādyutistutivyavahāramodamadakāntisvapnagatiṣu*— who sports, surging forth spontaneously by her own will;
likewise the Goddess who shines, making the word and its denoted meaning subordinate to the letters of her name.
Likewise, she is the Goddess (Devī), shining, for "shining" (dyotana) and "resounding" (dhvanana) are synonyms, thus she is known as Dhvani.
Likewise, she is the Goddess, worthy of praise by all and to be saluted because she is the very soul of poetry.
Likewise, she is the Goddess, acting everywhere with established conduct and never erring anywhere.
Likewise, the Goddess is radiant, bestowing supreme bliss by the mere hearing of her name;
likewise, the Goddess is intoxicating, generating a certain sense of self-identity in the poet and the connoisseur respectively through the faculties of perception and understanding;
and likewise, the Goddess is lovely, desired by all.

"Having a threefold exclusionary apprehension" (*trividhavigrahāṃ*) means that its mode of operation as a means of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇaprakāra*) consists of a threefold, three-pronged exclusionary apprehension (*vigraha*), that is, an apprehension by way of exclusion (*vyatirekeṇa grāhaḥ*) rooted in exclusion (*vyatirekamūla*).
For instance, in sentences such as "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the coolness, purity, and so forth perceived in relation to the hamlet are not denoted by the word;
for words such as "Ganges" do not directly denote meanings such as coolness.
It is not of the nature of *tātparya* (intentional import),
for the power of *tātparya* is exhausted merely in establishing the mutual connection [of words] for the purpose of understanding the relationship between the locus and the located;
it is not *lakṣaṇā* (indication).

Because the three causes, such as the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*), are absent, the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*)—which is not distinct from denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*tātparya*), or indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and which resides in a fourth stage—is pervasive; this very point he will examine further on. Furthermore, since the suggested meaning is well known to have its basis in both word and sense, it is "threefold" (*trividha*); or rather, it is that in which there is a "grasping of distinctions" (*viśeṣaṇānāṃ bhedānāṃ grahaḥ*), that is, a grasping of the various specific qualities.

Having paid homage to such a work merely by way of a brief introductory salutation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*), and not by means of an extensive investigation characterized by the exposition of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) through both sūtras and commentary (*vṛtti*), he states the intended meaning of his own *alaṅkāra-sūtras* by means of a commentary (*vṛtti*).
His intention is this: thus, he provides only a brief mention of *dhvani* with the words "In this [work], first of all, Bhāmaha... and so forth.
Let that matter rest for now.
The sense is that there might even be a failure to understand the intended meaning of the sutras belonging to others— that is, the compositions of others.
Likewise, it is also implied that such sūtras have not been composed by any others;
"tātparya" means the illumination of the condensed meaning.
Otherwise, one would not reach the end of the work by any means.
Now, it might be argued:
"The subject matter and the purpose must be stated in the opening sentence."
In order to inspire the audience to listen and ensure their sustained enthusiasm for the exposition.
According to this principle, the subject matter, purpose, and so forth are stated in every introductory sentence in order to incite the listener to action.
Since those have not been stated here, how could there be any inclination for listeners to engage with this work?
Do not say so.

For the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are indeed the subject matter here, since they are expressed directly in this work. And this treatise, titled *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, is the expression of those [figures]. Thus, by encompassing the restriction between the designation and the designated, there is an implied relationship characterized as that between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*).
Indeed, there exists no other such distinct section that expresses this [definition], for even when sought, it is not perceived despite being capable of being perceived.
For this very reason, in order to highlight its distinction from other treatises on poetics (alaṅkāra), it was stated: "The intended meaning (tātparya) is now declared," and so forth.

And the subjects to be treated here are the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), not those of common worldly usage; thus, by means of their embellishment of poetry, they serve indirectly [the following purposes]: "Poetry leads to fame, to wealth, to knowledge of worldly conduct, to the warding off of misfortune, to immediate supreme bliss, and to instruction through its resemblance to a beloved woman."

According to the principle stated above, since [the treatise] has as its intrinsic nature an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with that [subject], its purpose (*prayojana*) consists in the attainment of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*), which takes the form of the accomplishment of all human goals implied by the subject matter.
Furthermore, the relationship (*saṃbandha*) between these two is characterized by the nature of the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*).
Thus, it is established that the opening statement serves as the basis for generating in the listener the desire to hear and faith.

Now, one might object: "If the ornaments (alaṅkāras) are the subject matter here, then that which is ornamented must also be the subject matter. According to the principle that 'ornaments depend upon that which is to be ornamented,' what indeed is this very thing whose nature is expressed as being an embellishment for them? Anticipating this doubt, the author begins the introduction to that very point with the words "here" (iha), and so forth.

INTRODUCTORY DISCOURSE: Here, indeed, the ancient authors on poetics, such as Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, and others, consider the implied meaning (*pratīyamāna-artha*) to be included within the category of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) because it serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
This is evident in cases such as *paryāyokta*, *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, *samāsokti*, *ākṣepa*, *vyājastuti*, *upameyopamā*, *ananvaya*, and so forth.

They have explained that the mere matter (*vastumātra*), while being understood as a subordinate embellishment (*vācyopaskāraka*) of the expressed meaning, is presented through two modes according to the circumstances: "attracting another for its own establishment" and "surrendering itself for the sake of another. Rudraṭa also stated that the figure of speech *bhāva* is of two kinds.
In figures such as *rūpaka*, *dīpaka*, *apahnuti*, and *tulyayogitā*, ornaments like simile (*upamā*) and others are stated to function as embellishments of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
However, *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is said to be apprehended by itself [as a suggested sense].
In the case of *rasavat*, *preyas*, and so forth, however, rasa, bhāva, and the like are stated to be causes for the beauty of the expressed meaning.

Thus, all three types of *pratīyamāna* (suggested meaning) have indeed been declared to be figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) by Daṇḍin and others through the use of the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*). The word "tāvat" indicates the absence of any disagreement.
The phrase "ancient," and so forth, implies that the opinion of the author of the *Dhvani* has not been seen by these [authors].
Regarding the term "the suggested" (*pratīyamāna*): [it refers to that which is apprehended through suggestion].
The meaning is that it is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as being distinct from the expressed object.
"The object" (*artha*) refers to that which is characterized by being the supreme thing to be attained, by virtue of being the locus of rest.
"By way of being an embellisher of the expressed meaning"—
for the state of being an embellisher of the expressed meaning is indeed the very essence of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*). Thus, it is included within the category of figures of speech.
The meaning is that it is included within the various ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) themselves, and not something separate from them.
"They consider" means they consider it to be such, but it does not actually exist in that way.
The point is that the transformation of entities does not occur merely through mental conceit (*abhimāna*).
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "By them, the mere thing (*vastumātra*) being perceived is presented as a refinement of the expressed meaning (*vācya*)."
It is merely the matter itself, and not the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) nor the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of their own establishment":
in such cases as "the spears enter," for the sake of establishing their own entry, the persons joined with the spears are implied by the spears themselves.
Without them, their entry [into the primary meaning] would not be established.

However, in cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the word *gaṅgā* surrenders itself to the further bank (*taṭa*) in order to establish that the bank is the locus of the hamlet;
for it is impossible for the word itself to be the locus of the hamlet.
Regarding the phrase "according to the requirements":
in some cases, the expressed meaning implies a suggested meaning for its own establishment; and in other cases, being itself untenable, it surrenders its own sense into the suggested meaning alone.
The meaning is that, therefore, wherever [a particular feature] occurs, it should be applied in exactly the same way.
In that regard, an example of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is as follows:
"He has burnt Laṅkā for us; he has crossed the ocean; he has brought from the medicinal forest the arrow-head of the son of Sumitrā."
Thus, repeatedly recollecting Hanumān, who was painted upon the wall of your enemy’s palace, the enraged host of Rākṣasas bites them with their teeth.

In this case, the account of the host of Rākṣasas—which is itself the subject to be described—implies the flight of the enemy and so forth, which serves as the primary cause for its own establishment; for without that flight and so forth, the account of the Rākṣasas would be incoherent.
An example of Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description) is as follows:

"O brother, you who by your strength surrendered your very life-breaths to him, by whom you were raised up, upon whose shoulder you long remained, and even for whom you performed worship— by producing the act of taking his life with a mere smile, you act as the supreme leader among those who requite favors, sporting like a Vetāla."

In this instance, the story of the Vetāla—which is irrelevant and, by the force of the context and other factors, inherently inconsistent with the subject at hand—voluntarily surrenders itself to the relevant narrative of the ungrateful man.
An example of *samāsokti* (condensed expression) is as follows:
"The tooth-marks and those torn by fingernails upon your body, which is covered in emerging, thick horripilation..."
These were offered with a devoted heart by the queen of deer, and even the sages gazed upon them with longing.
In this case, since the designation "leader" (nāyaka) is not applicable to the Bodhisattva [in the literal sense], he invokes the status of a leader for the sake of establishing his own position.
The invocation is as follows: "What shall we say? It is said; or rather, what is the use of saying this?"
"You will be spoken to anyway; or rather, what is the point of my speaking, since you have already been spoken to?"
"What shall we say? How much more could be said? Or what is the use of saying this?
Even so it shall be said; or rather, I speak—have I not already spoken?"

In this context, the prohibition of speaking regarding the subject matter about to be described—which, being something that ought to be spoken, cannot logically be prohibited once the act of speaking has already commenced—is itself unable to find rest; thus, by surrendering its own nature, it implies three further meanings: "I shall die for you," or "I am dying," or "I have died.
These constitute three distinct injunctions implied by the sense.
As for what others have stated here—that "the expressed meaning implies another meaning for its own establishment"—that is indeed incorrect.
For if that were the case, the figure would terminate merely as a negation rather than being a semblance of negation, and thus it would not be the figure of speech known as *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).
Indeed, the definition of *ākṣepa* is: "a negation that appears at first sight [but is subsequently sublated]."
Furthermore, because of the contradiction between affirmation and negation, a relationship of probandum and probans is not tenable.
An example of *vyājastuti* (ironical praise) is as follows:
"O Lord of the Gods, what is the use of the status of being the ancient Lord for one who is already the Lord of the gods?"
"Virtues became faults and faults became virtues; these were not brought about by them."
"Now, what is the power, the source, or the sovereignty of those ancient lords?
Indeed, virtues have not been made into faults, nor have faults been made into virtues by them."
In this case, the censure of the ancients, while being expressed, is itself untenable and thus surrenders itself to praise;
for censure directed toward them cannot possibly exist as a factual reality.
Likewise, the praise of the moderns surrenders itself to censure.
Furthermore, because that [reason] is impossible as residing in that [subject] due to its being contrary [to the thesis],
the interpretation offered by others here— namely, that there is an implication of another [reason] for the sake of establishing their own position— is simply to be disregarded;
for in this case, it would ultimately result in an implication of what has already been stated by the ancient masters, and thus this is not tenable.
Furthermore, even in the case of secondary signification (lakṣaṇā), it is not logical to invoke another [meaning] for its own establishment;

for if that were so, there would be a loss of the very nature of secondary signification itself. This is because, since the secondary signified meaning is already established as such, there is no sublation of the primary meaning.
Furthermore, it is not logical to say that for a single [word], there can be both sublation and establishment at one and the same time;
for this is a contradiction.
If what is established here is indeed the expressed meaning (*vācya*), then it would be primary denotation (*abhidhā*) itself, not indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) is indeed the very lifeblood of that [metaphorical indication].

In cases such as "The spears enter," since it is impossible for the spears themselves to enter, there is indeed a sublation of the primary meaning; thus, the primary status belongs to the indicated object itself, which possesses the form of the spears.
Consequently, it is only logical that in metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the primary meaning, being sublated, surrenders its own nature to the other, which is the indicated object itself.

Now, if this is so, then it would be more logical to say that in *paryāyokta* and similar figures, there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of another, implied meaning (*lakṣya*) for the sake of establishing the expressed meaning (*vācya*).

Or rather, if this is so, then it would be more logical to say that in *paryāyokta* and similar figures, the expressed meaning itself surrenders its own nature to the other, which is the implied meaning, for the sake of establishing itself.

Now, if this is so, then in *paryāyokta* and similar figures, since an implication of another, implied meaning is perceived for the sake of establishing the expressed meaning, what should be understood in that regard?
This is how it should be understood: for here there is no room for indication (lakṣaṇā) at all.

In that case, since one must state "How could I [the cause] exist?", the effect, being inseparable from it, implies the supreme cause; thus, because the goal is established through this very implication (ākṣepa), indication is of no use.

Just as in the case of the injunction "A cow is to be sacrificed," where the thought "How may my tying, as enjoined by the Veda, be accomplished? leads to the implication of the individual animal through its inseparability from the genus (jāti), and not to its indication—exactly so it is here as well.
This should be understood as applying to both the cause and the effect.

Thus, even in the case of *samāsokti* (synecdoche), the behavior of the hero (*nāyaka*) implies his status as a hero precisely because it is invariably concomitant with it; therefore, one should not suspect that this too is rooted in *lakṣaṇā* (indication). However, the author [of the present work] has stated this merely for the purpose of restating the views of the ancients.
We have, however, examined the matter incidentally; enough of this prolixity.
The *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) is as follows:
"With dust raised by chariots and with elephants resembling clouds..."
Making the sky like the surface of the earth, and the earth like the sky.

In this case, the mutual relationship of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) between two things, while expressed, is itself untenable; thus, it transfers its own nature to another entity elsewhere, which serves as a different standard of comparison.
An example of *ananvaya* (non-repetition) is as follows:
"O Lord, if you alone were to become like yourself, then [only then would there be a comparison]."
The creation and withdrawal of the three worlds are brought about by the arraying and re-arraying of his own powers.

In this context, the relationship of being both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison belongs to one and the same thing; having abandoned its own nature in another object due to the absence of a second [object], it offers itself [as the standard].
The word "ādi" (and so forth) indicates a variety of types;
by it, there is the inclusion of the semblance of an injunction for the undesirable, the implied (ākṣepa), and others.
For example:
"Let it be; enough with these useless words, my dear, you may go. There is not even the slightest fault in you; our quarrel has turned away from you.
If your love for me has grown so deep as to have reached this state, then what shame is there for us when our wretched lives, fickle by nature, depart?"

In this context, the departure of the beloved is the expressed meaning (vācya), yet because it is impossible for that which has been commenced as a prohibition to be established as a positive injunction, the [meaning] itself, not finding rest therein, implies the prohibition by surrendering its own form.
Thus, it has been stated that the mere fact (vastumātra) suggested through these two modes serves solely to embellish the expressed meaning.

Nevertheless, fearing that the suggested meaning might not be established as falling within the scope of the figures of speech (alaṅkāra) due to the perception of a distinct separate object, he says "by Rudraṭa," and so forth.
"Of two kinds" means by way of having as their objects things that are either subordinate or non-subordinate [to another].
As it is said:
That entity whose modification, arising through an unimpeded cause,
indicates both that [cause's] intention and its connection, is [the signifier].
As she gazes upon the village youth whose hand holds a fresh cluster of *vañjula* blossoms,
the luster of her face becomes increasingly pale.

That sentence which, while expressing its own denoted meaning, causes another meaning to be understood— possessing qualities and defects dissimilar to that [first meaning]— is the other type of figurative expression (bhāva).
"Since I am alone, a young woman, and likewise my husband has gone abroad, whom can you ask here for lodging? This poor mother-in-law of mine is indeed blind and deaf, O foolish traveler!"
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, the phrase "in two ways" should be explained as before, based on the two types of indication (*lakṣaṇā*): thus,
in the first case, there is the projection of another for one's own sake, whereas in the latter, there is the surrendering of oneself for the sake of another.

As for the explanation given by others that the figure of speech *bhāva* (emotional state) is twofold— consisting of the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*)— as characterized here by states such as world-weariness (*nirveda*) and so forth, that is indeed contrary to the sūtra; for Rudraṭa did not present it in that manner,

and furthermore, it would have been more appropriate to mention it at the point when he was discussing how a mere fact (*vastumātra*) serves as an embellishment (*upaskāraka*) of the expressed meaning.
Thus, the two types of subject matter—namely, that which is subordinate and that which is non-subordinate—have been presented as serving to embellish the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Now, he demonstrates that even the suggested figure of speech (*pratīyamāna-alaṅkāra*) serves to embellish the expressed meaning, beginning with the words "rūpaka" and so forth.
Among these, an example of *rūpaka* (metaphor) is as follows:

May the eye of Śiva protect us— that eye which is the blazing crest-jewel of the serpentess of his furrowed brow, the fierce funeral pyre for the body [of worldly existence], the lord of the circle of moon-stalks coiled like a bracelet, a red lotus upon the forehead-pavilion familiar with the jasmine-flower of the nose, and a radiant flame of light.

In this instance, the comparison between the eyes and so forth, and the jewels and so forth, is understood as a verbal embellishment (*vācyopaskāra*), because without it, the similarity would not be apprehended. An example of *dīpaka* (the illuminator) is as follows:
"Only a few indeed know how to read a book, how to tie a knot, how to gather flowers from a dwarf tree, and how to enjoy the company of a young woman."
Here, the comparison between the non-contextual (aprakṛta) reading of Prakrit verses and so forth is understood as a means of embellishing the expressed meaning (*vācya-upaskāra*),
because both are presented solely for the purpose of establishing a similarity with the contextual subject (*prakṛta*), such as the delighting of mature women.
An example of *apahnuti* (concealment) is as follows:

From their breasts, which were bristling with thrill, the women somehow managed to part the circle of their bosoms from their chests— breasts that were twice the width of their pillows— and they parted their lips from their faces, which were pressed half-way together.
In this case, because the similarity of the arms and so forth is perceived, the simile (*upamā*) is understood as a verbal embellishment (*vācyopaskāra*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in *tulyayogitā* and so forth," figures such as *nidarśanā* are included;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "simile and so forth," figures such as *upameyopamā* are included.
It was as follows:
"The tremulous glance of the large-eyed woman, indistinguishable from a blue lotus swaying in the wind—
was it taken from the female deer by her, or was it taken from the female deer by her?"
Here, the apprehension of the object of comparison (*upameya*) functions as an embellishment (*upaskāra*) for the expressed simile (*nidarśanā*);
for without it, the expressed meaning would lack repose, as its connection with the actual thing would be impossible.
Therefore, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) established here is that which is apprehended, not the mere thing itself.
Therefore, the example cited by others in order to justify the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the preceding [definition] is indeed incorrect;
for in that case, it is the mere fact (*vastumātra*) that is intended to be conveyed as an embellishment of the expressed meaning (*vācyopaskāraka*).
The logical connection is that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is described precisely as an embellishment of the expressed meaning.
But she,
O fortunate one, not finding entry into your heart which is filled with thousands of women,
makes her already slender body even more emaciated throughout the day, having no other object of affection.
Thus:
"O fortunate one, in your heart already filled with thousands of women, that lowliest woman makes her slender body even thinner throughout the day, having no other occupation."
Thus, it has been stated that even a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), when being suggested (*pratīyamāna*), serves as a cause for the beauty of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Now, in order to demonstrate that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) also functions as an embellishment of the expressed meaning, he says "rasavat," etc.;
by the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), [figures such as] *ūrjasvin* and others are included.
And by the word "etcetera" (ādi), [figures such as] *tadābhāsa* and others are included. Among these, the *rasavat* ornament is as follows:

"Having with difficulty passed between her pair of thighs, and having wandered for a long time upon the region of her hips, [the gaze] comes to a standstill at her waist, which is uneven with the waves of her three folds."
Like a thirsty woman, my gaze has now slowly ascended her lofty breasts and gazes repeatedly with longing at her eyes, which are dripping with drops of water.

Here, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) called love (*rati*), consisting of the mutual bond of affection between the King of Vatsa and [Vāsavadattā], having become aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through the conjunction of determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning (*vācya*),
because the expressed meaning is apprehended with aesthetic charm (*sacamatkāra*) by virtue of being permeated by that [flavor]. An example of the *preyas* ornament is as follows:
"Stay! She does not remain angry for long, her power obscured by the force of her indignation; she might even fly up to heaven, yet her heart remains moist with affection for me.
Even the enemies of the gods would not have been able to carry her off while she was standing before me; and now that she has gone utterly beyond the range of my eyes—what is this fate?"

In this case, the transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) called *vitarka* (reflection/doubt) serves solely to enhance the beauty of the expressed meaning. An example of the *ūrjasvin* ornament is as follows:

"If your mind is full of curiosity regarding the playfulness of my glances, then let my twenty eyes behold you; if there is a desire for an uninterrupted embrace, then let the circle of my arms see you."
O Vaidehī, if there is pleasure in kissing, let it be tenfold;
behold now the great difference in treatment between Rāvaṇa and Rāghava before you.
In this instance, Rāvaṇa’s passion for Sītā proceeds with such impropriety that it constitutes a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa), serving as an embellishment for the expressed meaning (vācyopaskāraka).
The rest, however, should be inferred by oneself.
He concludes this very point with the words "tadittham" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of three kinds": in *paryāyokta* and similar figures, it is a matter of fact (*vastu*); in *rūpaka* and similar figures, it is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
In the *rasavad* and other [figures], there is *rasa*.
Thus, the ancients have stated that the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*) is indeed included within the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
However, they did not accept that its very essence (*ātman*) is something to be embellished by those [figures].

However, by Vāmana, who asserts that *lakṣaṇā* based on similarity constitutes the figure of speech *vakrokti*, a certain variety of *dhvani* has been stated as nothing other than a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
Furthermore, he declared that *rīti*—consisting of the arrangement of words characterized by specific qualities (*guṇas*)—is the very soul of poetry (*kāvyātmatva*).
On the other hand, Udbhaṭa and others indicated that there is essentially no difference between the qualities (*guṇas*) and the figures of speech (*alaṅkāras*).
Because the distinction is established by the mere object itself,
and because it functions as the nature of composition;
thus, the view of the ancients is that the ornaments alone are the primary element in poetry.

Although Vāmana asserts that what is suggested (pratīyamāna) is included within [the categories of] figures of speech (alaṅkāra), he nonetheless states that there is a certain "self" (ātman) which is embellished by them; thus he says, "by Vāmana," and so forth.
The word "but" (tu) indicates a distinction from the previous [views], because the self is also something to be communicated.
Regarding the statement "by speaking":

as it was said—"'Indirect expression (vakrokti) is metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) based on similarity'"; and he cited this very example: "'The lotus of the lakes opened its eyes, and the night-lily closed its eyes for a moment.'"
"A certain variety of sound" refers to "that whose expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed," and so forth.
"Merely" means...
The meaning is "at most.
Regarding *gumā*:
as it has been said, "Rīti is a distinguished arrangement of words."
Regarding the phrase "by way of being the soul of poetry":

as it has been said, "Style (rīti) is the soul of poetry," once style is accepted as the essence of poetry, then—according to the statement "the ornaments (alaṅkāras) are the causes of its excellence"—the ornaments, which include the implicit suggestion (dhvani), serve as embellishments;
this is that [opponent's] view.
He states that others have further refuted this as well, beginning with the words "by Udbhaṭa and others. The term "mostly" (prāyaśas) means "for the most part" (bāhulyena).
Regarding the phrase "by the mere object":
for it is logically impossible for things of different status to stand in the relationship of the embellisher (upaskāraka) and the embellished (upaskārya).
If that were the case, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that even poetic figures (alaṅkāra) would be embellished by the qualities (guṇa).
Because the same logic applies,
the followers of Udbhaṭa are precisely those who maintain the equality of those [poetic] qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras).
Thus, since *dhvani* is included within the very midst of the ornaments that depend on the expressed meaning (*vācya*), *dhvani* is indeed within the scope of the function of denotation (*abhidhā*).
It has already been stated that the opinion of the ancient masters is that there is no such thing as *dhvani* distinct from those [other elements].
Now, in order to demonstrate that which others have also asserted—namely, its inclusion within *bhakti* (suggestion by secondary indication)—the author says "vakrokti," and so forth.

Furthermore, the author of the *Vakroktijīvita* has declared that various forms of *vakrokti* (oblique expression), whose nature consists of clever and artistic speech, are primarily the very life of poetry.
Furthermore, the primacy of the poetic function (*vyāpāra*) was established for poetry;
indeed, figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are nothing other than specific modes of expression.
Even though the threefold division [of meaning] is perceived, it is the verbal expression itself, consisting of that function, which constitutes the domain of the poet’s creative effort.
Through such devices as metaphorical transference (*upacāra*) and *vakratā* (poetic curvature), the entire expansion of *dhvani* has been appropriated.
Their established doctrine is that poetry has its life solely in the variety of expression (*ukti*), not in the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
By the word *vaidagdhya* (ingenuity), the essential nature of *vakrokti* (oblique expression) is stated.
As it has been said: "Oblique expression is defined as speech characterized by the graceful artistry of ingenuity.
The particle *eva* (only/just) serves to exclude anything else from being the life-force (*jīvita*) of poetry.
"Life of poetry" means that which vitalizes poetry;
the meaning is that without it, there would be no poetry at all.
As it has been said: "Wherein a variety of *vakrokti* (oblique expression) acts as the life-force."
Regarding the phrase "of the operation": this refers to the action fashioned by the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*).

For, were it not brought about by the poet’s creative intuition, there would be no *vakrokti* (curved expression) at all; thus, since it is the very life-force of the [poetic figure], its predominance is intended here as being necessarily connected [to that intuition].
Consequently, one should not suspect that the predominance of both [the intuition and the operation] is difficult to establish in this context.
Regarding the phrase "the ornaments" (*alaṅkārā*),
the words "were stated by him" (*tenokta*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the specific varieties of *dhvani* taught by the ancient masters.
"Even though it exists" means even though it is being perceived, it is disregarded.
"Having the nature of an operation" means having a circuitous (or indirect) nature.

"Bhaṇiti" means "utterance"; "kavi" refers to one who is intensely engaged (*saṃrabdha*) therein. For, without such intense engagement, there would be no *vakrokti* (oblique expression) at all, as in the verse beginning with "cāru" and so forth.
The intended meaning is that *dhvani* (suggestion) is included within the very midst of [the poetic figures] such as metaphorical transference (*upacāra*) and *vakratā* (poetic deviation).
As it has been said:
"Where a commonality is metaphorically transferred from one thing to another that is far removed..."
One might even, to a slight degree, act with some degree of excessive conduct.

"That poetic figure (alaṅkāra) such as metaphor (rūpaka) and the like, which is rooted in the suggestion of rasa and primarily consists of figurative usage (upacāra), is considered a certain kind of 'crookedness' (vakratā)."
Thus he spoke, citing this very example:
"The sky with its intoxicated clouds, and the forests with their Arjuna trees shaken by the downpour."
The moon, free from ego, and the dark nights captivate us.
"The sky filled with intoxicated clouds, forests where the *arjuna* trees are drenched by torrents of rain,
the moon devoid of egoism, and the dark nights— all these captivate the heart."
Here, the absence of passion and egoism are metaphorical; thus, this is "curvature through metaphor" (*upacāra-vakratā*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), curvature of action (*kriyā-vakratā*) and the others are also included.
In this way, the entire expansion of *dhvani* remains established as being subsumed precisely within these forms of "curved speech" (*vakrokti*).
He says "merely," and so forth, to show that it possesses no preeminence whatsoever.
"Tadīyam" means belonging to the author of the *Vakroktijīvita*.
Thus, by its inclusion within the *vakrokti* (oblique expression) rooted in *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the true essence of *dhvani* has been established.
[The author] says "Bhaṭṭanāyaka," etc., because some have claimed that this [dhvani] is not to be defined since it is beyond the scope of speech.

Bhaṭṭanāyaka, however, while asserting that the function of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*)—which he accepted through bold assertion—is a constituent part of poetry, declared that the function alone, in which the nature of word and meaning is subordinated, possesses primacy.

Even there, a function consisting of the savoring of rasa— which transcends the two functions characterized as denotation (*abhidhā*) and manifestation (*bhāvakatva*), and which is synonymous with enjoyment (*bhoga*)— is accepted as the primary locus of repose.
This is stated by way of a bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*),
and not by means of providing a formal definition (*lakṣaṇakaraṇa*).
It is for this very reason that the maturity of the statement consists in its acceptance even of that which cannot be defined;
it is a constituent part of poetry (*kāvyāṃśatva*), but not its very soul (*kāvyātmatva*). As he said:
"Even though there is another operation called *dhvani*, which consists of suggestion (*vyañjanā*),
even if its distinction [from other operations] were established, it would not be characterized as a constituent part of poetry."
Thus:
"of the operation" means of the poet's work.
Otherwise, there would be no distinction between poetry and the Vedas and other texts where sound is predominant, as well as the Itihāsas and other works where meaning is predominant.
As it has been said:
"Relying on the predominance of sound, they know that [the former] to be a distinct category of scripture (śāstra)."
However, they say that this narrative concerning these two is endowed with the true meaning of reality.
When both are qualities and the operation is predominant, there arises the cognition of poetry (kāvyadhī).
Thus:
"even there" means even when the operation in the form of the poet's work is predominant.
"Denotation (abhidhā), suggestion (bhāvanā), and another, namely the enjoyment (āsvādīkṛti)—thus poetry has been said by him to have three components.
Furthermore, regarding those:
"Denotation (abhidhā) is the power of intentionality; indication (lakṣaṇā) and inference are twofold."
In some cases, there is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), while in others, there is the poetic figure of synecdoche (samāsokti) and so forth.
"The fact that rasa is an effect, its being produced by a process, and the exclusion of other functions—
thus there are twelve such points of controversy regarding this dhvani."
Thus, although many types of divergent views are possible according to this logic, nevertheless:
"Others have declared the non-existence of that which was previously proclaimed by the wise as 'dhvani is the soul of poetry'; others say it is merely figurative."
"Some have said that the reality of those [words] resides in the non-objective"—according to this very principle, this mode of disagreement regarding *dhvani* has been stated here as the primary one.

In this way, now refuting these three modes of disagreement, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* establishes that *dhvani* alone is the soul of poetry, beginning with the words "The author of the *Dhvani*," and so forth.

Furthermore, the author of the *Dhvani* [speaks of] that which transcends the three operations known as denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and is designated by such terms as "resounding" (*dhvanana*) and "illuminating" (*dyotana*).

Since the operation of the *vyañjana* (suggestive function) must necessarily be admitted, and since this operation itself does not constitute the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and since it is precisely the suggested form of the sentence-meaning that—being embellished by *guṇas* and *alaṅkāras*—is primary, the locus of repose, and the very soul [of poetry], this has been established as our tenet. Because the nature of the operation is apprehended through its object, its primacy depends on the primacy of that object; and since the operation cannot be investigated in its own form [independently], the object alone is capable of bearing the entire burden [of poetic significance].
Therefore, it must be stated that the object alone, designated as the "suggested" (vyaṅgya), is the life-force [of poetry],
whose splendor consists in its being embraced by the beauty produced by qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras).
However, rasa and the like, being the very life-force itself, should not be described as ornaments.
Because ornaments serve as embellishments,
while rasa and the like are primarily that which is to be embellished;

therefore, it is the suggested meaning alone, having become the sense of the sentence, that constitutes the life of poetry— this is the very position that wins over those connoisseurs who understand the meaning of sentences.

Since the operation of the phonemes (*vyañjana*) cannot be denied by anyone, and since no alternative position can be established on that basis, [the following is stated]: "Denotation" (*abhidhā*) is the capacity for the comprehension of meaning dependent upon convention (*samaya*). "Intent" (*tātparya*) is the capacity for the cognition of a specific meaning through the mutual connection of generalities (*sāmānya*).
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the capacity for the manifestation of a meaning that depends upon auxiliary factors such as the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).
The meaning is that [the indicated sense] is something distinct from what has been excluded by these three operations.

Thus, in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the word *gaṅgā* and the word *ghoṣa* are conventionally established (*saṃketita*) respectively for the flow of water and a cluster of houses, both of which possess a general nature.
This is because effort is directed toward the universal alone;
for if a convention were made for a particular, there would be both infinity and ambiguity.
Consequently, through denotation (*abhidhā*), one perceives merely a flow of water and merely a cluster of houses; this constitutes one stage.
Even for the purpose of conveying something other than its own primary denoted meaning, the denotative function (*abhidhā*) is not capable [of doing so], according to the maxim:

"The denotative function does not reach the qualificand, for it has exhausted its power while conveying the qualifier. Therefore, by means of the power of *tātparya* (implicatory function), it conveys the specific [entity]—such as the Ganges-bank or the sound [of the cowherd settlement]—which exists in a relationship of locus and located with the general [meanings], through the operation of *tātparya*.
The second [type of indication] is when only the mutual connection [of the primary meanings] is perceived.

The third is when the word *gaṅgā*, being contradicted by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—since it is illogical for a stream of water to be the locus of a hamlet—indicates the bank, which is suitable to be its locus.
Regarding these, it is said: "When there is a contradiction of the primary meaning, and a connection [with another], then through conventional usage (*ruḍhi*) or through a purpose (*prayojana*)."
That function by which another meaning is indicated is called "superimposed" (āropitā) indication (lakṣaṇā).
Thus.
Indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs only when three conditions are present.
Among these, the sublation of the primary meaning is rooted in other means of valid cognition such as direct perception;
likewise, the relationship of proximity and so forth is also to be understood through other means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, as for this purpose that is perceived— characterized by the purification of the listener's ears and so forth— which is not stated by another word and is not established by any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), from where has it come?
It cannot first be known through perception alone, because its comprehension is not established from this very word itself.
Furthermore, it does not arise from the word-meaning itself because the word does not apply to that [proximity].
Nor does it arise from inference, because even when proximity exists, qualities such as coolness and purity are impossible; thus, [the reason] is inconclusive.
There would be no memory,
because there is no experience of that [object];
or even if it were real, there would be no recollection of the rule regarding it.
And what is the reason that this very thing is understood from this very word?
Therefore, this specific operation of this very word must be admitted;
for that which is devoid of an operation lacks the capacity to bring about the cognition of an object.

It is not, first of all, the nature of the individual self (*pudgala-ātman*), because of the absence of a [corresponding] convention (*samaya*). Nor is it the nature of the intended object (*tātparya-ātman*).
Because it is completely exhausted by the very cognition of its derivative meaning (*anvaya*),
it does not consist of indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
for there is an absence of the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) and so forth.

Therefore, the proponent of *abhihitānvaya* (the theory that words express meanings which then connect) must necessarily admit a fourth-order function of manifestation (*vyañjanā*), residing in the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which is distinct from denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Even for the proponent of *anvitābhidhāna* (the theory that words express meanings as already connected), who—like an arrow—desires the operation of denotation to be as far-reaching as possible according to the maxim "that which is the purpose of a word is its meaning," causes (*nimitta*) must be postulated in accordance with the resulting effects (*naimittika-artha*); thus, in the postulation of these causes:
Since this entire process must be followed in its entirety, the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is established in both ways;
and thus, as it is exceedingly profound, it has been stated here according to the logic of "established flavor" (*siddharasa*), like a mantra.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of "causing to understand," "comprehension," and so forth is also intended.
"Because it is necessary":
for without that [denotation], the meaning to be suggested (vyaṅgya) could not be included.
"Of the function" (vyāpārasya): [refers to the function of suggestion].

The meaning is: [this refers] to action consisting of phonemes (*vyañjana*). Since that [action], by virtue of being in the process of accomplishment, possesses parts arranged in a temporal sequence (prior and posterior), it cannot be perceived in its own essential nature; thus, it does not even dare to enter the path of critical inquiry itself. Therefore, the point is: how indeed could such [an action] constitute the meaning of a sentence?

As he will state: "Because the nature of an operation is acquired through its object, it is predominant by virtue of that [object's] predominance; since there is no need to investigate the nature [of the operation] itself, the object alone is capable of bearing the entire burden.
This is what is meant by "as that which is to be embellished."
The meaning is that it is established through being intent upon that;
as it has been said:
"Of the various causes of beauty consisting of the expressed, the expressive, and the aesthetic..."
Where there is a preoccupation with rasa and so forth, that is considered the domain of dhvani.
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, it is said "because it is the locus of rest.
Regarding "selfhood" (ātmatva),
the meaning is "the state of being the essence" (sārabhūtatva).
Therefore, the intended meaning is that without that [suggestion], poetry would not be poetry at all;
for a lifeless body is of no use anywhere.
Now, if this is so, then in the case of "A hamlet on the Ganges," the status of being poetry would follow as a consequence, since the suggested meaning is present there as well.
This is not so.

Just as here, because the self is all-pervasive, although it exists in jars and other objects, the conventional usage of "living being" (jīva) applies only to the body—specifically that body characterized by the senses and so forth—and not to jars and the like;

similarly, for this [poetry] as well, the conventional usage of "soul" (ātman) applies only when it resides in a body consisting of words and meanings that are beautiful through the ornaments of various qualities and propriety, and not elsewhere. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Now, one might object: "Is it not well known that in all cases the action alone is predominant, whereas here it is said to be the object? What does this mean? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the operation," and so forth; [the phrase] "by way of the object."
In response to the doubt—"How is it so? As in the case of the softening of rice and the like"—he says "of the operation," and so forth.
"By way of the object" means that, for instance, the nature of an action such as cooking is apprehended by way of the softening of the rice and so on.
"By its predominance" means by the predominance of the object; the sense is that,
therefore, the predominance of the operation is merely figurative.
"By its own nature" (svarūpeṇa):
for its own nature—such as being that which is to be proven—is impossible to investigate. The point is that investigation occurs only regarding that which is already established.
The particle *eva* excludes the operation of the phonemes. Regarding the term *samagra*:
it means the capacity for endurance (*sahanaśīlatva*) in such conventional expressions as "the self of the entire burden" (*samagrasya bhārasyātma*).
He concludes this very point with the words beginning "tatsāt" (therefore, etc.).
Regarding the phrase "yasya" (of which):
it refers to the object, namely the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which is the name of that which is manifested.
Regarding the phrase "having produced the qualities and ornaments":
the qualities (*guṇas*) are those various natures that serve as the causes for the beauty of both the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*).
Where there is a predominance of rasa and so forth, that is considered the domain of dhvani.
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, it is said, "because it is the locus of rest.
Regarding the term "selfhood" (ātmatva),
the meaning is "the state of being the essence."
Therefore, the intended meaning is that without that [suggestion], poetry would not be poetry at all;
for a body devoid of life is of no use anywhere.

[Objection: If this is so, then in the case of "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the status of being poetry would follow as a consequence, because of the presence of the suggested meaning there as well.
This is not so.

Here, although the Self (ātman) is all-pervasive and thus exists within bodies as well as in jars and other objects, the conventional usage of the term "living being" (jīva) applies only to the body as qualified by the instruments [of perception] and so forth, and not to jars and the like;

likewise, since this [poetry] also resides in a body consisting of words and meanings that are beautiful through their appropriateness and the ornaments of various qualities, the conventional usage of the term "Self" applies only to it and not to anything else—thus there is no fault whatsoever.

Now, one might object: "Is it not well known that in all cases it is the action alone that holds primacy, whereas here it is said to belong to the object? What does this mean? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the operation," and so forth; [and] "by way of the object."
For just as the nature of an action such as cooking is apprehended by way of the softening of rice and so forth,
[the phrase] "by its predominance" means "by the predominance of the object."
The sense is that, for that reason, the primacy of the operation is merely figurative.
Regarding the phrase "by its own nature":
for its own nature cannot be investigated because it is currently being accomplished.
The sense is that analysis occurs only when [the object] has been established. The particle *eva* serves to exclude the operation of phonemes (*vyañjana*).
[Regarding the term] "complete" (*samagra*):
The sense is that investigation occurs only when [the conditions] are complete. The particle *eva* excludes the operation of the phonemes.
Regarding the term *samagra*:
The meaning is that it possesses the quality of endurance, such as being designated as the "self" of the entire burden.
He concludes this very point with the words beginning "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
As for the phrase "of whom" (*yasya*):
Of the suggested object, whose nature consists of rasa and so forth;
"produced by the qualities and ornaments"—
of the qualities—
"Those properties of the aesthetic flavor (rasa), which are like the qualities of bravery and so forth belonging to the self,
and which serve as causes for its excellence while remaining fixed, are called *guṇas*."

According to the principle stated in [Kāvyaprakāśa 8], "Because they are directly its properties," this applies even to the ornaments: "May those which occasionally assist that virtuous work by way of being its constituent parts [be honored]."
"Figures of speech such as alliteration (anuprāsa) and simile (upamā) are ornaments like necklaces and other such jewelry."

According to the principle stated in [Kāvyaprakāśa 8], because they serve as embellishments by means of the excellence of the word, the meaning, and the defining characteristics of the constituent parts (*aṅga*),
the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) possess their status as ornaments primarily through their function of adorning the suggested meaning (*dhvani*) in the form of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth;
for that [status] is dependent upon the existence of the object to be adorned.
Furthermore, since it is precisely the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), consisting of rasa and so forth, that is established as the primary object of ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*);

for this very reason, in cases where there is an absence of a manifest suggested meaning, these [figures] possess only a secondary status as ornaments (*gauṇam alaṅkāratvam*). This is because, according to the principle stated in [Kāvyaprakāśa 8], "But their function regarding word and meaning is held to be by means of metaphorical indication (*guṇavṛtti*"), they are based solely on word and meaning and thus terminate merely in a variety of expression (*uktivaicitrya*).
And it is precisely with this intention that the nature of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) will be defined as a variety of the type of poetry known as *citra* (pictorial).
For this very reason, others have stated that "alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like are poetic figures [in the *citra* type]," and so forth.
Furthermore, although that suggested meaning (*pratīyamāno 'rtha*) is threefold—consisting of a fact (*vastu*), a figure (*alaṅkāra*), or aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—
Nevertheless, since poetry lacks its very essence without it, it is logical that rasa alone possesses the status of the soul (ātman).

Therefore, let us set aside what others have said—that because it consists of both matter (vastu) and ornament (alaṅkāra), it falls under the category of ornament; for it is absolutely improper to say that rasa, the soul of poetry, is itself an ornament. Thus he says: "rasādayaḥ," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), things such as existence and its appearance are included.
"They are not to be expressed" means that they are simply not applicable to a real entity.
For that which is to be embellished cannot itself be the ornament;
and if it were described as an ornament, another thing to be embellished would necessarily follow,
since ornaments cannot exist without something to be embellished.
He concludes this very point with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
"The suggested" (*vyaṅgya*) refers to that which consists of rasa and the like,
because it is precisely that which was introduced at the outset.
Regarding the phrase "having become the meaning of the sentence":
however, that which has not become the meaning of the sentence—such as rasa and so forth—may also be an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
As it has been said:
"In that poem where rasa and the like are subordinate to another sentence-meaning as a mere constituent part, my view is that rasa and the like function as an ornament (alaṅkāra)."
Thus [it is said].
And this we shall determine precisely in the context of the discussion on figures of speech such as *rasavat* and others.
The word "iti" marks the completion of the subject matter (*prameya*).
He states, "This alone," and so forth, to show that this [view] is indeed the correct one.
"By all" means by those who do not know the meaning of sentences (*avākyārthavid*), that is, by those who are for the most part lacking in aesthetic sensitivity (*asahṛdayaprāya*).
"Of another position" means...

In that regard, among the figures of speech (alaṅkāra) which depend solely on the relationship between the expressed (vācya) and the expressive (vācaka), its inclusion is not appropriate because it is established by relying on the relationship between the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the suggester (vyañjaka).
As it has been said:
"Because Dhvani is based upon the connection between the suggested and the suggester..."
How could it fall within the scope of the expressed, the expressive, or the causes of beauty?
Thus it is said.
Its inclusion even within *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is not tenable;
for it exists even when that [indication] is absent, and it is absent when that [indication] is present.
As it has been said: "Otherwise, because of over-extension or non-extension, it is not indicated by that [indication]."

Nor is it logical that this [dhvani] lacks a defining characteristic, for the learned have declared: "That particular type of poetry in which a meaning or a word manifests another meaning while subordinating their own meanings is called *dhvani*."
Thus it is said.
Thus, it has been established that these three types of misconception are untenable.
Now, [the author] says "But as for... and so forth, to show that even any other mode of misconception stated by some others is likewise untenable.

As for the claim made by the author of the *Vyaktiviveka* that suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is included within inference (*anumāna*) because the expressed meaning (*vācya*) serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*), that is an unexamined statement, since there is no identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between the expressed meaning and the suggested meaning.
This matter is exceedingly profound and must be scrutinized by those whose intellects are as sharp as the tip of a blade of kuśa grass; therefore, it is not elaborated upon here.

The author of the *Vyaktiviveka* lived after the author of the *Dhvani*, and thus his view is presented later in this work. Although the authors of the *Vakroktijīvita* and the *Hṛdayadarpaṇa* also lived after the author of the *Dhvani*, their views were mentioned earlier because they followed ancient doctrines.
Furthermore, this has been stated by him as his own original formulation:
that [perception] is included within inference;
the meaning is that it possesses the very nature of inference.
"He has declared" means as it was said:
"Where a meaning that is either directly expressed or intended by implication reveals another meaning..."
"Due to some connection, that [cognition] is called poetic inference."
Thus it is said.
Regarding the statement "it is an unexamined assertion":

here, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is determined solely through identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). And it is precisely by the determination of that [connection] that the probandum (*sādhya*) is established.
Otherwise, the proof of the probandum would not occur due to deviation.
In that regard, identity [is the basis of pervasion], as in the case of being produced and impermanence;
origination from that [is another basis], as in the case of fire and smoke.
Furthermore, the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) do not exist between the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*). To illustrate:

"The sandal-paste has completely vanished from the slope of your breasts; the redness is wiped away from your lower lip; your eyes are entirely devoid of collyrium; and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation."
"O messenger who speaks falsely, you who do not know the arrival of your kinsmen's distress, you have gone from here to bathe in the pond, but not to the presence of that base man."
In this case, a negation is understood through an injunction, or an injunction through a negation; however,
there is no identity between that [negation or injunction] and the expressed meaning,
because they are contradictory.
For non-existence does not have the nature of existence, nor does existence have the nature of non-existence; nor is there the production of one from the other,
because it is logically impossible for non-existence to be either produced or productive.
Nor is it logical that the qualifiers such as "the sandalwood paste completely wiped away" and so forth should serve as an inferential mark for her approaching his presence,

because they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since they can also exist during activities such as bathing. And this point, which the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* did not criticize, has been refuted by the present author himself in his own words.
For this very reason, other conflicting views have not been refuted by him.
Regarding the word "this":

the meaning is that the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*) is not elaborated upon here, as I have already determined this at length in my *Vyaktiviveka-vicāra*.
Thus, by rejecting the superimpositions and denials imagined by others, he states that sound is established in its own nature, beginning with the words "It exists" (asti) and so forth.
First of all, the function of manifestation (*vyañjana-vyāpāra*) culminates in the manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
Therein, based on the predominance or non-predominance of the manifested, there are two varieties of poetry called *dhvani* (suggestion) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion).
When the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is not clear, there is the third variety of poetry called *citra* (pictorial), which is considered a mere ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

Among these, the highest is *dhvani*. Based on whether it is rooted in indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or expression (*abhidhā*), it has two divisions: that in which the literal meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*) and that in which the literal meaning is intended but subordinate to another meaning (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*). The latter [division] is further named *vivakṣitānyaparavācya*.

The first [type of suggestion] is also twofold, by way of being "suggestion where the sequence is perceptible" (*saṃlakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*)—which includes "transferred" (*arthāntarasaṃkrama*), "merged" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), and "completely set aside" (*atyantatiraskṛta*) literal meaning—and "suggestion where the sequence is imperceptible" (*asaṃlakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*).

The second [type] is also twofold, by way of having its suggested meaning either "with imperceptible sequence" or "with perceptible sequence. Thus, there is suggestion based on indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*) and suggestion based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*), which is the suggestion of a fact (*vastudhvani*).
The *dhvani* based on the power of meaning (*artha-śakti-mūla*) with imperceptible sequence of suggestion (*asaṃlakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya*) consists of rasa and so forth;

the *dhvani* with perceptible sequence of suggestion (*saṃlakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya*) consists of the *dhvani* of a fact (*vastu-dhvani*) and the *dhvani* of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-dhvani*), both based on the power of word, meaning, or both.
Among these, the *dhvani* of rasa and so forth has been demonstrated in the *Alaṅkāramañjarī*.
Because poetry has *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) as its primary sentiment,
the remaining [sentiments] are distributed therein according to the occasion.

Furthermore, *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (poetry where the suggested meaning is subordinate) has been demonstrated, as far as possible, in instances such as *samāsokti* (speech of condensed expression), based on distinctions such as being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the expressed meaning.
The word "tāvat" indicates the absence of any contradiction.
To provide a specific explanation of this very point, he says "tatra" and so forth;
the meaning is: even though the function of manifestation (vyañjanavyāpāra) is directed toward that which is manifested (vyaṅgyaniṣṭha).
Regarding "predominance and non-predominance":
as it has been said—
"In that [context], both word and meaning are directed toward that [suggested sense] and abide with respect to the suggested."
That alone, free from any confusion, should be considered the object of the suggestive word (dhvani).
Thus it is said.
As it is said:

"Another variety of poetry is seen in which the suggested meaning is subordinated (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya); in that case, when there is a connection with the suggested, the beauty of the expressed meaning becomes preeminent."
Thus it is said.
Regarding the term "asphuṭatva" (non-manifestation): it means when the suggested meaning is not intended to be expressed. As it has been said:

"When there is an absence of the intention to express objects such as rasa or bhāva, that composition which consists of poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra) is considered to have *citra* (pictorial poetry) as its domain."
Thus;
"therein" means in the selection from among three.
The word "tasya" (of that) refers to the highest type of *dhvani*.
"The first" refers to that in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*).
The meaning of the particle "api" (also) is that not only is *dhvani* twofold, but its source (*tatprabheda*) is likewise twofold.

As it has been said: "The expressed meaning (vācya) of the dhvani in which the literal sense is not intended to be conveyed is considered to be of two kinds: that which is transferred to another meaning, or that which is completely set aside."
Thus.
"The second" refers to that which has an intended meaning other than the literal one (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
As it has been said:

"The soul of *dhvani*—whose intended meaning is to be expressed—is considered to be of two kinds: that which shines forth with imperceptible sequence, and that which is manifested through a sequential process."
Thus [ends the previous section].

In this very context, in order to demonstrate that the *vastu* (subject matter), *rasa* (sentiment), and *alaṅkāra* (ornament) function as *dhvani* (suggested meaning), he says: "based on indication" (*lakṣaṇāmūla*), etc.
By "based on indication," he means that the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary (*avivakṣitavācya*).
It is rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*), and not, however, rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*).

Although the power of the meaning is also present in that which is rooted in the power of the word, nevertheless, because it is established there as a mere auxiliary (*sahakāritayā*), it is described as being rooted in the power of the word due to its predominance.
This should be understood likewise in the case of being rooted in the power of the meaning.
Regarding "suggestion of a fact" (*vastudhvani*): this is so because a mere fact (*vastumātra*), distinct from rasa and poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), is being suggested.
Among these, an example of suggestion of a fact where the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) is as follows:
"The sky is filled with clouds of glossy, dark luster, with cranes wheeling about; the winds are laden with spray; and the soft, joyous cries of the peacocks—the friends of the clouds—resound.
Let it be so; I, Rāma, am of a heart truly hardened and shall endure all. But what will become of Vaidehī? Alas, alas! O Queen, be firm!
In this passage, the word "Rāma" suggests through resonance (*dhvani*) the reality of being the vessel for countless sufferings, such as exile from the kingdom and the like.

An example of the *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (where the expressed meaning is completely set aside) is as follows: "The moon does not shine, its beauty transferred to the sun and its orb shrouded by frost; it is like a mirror blinded by one's own breath."
Here, the word "blind" (*andha*), taking its own literal meaning as the cause, reveals the nature of the object— a collection of qualities such as lack of visibility, commonality, and lack of luster.
Regarding the phrase "rasa and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes aesthetic states (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and others.
Among these, an example of *rasadhvani* (suggestion of aesthetic flavor) is as follows:

"Having painted you on a rock with mineral pigments while feigning anger out of love, and wishing to depict myself fallen at your feet, my vision is repeatedly obscured by mounting tears. Cruel Fate does not tolerate our union even in that [painting]."

In this context, rasa is manifested precisely by means of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*). An example of the suggestion of emotion (*bhāvadhvani*) is as follows:
"I know that today in a dream I saw my beloved turned away in anger; weeping, she cried out, 'Do not touch me with your hand! and then began to walk away."
"O brother, before I could embrace my beloved and comfort her with hundreds of endearments, I have been robbed of sleep by that deceitful Fate."
In this case, there is the transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) called envy (*asūyā*) directed toward the ritual injunction.
An example of *rasābhāsa-dhvani* (suggestion of a semblance of rasa) is as follows:
"Whom shall we praise, O fair-eyed one, without whom you do not find delight even for a moment? Who has surrendered his life at the front of the sacrifice, whom you seek as your prize?"

O moon-faced one, who was born at the time of the rising of the sun (the ascendant) that you embrace so forcefully? This is the splendor of your asceticism; as for him whom you meditate upon, he is the city of Love itself.
In this case, because the longing is directed toward many lovers, it is a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa). An example of the suggestion of a semblance of emotion (bhāvābhāsadhvani) is as follows:
"She, whose face is like the full moon, whose eyes are tremulous and long, and whose limbs possess the playful grace of youth rippling with smiles—"
What then shall I do? How can I practice loving-kindness toward him? What indeed is the means for engaging with his acceptance of that [offense]?
"In this case, the thought proceeding from impropriety is a semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*).

An example of the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvapraśama*) is as follows: 'On a single bed, they lie with their backs turned to one another, suffering in silence; though the conciliation resides in each other's hearts, they both maintain a sense of dignity.'"

The strife of pride between the husband and wife was broken by their eyes slowly meeting in the exchange of sidelong glances, as they laughingly and impetuously turned toward one another and grasped each other's necks.
Here, "the pacification of resentment" constitutes a suggestion (dhvani) of the pacification of an emotion (bhāva).
There are also the suggestion of a fact (vastu-dhvani) and the suggestion of a poetic figure (alaṃkāra-dhvani).
Among these, an example of the suggestion of a fact based on the power of words (śabdaśaktimūla-vastu-dhvani) is as follows:

May the sons of Pāṇḍu rejoice together with Mādhava, their enemies extinguished by peace and the fire of enmity toward Nirvāṇa; and may the sons of the Kuru king, along with their servants, be restored to health, their wounds healed and the earth adorned with blood.
In this instance, the fact that the Kauravas have their bodies wounded and so forth—which is the actual subject matter (*vastu*)—is perceived through the power of the word alone.
That same [type of suggestion], rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthāśaktimūla*), is as follows:
"O daughter, you are the crest-jewel of the indolent and the foremost among rogues, possessing an abundance of wealth."
"By this being said here, Nāyaṅgī’s eyes have become wide with blossoming joy."
"O crest-jewel of the indolent, leader of the rogues, filled with the abundance of wealth"—
at these words, the slender-limbed woman’s eyes blossomed wide.
Now, by the power of the meaning (*arthaśakti*), the fact that "this [place] is to be enjoyed by me alone" is suggested.
That same [suggestion], which is based on the power of both [word and meaning], is as follows:
"O traveler, there is no bedding here in this village, whose ground consists only of stones."
"Having seen the one who carries away [even] the wind, if you wish to dwell [here], then dwell."
"O traveler, there is not even the slightest bedding here in this village on a stony ground;
if you would stay upon seeing these towering clouds, then stay."

In this case, the statement "if you are capable of enjoying [this], then sit" is manifested through the power of both word and meaning by resorting to the propriety of the situation (*vastu-vakraucitya*); thus, it is based on the power of both.
An example of *alaṅkāra-dhvani* (suggestion of poetic figure) based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) is as follows:
"High, with shimmering necklaces, dark like black aloe-wood paste..."
Whom did the weight of the breasts of that woman with drooping bosoms not make full of longing?

Here, by the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*), another meaning characterized as a cloud is perceived. Lest there be the contingency of the expressed meanings—the contextual and the non-contextual—being unrelated, their similarity is inferred; thus, this is *alaṅkāradhvani* (suggestion of a poetic figure). An example of that same [type] based on the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*) is as follows:
