The flower-arrowed god (Kāma) has fixed the hearts of beloved women— whose sole delight is in ornaments of jewels that are sisters to his own splendor— upon her bimba-red lips.
"Their hearts, which had been single-mindedly intent on seizing the jewel-like earrings of Śrī, have now been directed by the flower-arrowed god toward the lips of their beloveds."

In this case, the meaning-power-based suggestion of poetic figure (*arthaśaktimūla alaṅkāradhvani*) consists in the fact that the comparison between the reflection of the *kaustubha* gem and the lower lip is understood through the power of the meaning alone, or even through the power of the word alone.
An example based on the power of both [word and meaning] (*ubhayaśaktimūla*) is as follows:
"O you who rend the hearts of people, you do not delight me in such a way [when you are] drenched by the water of the rain-shower..."
Know that your fame is as abundant as the mass of hair on the enemy’s sword-blade.

"Your gaze, O lover, does not take such delight in the eyes of your beloveds— tremulous with tears that rend the hearts of men— as it does in the sword of your enemy, shimmering with the water dripping from its edge."
Here, by the power of both [the literal and the suggested], the identity (*aupamya*) between the mass of hair and the sword is understood;
thus, the word [“like”] is redundant because the object of cognition has already been fully encompassed.

Having thus demonstrated the various types of *dhvani*, he proceeds to apply the category of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinated) in another way, beginning with the words “guṇībhūta,” etc.
This has been shown by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*,
who said:
"Where the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is subordinate and merely follows the expressed meaning (*vācya*)."
"In that [context], figures of speech such as *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis) and others are clearly expressed."
Thus.

Having thus applied the various types of divisions to the *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) as well, he says "The *citra* [suggestion]," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the various types of divisions of the *citra* [suggestion] as well:
"But the *citra* has many more subdivisions because its nature consists of word-ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) and meaning-ornaments (*arthālaṃkāra*)."
For instance, there are three types of redundancy here: redundancy of meaning, redundancy of words, and redundancy of both word and meaning.

The statement at the outset regarding the manner of repetition is for the purpose of establishing the classification of the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) that are about to be described. Although sound is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than meaning in the process of cognition, the definition of "resemblance to the repetition of the same" (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*) is given first because of its long-established tradition;
the word "here" (*iha*) refers to the present context.
The word *iti* denotes a manner;
for the completion of the number [of types] is already established by the word *tri* (three) itself.
The word *tu* (but), however, indicates the distinction of this [type] from the two other varieties of poetry.
For this very reason, it is said to have "many more subdivisions.
[In the compound] *śabdārtha*, there is an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member);
by that, both types of ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) are included.
To demonstrate that very point, he says "tathāhi" and so forth.

Anticipating the objection—“At the occasion of defining the varieties of poetry known as *citra*, what is the purpose of stating the types of *paunaruktya* (repetition) here?”—he says “ādau” and so forth.
The ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) to be discussed later are five, beginning with *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the semblance of repetition).

Anticipating the objection that since the cognition of an object is preceded by the cognition of the word, it is logical to first specify the property as residing in the word itself rather than in the object, he says "the object," etc.
The meaning is that [the object] is well-known through its own nature,
and not merely by virtue of being connected [to a word].
"The appearance of tautology (punaruktavadābhāsa) as well as alliteration (chekānuprāsa)"—this is the traditional consensus of the ancients.
Since it is a figure of sense (arthālaṅkāra), its proper placement is within the section on figures of sense.
But surely, at the outset, it was [classified] as residing in sound?

The claim made by others—that "the exposition of the poetic figures (dharmanirdeśa) should be performed later, as it pertains to the meaning, and thus we see no purpose for this sequence; so what is the use of it?"—is incorrect. This is because since word and meaning appear in cognition only through a sequential order, the exposition of the poetic figures is logically established precisely in that manner. Furthermore, according to the maxim that "treatises flourish as they increase in excellence," the poetic figures of meaning (arthālaṅkāras), which possess limited charm, [must be treated accordingly].
The sequence is indeed purposeful, as the detailed exposition is to be performed later;
furthermore, since we have proceeded without transgressing the views of the ancient masters, the author has relied upon that opinion even though it is incorrect.
He will certainly rely upon that opinion again later for this same reason.
Therefore, whatever we shall explain as being based on the ancient tradition is indeed appropriate.
To determine this very point according to its subject matter, he says: "In that regard," and so forth.
In that regard, the repetition of meaning that has become fully manifest is a fault.
There is a twofold division based on whether [the realization] has taken root or not.
The first statement regarding what is to be abandoned is for the purpose of resting in that which is to be adopted.
The word "therein" (*tatra*) serves to specify among the three.
"Sprouting" (praroha) is the settling [of consciousness] according to how things appear.
Anticipating the objection—"What is the point of discussing defects in the context of a treatment of poetic figures?"—the author says "first," and so forth.
"To be adopted" (upādeya) refers to the essential nature of the poetic figure itself.
"Yathā" means that it is concluded exactly as it was perceived; "yathā"— [the meaning is] just so.

Behold the beloved woman at the conclusion of lovemaking, when the dalliance has ceased: she with eyes like a doe, eyes like a gazelle, eyes like a deer; with a face like a lotus, a countenance like a water-lily, a visage like a rose; her hair disheveled, her locks shimmering, her mass of tresses flowing.
In this context, repetition in instances such as "sāraṅgākṣīm" is considered *prarūḍha* (established).
However, when it is *aprarūḍha* (unestablished), it constitutes an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Nor should one suspect that its status as an ornament follows merely from the absence of a fault to this extent.
This is because there exists a specific excellence of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) appropriate for being an ornament according to the principle that will be stated hereafter.
He states this very point in the verse beginning with "āmukhena" and so forth.
Furthermore, the manifestation [of the object] before one's face appears as if it were being repeated over and over again.
The use of the masculine form (*āmukhagrahaṇam*) at the beginning is for the purpose of understanding that there is a change [in gender] at the conclusion.

In the definition of the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*), the word *saṃskāraḥ* is not in the neuter gender; this is intended to suggest, by contrast with worldly ornaments (*laukikālaṅkāra*), that poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkāra*) are dependent upon the object to be ornamented (*alaṅkārya*).
It should be understood that they are "ornaments of meaning" (*arthālaṅkāra*) precisely because they depend on the meaning, such as through the repetition of meaning (*arthapaunaruktya*).
The specific classifications are not stated here for fear of prolixity;
an example may be found in my *Śrīkaṇṭhastava*, as follows: "With the body of the lord of serpents, his arms serving as bracelets and armlets..."
The life story of Nandin, the leader of the Śailas, which shattered the pride of Kandarpa.
I bow to the Lord, the companion of Pārvatī, whose mark is the preeminent bull, whose eyes are like fire and the sun, and who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
"Born from wood, fierce, the supreme bringer of ashes and prosperity,
with red and crimson flames and intense heat— may the crested Fire protect you!"
"May Śiva, who wears serpents as earrings, whose cool rays are as bright as the manifest moon, and who captivates the heart, always protect the worlds from calamity.

[Regarding the phrase] "otherwise": *anyathātveti* / *anyathātva* means "being otherwise. *anyathātva* is derived from *anyathā* ("otherwise") with the suffix *tva*. *Anyathā* is formed by adding the suffix *thāl* to the pronoun *anya*. *Thāl* is a suffix prescribed for expressing the sense of "in what manner" (*katham*). The word *anyathā* is used here in the sense of "differently" (*prakārāntareṇa*). The suffix *tva* is added to form an abstract noun (*bhāve*) from that. Thus, *anyathātva* signifies "the state of being otherwise" (*prakārāntaratvam*). The particle *iti* indicates that this is a quotation of the opponent's view. The meaning is: "The opponent asserts that there is a difference in the nature of the object between the two cognitions. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows: the word *anyathātva* is a compound consisting of *anyathā* and *ātva*. *Ātva* is derived from *ātmā* ("self") with the suffix *tva*, signifying "the state of being the self" (*svabhāvatvam*). The prefix *anya-* is applied to indicate "difference" (*vailakṣaṇya*). Therefore, *anyathātva* means "the state of having a different nature" (*vilakṣaṇasvabhāvatvam*). The particle *iti* here indicates the reason (*hetu*). The meaning is: "Because there is a difference in the nature of the object between the two cognitions. Or, it may be interpreted as follows: the word *anyathātva* is a compound consisting of *anyathā* and *atva*. *Atva* is derived from *adverbial indeclinable* (*avyaya*) with the suffix *tva*, signifying "the state of being an indeclinable" (*avyayatvam*). *Anyathā* is an indeclinable expressing "manner" (*prakāra*). The prefix *anya-* is applied to indicate "difference. Therefore, *anyathātva* means "the state of being an indeclinable expressing a different manner" (*vailakṣaṇyaprakārābhidhāyakāvyayatvam*). The particle *iti* here indicates the cause (*kāraṇa*). The meaning is: "Because there is a difference in the manner of the object between the two cognitions. Or, it may be interpreted as follows: the word *anyathātva* is a compound consisting of *anyathā* and *tatva*. *Tatva* is derived from *tattva* with the suffix *tva*, signifying "the state of being reality" (*tattvatvam*). *Tattva* is a synonym for *svarūpa* ("own-nature"). The prefix *anya-* is applied to indicate "difference. Therefore, *anyathātva* means "the state of having a different own-nature" (*vilakṣaṇasvarūpatvam*). The particle *iti* here indicates the cause (*hetu*). The meaning is: "Because there is a difference in the own-nature of the object between the two cognitions. Or, it may be interpreted as follows: the word *anyathātva* is a compound consisting of *anyathā* and *itva*. *Itva* is derived from *idam* ("this") with the suffix *tva*, signifying "the state of being this" (*idantvam*). *Idantva* is a synonym for *svarūpa*. The prefix *anya-* is applied to indicate "difference. Therefore, *anyathātva* means "the state of having a different own-nature" (*vilakṣaṇasvarūpatvam*). The particle *iti* here indicates the cause (*hetu*). The meaning is: "Because there is a difference in the own-nature of the object between the two cognitions. Or, it may be interpreted as follows: the word *anyathātva* is a compound consisting of *anyathā* and *atva*. *Atva*
The meaning is that there is no final rest in the object exactly as it appears;
otherwise, indeed, a fault would arise according to the principle stated above.

Now, one might ask: since the word *punaruktavadābhāsa* stands in grammatical apposition with the general term *alaṅkāra*, and since it can take the masculine gender—just like *upamā* and other such terms due to its capacity for non-abandonment of gender (*ajahalliṅgatva*)—why has the neuter form not been used here?
Anticipating this objection, he says "of the *lakṣya*, etc.

The meaning is: the *lakṣya* is that which is to be characterized; "resemblance to a tautology" (*punaruktavadābhāsa*) refers to its designation or statement with regard to the word "again" (*punaḥ*).
[The phrase] "dependent upon the object of ornamentation" (*alaṅkāryapāratantre*) [is used].
Because they are designated as being in grammatical apposition with "poetry" (kāvya),
the necklaces and so forth are worldly ornaments;
for these have a connection, namely a conjunction, with that which is to be ornamented.
For this very reason, even their dependence upon that [substratum] would not exist.
Furthermore, the relationship of poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkāra*) with that which is to be ornamented (*alaṅkārya*) is one of inherence (*samavāya*).

Therefore, because they are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), it is logical that they possess only dependence upon the object to be ornamented; thus, their difference from worldly ornaments is indeed the correct principle.

Since the relationship between the adorned and the adornment (alaṅkāryālaṅkaraṇabhāva) is established through the relation of substratum and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva), [the author] states "artha... and so forth to address the doubt: "What is the basis for its being an ornament? The particle *eva* indicates the exclusion of verbal repetition (*śabdapaunaruktya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that because there is no verbal repetition, this is neither a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) nor an ornament of both (*ubhayālaṅkāra*).

It should not be argued that there is tautology because, at the conclusion, the object (*artha*) does not exist in reality and, in the absence of a substratum (*dharmin*), the attribute (*dharma*) would lack a locus—asking "of what would it be the attribute?"—for at the moment of presentation (*āmukhe*), the object appears as existing, and we do not deny the relationship between substratum and attribute; furthermore, the existence or non-existence of the object is irrelevant [to the poetic figure]. Moreover, the cognition that serves as the seed of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-bīja*) is precisely that which is apprehended at the moment of presentation, not that which pertains to the final conclusion.

For if that were the case, there would be no distinction between metaphors (*upamā*), poetic figures of identification (*rūpaka*), and so forth. Furthermore, even when the final meaning is reached—as in "born from wood" (*dāruṇaḥ kāṣṭataḥ*)—since the sense of "fuel" (*indhana*) is present, there is no lack of pervasion (*anaikāntikatva*); thus, its non-existence cannot be asserted as being like a hare's horn. Even if the sense of fuel is not the primary factor at the conclusion, it does not cease to be a cause for the status of a poetic figure; therefore, it is the same as in cases such as "whose body is the slaughter of enemies" (*arivadhadehaśarīraḥ*), where there is no distinction because of the presence of the sense of "body" (*kāya*), even if it is not [the primary intended meaning].
Or rather, why would there not be a lack of reality for an object that does not reach a conclusion?
For here, since the essence of poetry consists in mere cognition (*pratīti*), there is no dispute that whatever is perceived in a certain way exists exactly in that way.

Even when that [perception] is sublated, because the object—which appears as a redundancy—still manifests, its existence is indeed established, just like the perception of two moons by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*).

For even when a hundred [instances] of objects such as cruel things are perceived, there is no appearance of the object—such as a piece of wood—as something not already expressed [by previous perceptions].
Rather, because sublation arises, there is simply the impossibility of perceiving it as a repetition, just as in the case of the perception of two moons;
it is not that the cognition is non-existent in its own nature from the very beginning, as is the case with the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl.
For this very reason, although there is the appearance of repetition, the cognition of this [object] results in non-repetition; such is its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
If it is argued that even so, the actual absence of objects such as the body remains the same, that is true.
However, although a second moon is not possible externally in reality, it nevertheless serves to impart a certain distinction to the cognition.
It is not possible [to claim] that here, too, there is no difference in the cognition even when, according to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*), an object such as the body is non-existent;
thus, the search for reality is merely the passion of a *diṇḍika*.
Therefore, in this case, the very fact of appearing (*avabhāsamānatva*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of the object.

If it is argued that since manifestness (*avabhāsamānatva*) is a property of the cognizer (*pramātṛdharma*), how can a property based upon it be a figure of speech (*kāvyālaṅkāra*)? This is incorrect; for manifestness is understood to reside in the object being manifested, and thus it is a property of the object (*arthadharma*).
For instance, according to certain proponents of cognition (*pratītivādinaḥ*): [text continues]
"For indeed, what is called 'knowability' is the very innate form of the object itself;
for what is it that appears here [in consciousness] when one thinks, 'I know what is to be known by Caitra'?"
By the reasoning stated above, just as the followers of Kumārila maintain that "blueness" is a property of the object, so too must "cognizability" (*vedyatā*) be accepted as a property of the object;
and since this [property] begins precisely at that point, it is not logical for it to have any contact with the theory of the reality of external objects (*vastuvāda*).

Furthermore, if it is argued that this constitutes a figure of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*) because its meaning is equivalent to the "opening" (*āmukha*) and thus, being a property of the word, it resides in the word itself.

Nevertheless, since in the final analysis it is impossible for them to have an identical meaning in reality, the relationship between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) would be as flawed as that of a hare’s horn.
Even if they did exist, the flaw remains; thus, there is scope for all the objections raised against our position.
If you claim that the resolution here is simply that they appear to have a single meaning on the surface, then what has our own position done wrong?

And thus, even though there is a contradiction, since a contradiction in reality is impossible and the quality of having contradictory meaning is a property of words, it would follow that this is a verbal figure (śabdālaṅkāra). If you argue: "In that case, although a contradictory meaning is impossible, there is a determination (adhyavasāya) of it as being denotable by the agent and so forth; but here, because the basis of the tautology lacks syntactic connection (ananvitatvena), it is not denotable."
This is not so;

for in cases such as "the fierce one born from wood" (*dāruṇaḥ kāṣṭato jātaḥ*), since the meaning of the word *kāṣṭa* (wood), which is the locus of the perceived redundancy, is understood to be co-existent with the state of being "born" (*jātatva*) and so forth, its status as the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*) exists indeed through the primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*).

However, in cases such as "whose body is the destruction of enemies" (*arivadhadehaśarīraḥ*), although the physical body (*kāya*) and so forth are not actually the expressed meaning, they are intended as the expressed meaning because—by virtue of appearing as the locus of the perceived redundancy—they result in the beauty of the non-artificial sense.
In this context, a non-artificial meaning, when embellished by an artificial meaning, produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) in a manner that it would not if expressed without such embellishment.

For instance, according to the view that "necklaces, which are ornaments for women, further adorn even their breasts," although a necklace is an ornament of the neck, it functions as an ornament for the breasts as well— due to its proximity and because it imparts an excellence of beauty to them.

In the same way, even though it relies on a fabricated meaning, the fact that the apparent tautology serves to embellish a non-fabricated meaning is indeed perceived; thus, one must not deny the experience.
And so, this is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) only in those cases where the meaning based on the tautology is intended to be expressed as a poetic figure (*vācyatvena*), and not otherwise.
"With a face like the moon of the bright fortnight and the luster of a *bandhujīva* flower upon her lips—
who would this playful woman not delight with a festival for the eyes?"
"In this case, although the redundancy of meaning—namely, that it is not black—is possible, this is not a figure of speech because it is not intended to be expressed as such.
Likewise, for all the figures of speech to be mentioned hereafter, the poet’s intention alone should be understood as the authority establishing their specific nature.
To say more: since all figures of speech possess the quality of having a meaning that is compared and so forth, which is a property of words, they would consequently be verbal figures of speech."
Therefore, its status as a figure of sense (arthālaṅkāra) is superior,
for its very life consists in the appearance of repetition within the sense itself at the very outset;
for this reason, it is given the etymologically meaningful name *punaruktavadābhāsa* ("the semblance of repetition").
There is no dispute among anyone regarding the perception of tautology in the case of meaning;

for you yourselves have stated that this very [tautology] constitutes a verbal figure of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*). And thus, by virtue of proximity, it is logical that its status as a figure of speech consists precisely in its being based on that [meaning].

Otherwise, since even the state of having words with identical meanings would be a property of the sentence, it too would depend upon that [property], leading to the consequence of an infinite regress. Now, if it is argued that the capacity to produce aesthetic charm (camatkāra) here is based on a specific excellence in the nature of the word itself, and therefore constitutes an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) of the word—
then what, precisely, is this excellence in the nature of the word?
Is it tautology, or is it the expression of a redundant meaning, or is it the state of being a pun through words that are both *sabhaṅga* (with word-splitting) and *abhaṅga* (without word-splitting)?
In this regard, first of all, the first position is not tenable,
because there is no double utterance of the word and thus it does not appear as such.
Nor is the second [position] tenable.

Since the relationship of ornamentation exists through the relation of the expressed and the expresser (*vācyavācakabhāva*), it is not tenable for that [ornamentation] to exist in the relationship of the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*).

For this very reason, it has been stated that since all poetic ornaments of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*)— such as simile (*upamā*) and the like— denote meanings that have already been compared, they would consequently become ornaments of the word (*śabdālaṅkāra*).

Nor is it the third [alternative], because the designation "appearing like a tautology" (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*) is adopted according to its etymological meaning; for the figure of speech was introduced by taking the property called "tautology" as its defining cause, and here, the quality of being "paronomastic" (*śliṣṭatva*) is not relevant to that purpose.
Furthermore, in this context, the understanding of the repetition of meaning is merely the cause [of the figure];
and it is undisputed that the relationship between a cause and its effect is not what constitutes a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Therefore, since the repetition of meaning rests upon the sense (*artha*), it is logical that it attains the status of an ornament.

In this way, even the status of [the *vaktra*] as a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is refuted; for since all [figures of speech] consist in a particular excellence of the speaker, it is logical that they possess that same nature.
[The phrase] "for fear of prolixity" [is used].
But it is not because of an absence of variety;
"they are not mentioned" means that,
in reality, they certainly do exist.

Therefore, this [type of *śleṣa*], primarily because it relies on both the meaning of the sentence and the meaning of the words, first divides into two types; then, by way of being composed of either compound or non-compound words, it becomes fourfold.
For example, in order:
"May the mountain of snow, renowned everywhere, protect you."
May Himavat, who has attained renown everywhere, always protect you.
He embraced the river-banks yet did not abandon his charming trunk;
he bore the luster of a well-saddled horse yet was worthy of worship everywhere;
and he moved about with both a water-pot and a ceremonial jar.
He was one whose teeth were perpetually gnashing and stained turbid with rut,
bearing a certain cheek that bore the likeness of a door-panel,
possessing a luster increased by the pride of the elephant herd, and agitated by the restless longing for battle with other elephants.
"He who brings about discord among princes yet shines resplendently;
who has become like a female elephant yet is dappled with the ichor of rut"—
thus, in the *Anaṅgalekhā*, the description of the elephant contains a repetition of its basis.
The time that destroys the darkness is black, possessing the radiance of Govibhāvasu;
it casts away the two wings at the end of the fortnight, terrifying both the enemy and the glory of the other king.

However, the author of the treatise has cited an example of non-compounded words: "Verbal repetition consists of the repetition of individual consonants, the repetition of individual vowels, and the repetition of the combination of vowels and consonants. (Sūtra 4)
In the discussion of ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), mere repetition of sounds (*svarapaunaruktya*) is not counted because it lacks beauty; thus, there are only two types [of *anuprāsa*].
Anticipating the objection—"Why is mere repetition of the phonetic form (*svarūpa*) not counted?"—he says: "In the discussion of ornaments," and so forth.
For example:
"Yogīndra has a resolve similar to that of Indīvara, Indra, Indrāla, the host of Indriya, Indidira,
and Indra."
In the verse "indāvarammi...", there is no status as an *alaṅkāra* because the repetition of vowels lacks aesthetic charm (*cārutva*).
In that regard, he defines two types of *alaṅkāras* based respectively on single consonants and combinations of vowels and consonants by means of number and so forth.
START Sūtra 5:
When there is a restriction on the number [of syllables], alliteration (*che kānuprāsa*) occurs first. // RuAss_5 //
The rule of numerical restriction regarding the mutual similarity of two groups of consonants in manifold ways is as follows:
first, that which depends on a group of preceding consonants, for example:
"O frog of wicked resolve, why indeed do you produce such a sound by crushing your body in the evening, as if out of anger?"
Having heard these sweet, black-throated warblings of the swans in their play, are you not ashamed?

Here, by the word *sāyam* (evening), there is a *saṃkara* (commixture) with *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration of phonemes), characterized by their being expressed through a single designation, based on the similarity of the mere letter *y*.
"Chekas" means the learned or clever.

Because the singular number would entail plurality by virtue of [referring to] a genus (*jāti*), and because the plural number [would apply] to three or more since they are inherently many, a restriction of number is possible only in the case of duality; therefore, it is said "of two."
Anticipating the objection that the similarity between two [sounds] in a single manner constitutes only *vṛttyanuprāsa*, he says "in manifold ways" (*anekadhā*).
By the phrase "by the mere letter *ya*," it is implied that the life-force of this [type of alliteration] consists precisely in the similarity between two [sounds].

Furthermore, although this is indeed *anuprāsa* because it falls under the general definition known as the repetition of mere consonants (*vyañjana-mātra-paunaruktya*), [it is distinguished by its specific variety].

Although it is thus included by others, the author of this work has nevertheless provided its definition here in accordance with the opinion of Udbhaṭa—beginning with "otherwise," and so forth: "But otherwise, it is *vṛttyanuprāsa*. (Sūtra 6)

Similarity consisting solely of consonants is one type; similarity of the whole [word] and mutual similarity among three or more [words] constitute another type. *Vṛtti*, however, is an operation directed toward rasa; the arrangement of phonemes possessing that [operation] is what is here termed *vṛtti*.
And that [alliteration] is threefold, because it is composed of harsh, soft, or intermediate sounds;
this *anuprāsa* is characterized by those [sounds].
For example:
"Even though that speech of a poet may sport at the outset with great and skillful bombast, it nevertheless does not bring delight to the minds of the wise;
for as long as there is no *rasa*—resounding with the tinkling of abundant, beautiful qualities and ornaments, and following the flow of a shower of overflowing, elixir-like essence."
Or for example:
"The fiery crests from the hissing of serpents, or even showers of iron arrows, or winds in the rainy season that release liquid poison—these may be unbearable;
yet not so are these glances of the fawn-eyed women, directed askance, languid, full of intent, and intoxicated, pierced by pride, with their white and dark luster flowing like straight shafts."
Explaining this very same classification of distinctions, he says "kevala" and so forth.
By process of elimination, the "aggregate" (samudāya) consists of the form of two consonants.
Furthermore, the word "ekadhā" (in one way) should be connected here with this very term.

Because this [similarity] pervades the single [syllable], as well as groups of three and so forth, in many ways; and thus, in terms of being composed of all or some syllables, there are generally six types. For example, in order: 1. *Sarvasarva* (all-similar-to-all): *rājate rājahaṃsānāṃ madhye rājati bhūpatiḥ* "He shines among the royal swans; the king shines. 2. *Sarvaikadeśa* (all-similar-to-one-part): *rājate rājahaṃsānāṃ madhye rājati bhūpatiḥ* "He shines among the royal swans; the king shines. 3. *Ekadeśasarva* (one-part-similar-to-all): *rājate rājahaṃsānāṃ madhye rājati bhūpatiḥ* "He shines among the royal swans; the king shines. 4. *Ekadeśaikadeśa* (one-part-similar-to-one-part): *rājate rājahaṃsānāṃ madhye rājati bhūpatiḥ* "He shines among the royal swans; the king shines. 5. *Sarvāvayava* (similar in all constituent parts): *rājate rājahaṃsānāṃ madhye rājati bhūpatiḥ* "He shines among the royal swans; the king shines. 6. *Avayavasarva* (similar in some constituent parts): *rājate rājahaṃsānāṃ madhye rājati bhūpatiḥ* "He shines among the royal swans; the king shines. [Note: The examples provided above illustrate the various forms of similarity (*sādṛśya*) through the repetition of phonemes in different configurations.]

"By whichever [means], by whichever, by whichever you [are]; whoever, whoever, whichever; by whom, by whom, by whom; he went, he went, he went; he went to the one who has gone; he went for the sake of the one who has gone; O you who are joined with the path!"
The author himself has cited an example of a verse consisting of non-compounded words:
"Day after day he gave gifts to the wretched and the destitute; he sounded his praises; he censured the joys of Nandana; he distressed the one who delights in the day."
The mind has long been struck with wonder by these rays— abundant, pleasing, ripened on the treetops, delightful, radiant with the brilliance of fresh lightning, and enduring for a long time.
Then, in the month of Somaśita, that virtuous woman, whose intellect was supreme and free from darkness, gave birth to a son who was always esteemed by the virtuous.
"The body of this lotus-eyed one is exceedingly pure, possessing a beauty as stainless, soft, and lovely as a lotus;
for even he who has fallen into the hands of Kamalā remains stainless."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of four-syllable [names] and so forth is intended. For example:
"May he, who is praised by the hymns of deities such as Vāsava, grant [your desires]..."
The divine Savitṛ always bestows upon the virtuous that excellent abode which has been spread out for them.
"In this context, 'function' (vṛtti) refers to the arrangement of phonemes";
the meaning is "by way of metaphor" (upacārāt).
"In three ways" (tridhā): [end of sentence].
As it has been said:
"That which is joined with the letters śa, ṣa, and the saṃyoga of ra, as well as with the ṭavarga, and combined with pa, ra, ṣa, ha, and so forth, is the style known as paruṣā (the harsh)."

The wise consider that [speech] which is joined with similar sounds (sarūpa), with conjuncts (saṃyoga), and with the last letters of the guttural class (mūrdhan-varga), as well as with the stops (sparśa), to be Upanāgarikā.
Those whose intellects are attentive to poetry praise the rustic style (*grāmyā vṛttiḥ*), which is composed with the remaining phonemes as appropriate, under the name *kopala*.
[From Udbhaṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha*, verses 914–6] For example:
"These elephants, with throats terrifying from the unobstructed flow of ichor, resplendent with drums beating loudly amidst flashes of lightning,
with swarms of bees eager for their dripping rut, and whose inner flanks are wounded at every moment by the friction of their girth-straps."
In this context, there are three types of *vṛtti* (modes of composition), wherein "mediocrity" (*madhyamatva*) arises from the repetition of vowels and so forth.

Having thus defined the two figures of speech based solely on consonants, [the author] now defines *yamaka* (chiasmus), which relies on both vowels and consonants, beginning with the words "svara... and so on.
Yamaka is the repetition of a combination of vowels and consonants.

In this regard, there are briefly three types: in some cases there is a difference in meaning; in some cases there is no difference in meaning; and in some cases one word is meaningless while the other is meaningful.
For example:
"Whosoever beholds those two lovely eyes, [in him] the lotus-born [Cupid] arises."
In each of those other eyes, only a lack of delight arises.
This is in the sense of being meaningful;
in this way, other [cases] are to be understood.
The phrase "of one," etc., is intended as an illustration.
Therefore, the fact that among many *yamakas* there exists both meaningfulness and meaninglessness is already included [in the definition].
However, if the reading were "meaningfulness in some cases and meaninglessness in others," then only the first two types would have been mentioned, and the third variety would not be.
Consequently, the text as it stands, which specifies the different varieties, is superior.

"Concisely" means that, because it would act as an obstacle to the savoring (*carvaṇā*) of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which constitutes the very soul of poetry, it is not suitable to be elaborated upon; thus, the intention is that it has not been defined by dividing its types, unlike the ancients' treatises on poetics (*alaṅkāra*).
This should be understood to apply to *citra* (pictorial poetry) as well.
"Another" refers to two types. Among them, that which is meaningless is as follows:

In the springtime, she bore a splendor resembling that of the goddess of the ocean, possessing a luster of most vivid passion, like a lotus pond whose waters are stirred by bees hovering with longing for the gently swaying red lotuses.
In this context, the word *tarāga* is meaningless.
To illustrate the distinction between meaninglessness and meaningfulness:
"Taking food, taking food, taking food—he knows the food that is well-prepared."
It is a continuity, a continuity, a continuity—a continuity of delusion.
In this context, the term *sajjasāhāram* is redundant;
however, since the other terms are meaningful, there is no fault whatsoever.
And this [type of *yamaka*] does not occur without a restriction of position (*sthānaniyama*).
As it has been said: "A word with multiple meanings and a syllable repeated [in a specific place] constitute *yamaka* when there is a restriction of position.
For this very reason, "yamaka" is an etymologically appropriate designation for that which possesses a restriction of position.
And that restriction of position is merely intentional (vaivakṣika), not real (vāstava).
For example:
"The splendor [of the city], fragrant with the flowers of the hearts of proud women who had been conquered by the swarm of bees..."
He went to a place where the flood of lotuses had been warded off by non-lotuses, and where the copper-colored groves were in full bloom.
In this case, due to the arrangement of the *yamaka* (rhyme) within these two syllables, the position is fixed.
Or, for example:
"May Kārttikeya cut away your pain of fear—he who, O Kārtika, conquered that moon."
The Lord of Gaṇanāyaka has his tooth pulled out, whereas the other [Lord] is for the counting of the Gaṇas.

And here, since there are two *yamakas* (rhyme figures) for these two meanings, the restriction of position is indeed twofold; thus, there is no impairment whatsoever to this poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
And therefore— "O Goddess whose waves of disease have been shattered by the swift power [of Your name], O You who destroy the dense darkness [of ignorance] with the net of Your compassion..."
And from that, O most deer-like one, may there arise for you a mass of fame spreading here and there.

In this case, although there is repetition, because there is no fixed position for the repetition of the collection of vowels and consonants, this is not *yamaka* (rhyme), but rather a semblance of *yamaka*, namely *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration).
START Sūtra 8:
“The repetition of word and meaning that has become habitual is a fault. (RuAss_8)
The inclusion of the term "established" (*praruḍha*) is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the various types that will be explained hereafter.
As they say: "The repetition of words or meanings is tautology (*punarukta*), except in the case of restatement (*anuvāda*)."
"Fully grown" means appearing as such because of [the mind's] resting;
for example:
"In his lineage was born Śuddhamati, the most pure of the pure;
from him came King Dilīpa, like the moon [born] from the ocean of milk."
Regarding the phrase "the moon here":
one should not think that this [simile] is not firmly established because the moon is twofold due to its birth from Atri’s eye and from the ocean;
for such a state is not perceived in poetic convention.
The followers of Akṣapāda say: "In a restatement (*anuvāda*). For when a restatement is made, the repetition of both word and meaning does not constitute a fault.
The meaning is that, on the other hand, failing to act leads to fault.
As it is said:
"The sun rises red, and red indeed it sets."
In both prosperity and adversity, the great remain uniform in their nature.
Regarding the word "rakta" (red) here:
"The head of Śarva fell from heaven; from the head of Paśupati it went to the mountain; from the lofty mountain to the earth; and from the earth even to the ocean.
Thus, like the Gaṅgā, this [blood] has descended lower and lower. Or rather, for those fallen from discernment (*viveka*), ruin indeed becomes hundredfold."
In this case, although there is a repetition of meaning, there is no fault regarding the non-repetition of words because they generate a different cognition.
He states that this very [repetition], when not yet fully established, is an ornament, beginning with the words "tātparya" and so forth.
"But *lāṭānuprāsa* consists in a difference of intended meaning. // RuAss_9 //
Tātparya is the state of being directed toward another meaning;
it is only that which differs, not the essential nature of the word or its referent.
As it is said:
"The virtues of those who are perceived by their own kin become manifest;
like lotuses bathed in the rays of the sun, they blossom."
"Then virtues arise when they are perceived by those with sensitive hearts; lotuses become truly lotuses only when graced by the rays of the sun."
"O lotus-eyed one, close your eyes for just a brief moment; I say this to you:
know that I have come here, having swiftly carried away that golden lotus from the enemy of the gods."

In such examples, although there is no tautology regarding the case endings (*vibhakti*) and so forth, because of the tautology of the meanings of many words, it is indeed *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration in the sense of the Lāṭa country). For example:
"The *kāśa* grasses shine like *kāśa* grasses; the lakes are like lakes;
and the rivers, like rivers, captivated the hearts of the youths."
In such cases, there is no *saṃkara* (commixture) with *ananvaya* (non-connection), characterized by their being expressed through a single statement;
for they are established as having distinct domains, since [the former] resides in both word and meaning while [the latter] resides in meaning alone, each depending upon the other.
Furthermore, in *ananvaya*, the identity of the word is incidental, arising from propriety.
In this case of *lāṭānuprāsa*, however, that very [repetition] is the direct cause.
Thus, there are five figures of speech regarding repetition (*paunaruktya*).
This has been explained by the [very] words [of the text].
Regarding the phrase "being intent on another":
it means that while one [word] comes to rest upon its expressed meaning (*vācya*), another [word] comes to rest upon either its indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) or its suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
The phrase "it is divided" refers to the final stage;
for at the outset, both the word and its meaning appear as if they were one and the same.
Therefore, he says: "not the intrinsic nature of the word or the meaning."
And thus, this is not merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) when the two [meanings] rest upon the expressed meaning;
for the mere absence of a defect is not the nature of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
For if that were the case, it would follow as an absurd consequence that even the absence of harsh words (*prapaśabda*) and so forth would constitute an ornament.
If "intentionality toward another meaning" (*anyaparatva*) is defined in general terms as "that which was stated in the primary sense is not stated again in that same [primary] sense," then—

just like contradiction (*virodha*) and other such figures— there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even in cases such as "The sun rises with redness" (*udeti raktiḥ savitā*), where there is merely the absence of a defect, this figure called "intentionality toward another meaning"— which is appropriate for being an ornament (*alaṅkāra*)—
would also have to be classified as an ornament.
Nor is any excellence perceived by this much alone; therefore, what has been stated is indeed correct.

One word, *kamala*, terminates in its denoted object (*vācya*), while the other is grounded in numerous qualities such as fragrance and loveliness; thus, there is a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*). We shall now state how much [of that difference] there is.
In this case, since the word *abja* (lotus) does not result in tautology, it should be considered as *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration of the same sound in different words).

For here, because both instances of the word *nayana* (eye) rest upon their literal meaning (*vācya*), they lack any other intended referent (*anyaparatva*); thus, there is no difference in their underlying purport (*tātparya*).
Indeed, that [difference in purport] is the very lifeblood of this figure.
Otherwise, it would be merely a case of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and not a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).

If it is argued that while the word *nayana* alone rests in its own primary meaning (*svārtha*), when included within a compound (*saṃsarga-pada*), it again subordinates its own meaning and functions toward the designated object (*saṃjñin*), thereby abandoning its own meaning and operating for the sake of another— thus possessing a state of being established in the indicated (*lakṣya*)— this is not so.
Because the collection of conditions for [the primary sense] is absent;
for here, since the referent of the other word is predominant, the word "leading" (nayana) is subordinated,
but there is no sublation of its primary meaning.

This is because [the word] rests solely upon its own primary meaning (*svārtha*). Furthermore, there is no identity between the state of being subordinate (*guṇībhāva*) and the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*);
for it is only when a primary meaning exists that it may become subordinate in relation to something else.
Furthermore, sublation (*bādha*) consists in not finding rest within itself; thus, there is a great difference between these two.
Nor is there any purpose here, nor is this a conventional usage (*ruḍhi*); it is merely a tautology.
Thus—
O Upholder of the Earth, your fame possesses a splendor as beautiful as the rays of the moon and the form of the sun;
that Lakṣmī who dwells in the lotus belongs to you alone, and to no other.
This same principle should be understood in cases such as those beginning with "ityādi.

Here, however, the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is to be recognized as being produced by alliteration (*anuprāsa*). Now, one might object: "Since verbal repetition is also observed in the figure of non-comparison (*ananvaya*), should that too be considered this very same ornament, or rather, is it that [other] one? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In non-comparison," and so forth.
"An incidental [factor]" means that it is not a direct motivator;
for it is established that there is no logical connection even in the absence of identity of expression.
The sense here is that the identity of words (śabdaikya), when not employed in certain instances, brings about a lack of propriety (anaucitya), while in others it does not. This is as follows:
"That which is the eye of the worlds like the thousand-rayed [sun], the abode of lights like the sun, the opened gateway for rising like the sun, and the destroyer of darkness like the sun..."
May the Self of all embodied beings, who is like the sun, like the sun of piercing rays, and who is the creator of time—He who is incomparable to any other maker of days—grant us auspicious speech.

In this context, since the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) and others appear as if they were something else, they obstruct the cognition of non-connection (*ananvaya*); thus, the absence of verbal identity brings about impropriety (*anaucitya*), but it does not, however, entail the absence of the figure *ananvaya* itself.

[As it is said: "The earth by its stability, the sky by its pervasiveness, the wind by being the life-breath of the entire world, the sun by illuminating the universe, and the moon by its simultaneous production of nectar and its refreshing nature..."

May that Eight-formed One (Aṣṭamūrti) be for your welfare—he whose comparison is Fire because of his power of withdrawal and Water because of his nourishing all people, even though his true nature is Reality itself.
In this case, since the non-connection (ananvaya) is perceived without any obstacle, the identity of the words does not lead to a lack of clarity;
the word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction; [the term] "directly" (sākṣāt) [is used].
Because this [repetition] does not arise without identity of word;
he concludes this very point with the words "Thus, in this way," and so forth.
Furthermore, that which appears as a repetition is based on the repetition of meaning.

The three beginning with *cchekānuprāsa* (alliteration) are based on the repetition of words (*śabda-paunaruktya*), whereas *lāṭānuprāsa* (rhyme) is based on both; thus, there are five ornaments based on repetition. Although, because speech pertains to both word and meaning and is distinguished by its utterance and denotation, there is no commonality [between them], how can there be a fivefold classification?

Nevertheless, because both [the universal and the particular] are followed by that [cognition], they are perceived as one; thus, the statement regarding the relationship between the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the qualified (*prakārin*) is based solely on a commonality of expression. Furthermore, the distinctness of the word itself due to the distinctness of its objects is unreal, because in cognition it appears only as a unity.
For this very reason, even in cases such as groups of words with multiple meanings (*anekārthavarga*), linguistic usage occurs precisely in that manner.
Sūtra 11:
It is marvelous that phonemes can be the cause of the formation of swords and other such objects.

In the context of repetition (*paunaruktakya*), "variegated speech" (*citravacana*) consists of the repetition of syllables associated with specific positions. Although written characters (*lipyakṣara*) possess a particular arrangement such as that of a sword and so forth, they are nevertheless perceived in common worldly usage as non-different from sound (*śabda*), which consists of syllables inherent in the auditory ether (*śrotrākāśasamaveta*). Therefore, this is an ornament of expressive words (*vācakaśabdālaṅkāra*).

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), compositions such as the *padmabandha* (lotus-arrangement) are also included, as far as their formation is possible according to linguistic convention.

"Just as it appears: 'O assembly, alas! It shines with the splendor of the gods, yet its divisions are destroyed; its essence is the manifestation of aesthetic flavor, while its nature is cultivated through the perception of impurity.'"
This is the seat of the eight-petaled lotus.
Here, in the petals of the cardinal directions, there is the quality of joined syllables (*śliṣṭākṣaratva*) due to both exit and entry;
however, in the intermediate petals, it is otherwise.
The syllable at the pericarp (*karṇikā*), however, is indeed joined.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the letters" (*varṇānām*) and so forth: since there is no presence of a configuration such as a sword composed of letters joined to specific points of articulation (*sthāna*) at the time of pronunciation, one might suspect that no repetition is perceived here. Anticipating the question, "What then is the basis for this figure of speech? he says, "Even though... and so forth.

The intended meaning is that this verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*) is figurative (*aupacārika*), because there is an apprehension of non-difference between the sounds of the syllables being heard and the reality of the ink-drop forms of the written characters.
To make the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) fruitful, he provides an example by means of a *padmabandha* (lotus-arrangement), beginning with "bhāsate," and so forth.
Furthermore, an example of a *khaḍgabandha* (sword-arrangement) is as follows:
"He shall become a worthy vessel for the splendor of liberation, which pierces through the ocean of the suffering of all living beings and destroys the cycle of worldly existence."
"It is indeed connected," [meaning] even though it extends in the eight directions, it remains so during both exiting and entering.
(Sūtra 12)
Metaphor (upamā) consists in the similarity between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison when there is an equality of difference and non-difference.

This is the section on figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*). The phrase "of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison" is intended to exclude cases where the object of comparison or the subject of comparison is not well-known. Regarding similarity (*sādharmya*), there are three types.
The predominance of difference is as in *vyatireka* and the like;
the predominance of non-difference is as in *rūpaka* and the like;
the equality of both is as in this [present case].
As they say: "That wherein there is some commonality and some distinction is the object of similarity.
Simile (*upamā*) alone, through its manifold variety of forms, serves as the seed for numerous other figures of speech; thus, it is mentioned first.
Regarding this, the ancients have described its great diversity based on the distinctions between the complete (*pūrṇā*) and the elliptical (*luptā*) types.

In that case as well, a common attribute may be described with a single form due to its pervasive attachment in some instances, while in others it is described separately through the relation of *vastu-pratibastu* (correspondence between objects).
And in the case of separate description, there is merely a difference in the related entities, as in the figure of speech *pratibastūpamā*.
Or, it is like the relationship between an object and its reflection,
as illustrated by examples in sequence:
"Like a flame with its crest of smoke, like a lamp with its wick, like the threefold path of the triple-streamed river."
By that very speech, which possesses refinement, the wise man is both purified and adorned.
"As she departed, repeatedly turning her neck and bearing that face which resembled a lotus with its stalk twisted back—
the side-glance of that long-lashed-eyed woman, smeared as it were with both nectar and poison, has been deeply embedded in my heart."
In this case, curvature and roundness are distinct due to the difference in their respective substrata;
however, with reference to the subject (*dharmī*) itself, they constitute nothing other than the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbatva*).
"This Pāṇḍya king has long necklaces resting upon his shoulders, and his body is anointed with yellow sandalwood paste."
With its ridges reddened by the morning sun, it shines like the king of mountains with a gushing waterfall.
Here, the necklace and the redness [of the lips] are indicated as reflections of a waterfall and the morning sunlight, respectively.
[Regarding the verse beginning with] "upamāna" etc.,
[the word] "artha" means...
The meaning is that [this topic] has reached its proper occasion immediately following the determination of verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*).

Now, one might object: "Since similarity (*sādharmya*) is possible only between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), and not between things such as cause and effect, what is the purpose of including those? Anticipating this doubt, he says "the standard of comparison," and so forth. In that regard, the ancients have stated that the non-apprehension of the standard of comparison arises from differences in gender (*liṅga*) and other such factors.
For example:
"Wicked people, hissing harshly and bringing impurity, pierce [the heart] excessively like fetters;
but the virtuous, with their sweet voices, captivate the mind at every step like jeweled anklets."
In this case, because it makes the attribute of "jingling" (*kaṇana*) and so forth different in the object of comparison (*upamāna*), the discrepancy in gender (*liṅgabhedo duṣṭaḥ*) is a defect.

Even though the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) can be connected to both [the subject and the object], since it is already established, its connection to the object of comparison is understood by itself; therefore, it is not proper for that [connection] to be expressed verbally (*śābdatā*). Thus, the modification of gender and so forth does not occur through dependence on the object of comparison.
The word "kāryam" (the effect) does not render the difference in gender and so forth defective;

nevertheless, because the sentence expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), the verbal connection with it is indeed necessary for the finality of the cognition.

For in cases such as "prabhāmahatya" and so on, there would be no rest in the syntactic coherence of the sentence expressing the standard of comparison without a connection to qualities such as purity (*pūtatva*).

The only distinction is that the common attribute (*samānadharma*) is predicated of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and is merely restated (*anūdyamāna*) with respect to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Since its connection to both is necessarily required, the persistence (*anugāmitva*) of the common attribute is indeed established. Consequently, it is also logical that discrepancies such as a difference in gender (*liṅgabheda*) constitute a defect.
The non-recognition of the object of comparison and the description of that which is not even fit for description;
for example:
"The fair, thickly swelling, shaven vulva of the widow."
The golden slopes of Mount Meru appear like young grass grazed by the horses of the sun.

In this [verse], while describing the beauty of the slender-limbed woman, the description of the Lord (Śiva) is inappropriate; thus, there is a lack of recognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*).

To explain the equality of difference and non-difference, he demonstrates the established arrangement of similarity (*sādharmya*) according to its specific domains with the words beginning "In similarity" (*sādharmye*), etc.
And by these very three modes, the entire class of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) based on similarity is fully subsumed.
By the phrase "like a vyatireka," [the author] includes Sahokti and others; by the phrase "like a rūpaka," he includes Pariṇāma, Utprekṣā, and so forth.

However, although both Rūpaka and Utprekṣā possess a predominance of non-difference (abheda), the distinction between them is caused solely by superimposition (āropa) and identification (adhyavasāya).
As he will state: "When there is non-difference through superimposition, identification is further intensified."
Therefore, among the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) that contain a process of determination (*adhyavasāya*), no fourth variety consisting of pure identity should be suspected;
for even there, it is precisely the non-predominance of identity that exists.
By this [definition] as well, *upameyopamā* and others are included under the category of "similarity" (*sāmānya*), which is caused by identity.
"Distinction" (*viśeṣa*) means that which is caused by difference.
Thus, it has been stated that the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśya-pratyaya*) which arises regarding the domain where difference and non-difference are equal is the province of simile (*upamā*).
Now, one might object: "Even though there are many other poetic ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*), why is this one mentioned first? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Simile alone," and so forth.
Many figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are based on similarity (*sādharmya*), because that [similarity] alone is their seed.
As it has been said:
"Similarity is simile (*upamā*); when there is a distinction [between the object of comparison and the standard], it is either complete (*pūrṇā*) or elliptical (*luptā*), the former being the first."
It may be expressed through the direct word (*śrauti*), through the sense (*ārthī*), in a sentence (*vākya*), in a compound (*samāsa*), and likewise in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
By such [passages] as these.
And thus, the sense is: "What is the use of our revealing that?
In this way, it is indicated that there is no such variety whatsoever in their enumeration.
Regarding the phrase "even there":
The meaning is: even though there is a description of distinctions such as "fullness" and so forth spoken by the ancient ones.
Regarding the phrase "of the common property" (*sādhāraṇadharma*): a *dharma* is that which is dependent upon another.
And because that [word] applies to both that and what is not that, it possesses commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*).
This very quality is the cause for the occurrence of similes and the like.

Furthermore, according to the method of the *Mahābhāṣya*—namely, "the fourfold application of words"—it occurs in this very manner with respect to the substrata (*dharmin*) consisting of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*).
And this is not contradictory;
for the relationship between a substratum (dharmin) and its property (dharma) is not ultimately real,
since even a substratum whose nature consists of a genus (jāti) and so forth may at times be dependent upon something else, and thus possess the status of being a property.

And thus, there is nothing whatsoever to be said regarding a common property (*dharma*) that exceeds these [four], since it has been stated that the application of words occurs only through these four categories. [As in the example: "The mighty-armed one ate this with compassion, thinking, 'She might go away suddenly in distress.'"
He regarded the earth, recently brought under his sway, as a bride newly taken by the hand.

In such cases, since qualities such as the nature of an action can be applied to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth, and because that [universal] alone is capable of encompassing the entire range of objects, [it serves as the common property].

If it is objected: "If the universal (*jāti*) were the common property, then because [the object of comparison] would belong to that same class, it would not be 'that' [i.e., the standard], but rather 'similar'; how then could it be a constituent of the simile?"—we reply: no.
Because there is no suchness [of identity] based on the relationship between an original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

For in that case, since it has been repeatedly taught that two types, such as necklaces and so forth, possess oneness by relying on the cause of non-difference—namely, whiteness and so on—their commonality would be based on the cause of similarity.
This we shall explain in detail further below.
In that regard, the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) as being of the form of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth is as follows:
"Like the shade of a dense grove from a desert path,
like a pool of icy water from a forest fire, like nectar from the ripening of poison..."
O Śaṅkara, when shall I, having crossed over this separation as if it were a natural state arising from intense madness, obtain devotion to you whose essence is incomparable?

In this instance, the standards of comparison—shadow (*chāyā*), pond (*vāpī*), nectar (*sudhā*), and primordial matter (*prakṛti*)—possess the nature of a genus (*jāti*), a quality (*guṇa*), a substance (*dravya*), and an action (*kriyā*) respectively.
As for shadow, because it is of the nature of a genus, its status as a quality need not be suspected.
Furthermore, the status of the object of comparison (*upameya*) in each case is to be inferred by oneself.
But as for the nature of things,
it is said: "O Vaidehī, behold the foamy ocean divided from Malaya by my bridge,
like the autumn sky, clear and bright with stars, revealed by the path of the moon."

In this context, the action-nature (*kriyātva*) of the word "divided" (*vibhaktam*), the substance-nature (*dravyatva*) of the path of the shadow of the Rāmasetu, the genus-nature (*jātitva*) of the foam and stars, and the quality-nature (*guṇatva*) of the clarity (*prasāda*) are all established by their being situated within the ocean, which is the substratum consisting of a substance.

Thus, having abandoned the very system of the *Mahābhāṣya* under discussion, what has been stated by others—relying on an entirely different and groundless system—is indeed improper; enough of this prolixity.
Furthermore, such a [system] is twofold, consisting of the nature of existence and non-existence.
And this [explanation] does not bring about such variety; therefore, it was not stated by the author of the treatise.
"By way of uniformity" means simultaneously.
As he will state: "In that regard, when there is a single mention [of the common property] upon the employment of 'iva' and so forth, it is simile (upamā).
"Separate mention" means more than once.
As he will state:

"Even when there is repeated instruction by way of the relation between the primary object and its counterpart, it is that very same [simile]. This [phrase] is also to be connected with the words "of the common property."

He states that even though there is the state of being a primary object and its counterpart (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*), there is still a twofold nature, beginning with the words "in the separate explanation" (*pṛthaṅ-nirdeśe*).
The phrase "merely a difference in relation" (*sambandhi-bheda-mātra*) means that there is no difference whatsoever in their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-bheda*).
As he will state later: "In the case of repeated mention, there is either the nature of a pure universal or the relation of the original and its reflection.

Furthermore, these three types of difference generally constitute the very lifeblood of all poetic figures (alaṅkāra) based on similarity; we shall illustrate this in their respective places as we proceed.
The phrase "in order" means according to the sequence of their enumeration.
"Due to the difference in the related entities" means due to the difference between the two related entities, namely the neck and the stalk;
it does not mean a difference in their own nature (svarūpa), as in the case of a pearl necklace and a mountain waterfall.
In reality, there is no difference between being bent (*valitatva*) and being turned away (*āvṛttatva*).

Now, one might object: "If the property known as being bent and turned away is presented in the case of the face and the hundred-petaled lotus as having the nature of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānya*), then what is the form of their substrata (*dharmin*)—namely, the neck and the stalk? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "With reference to the substratum," and so forth.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the nature of a pure universal.

Even though the neck and the stalk possess the status of subjects (*dharmin*) as previously stated, it is more appropriate for them to have the status of attributes (*dharma*) in relation to the "lotus-face";
for the relationship of subject and attribute exists by way of the relationship between locus and located.
It is for this very reason that its unreality was stated previously.

Therefore, it should not be explained as "in comparison with the hundred-petaled lotus," for it is precisely the linguistic convention of the relationship between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) that is appropriate here.
This being the case, the actual nature of the neck and the stalk would otherwise be rendered unintended.

Although the nature of the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) has been shown by this very [verse], the example beginning with "This is Pāṇḍya" was cited again with the intention of demonstrating it without confusion.
Regarding the phrase "of the necklace and the body-unguent," the words "of their own natures" (*svarūpayoḥ*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Nor should a fourth variety named "similarity of qualities" (guṇasāmya) be mentioned here as a distinct type of simile, by demonstrating that the relation of the original object and its reflection constitutes a different subject matter within the sentence-meaning.
For the very nature of simile is based upon a common attribute, and that attribute here is of two kinds: explicitly stated and unstated.
Furthermore, its threefold nature has been stated in the context of being demonstrable;
and since there is no diversity whatsoever in the context of its being non-demonstrable, the various types of distinctions based upon it have not been mentioned.
Therefore, since the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇadharma*) has been established as demonstrated here, what indeed is this conception of a fourth category?
Not even a trace of a sentence-based simile (*vākyārthopamā*) exists here;
for that occurs when several subjects, mutually distinguished from one another, are compared with other such subjects,
as for example:
"He was known as a source of fearlessness to his mother, his nurse, and his protector;
yet he remained like a hidden treasure to the serpent-like woman who brought him jewels."
In this [verse], the birth of jewels and so forth are employed as the points of comparison for the mother and the others;
their status as the subjects (dharmin) is indeed manifest.

Furthermore, the relationship of original image and reflection (bimba-pratibimba-bhāva) occurs between properties (dharmas) that are directed toward establishing the specific qualities of the subject.
Mutual delimitation occurs just as in this very example.
For here, the necklace and the body-unguent are employed solely for the purpose of bringing about a specific excellence in the Pāṇḍya king;
this is because he is intended to be presented to Indumatī as a distinguished objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*).
And because those two are thus oriented toward one another, they find no rest within themselves; what, then, can be said of their being objects of comparison?
In this way, the simile between the Pāṇḍya king and the King of Mountains is based solely on attributes such as the pearl necklace and the mountain stream;
for the similarity reaches its conclusion at that alone.

And since the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—such as the necklace and so forth—is related as an original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), this is indeed a primary example of the logic of the simile (*dṛṣṭāntanyāya*).
Now, one might object: "Since the necklace and the mountain waterfall do not share the quality of 'going to that' or 'not going to that,' how can there be a common property?
To this it is replied: the very lifeblood of this [poetic] property is its commonality.
And that [similarity] occurs when there is oneness of the property (*dharma*); yet in reality, there is no oneness of the property here,
for the very same property such as beauty that resides in the face does not reside in the moon and so forth.
Because its [literal] correspondence is impossible;
rather, there exists here another phenomenon belonging to that same class.
Thus, due to the difference between the two phenomena and the absence of commonality, the very establishment of the nature of the simile would not occur.
Now, if similarity is also admitted between two properties (*dharma*), then another cause for that similarity must be sought;
and since yet another would be required for that as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Consequently, even though the two properties are distinct in reality, because they are apprehended as a unity, one must rely on this "oneness" as the cause for the notion of non-difference despite their difference.
Otherwise, indeed, there would be no emergence of the *apahnuti* at all.

Likewise here as well, although there is a factual difference between the necklace, the waterfall, and so forth—which are employed as "thing" (*vastu*) and "counter-thing" (*prativastu*)—there is an intention to express non-difference; thus, their identity should be understood.
Otherwise, these [elements] would not even serve as the cause for the arising of the comparison (*aupamya*) between the Pāṇḍya king and the mountain king.
It was stated immediately prior that no analogy between these two is appropriate;
for this very reason, the designation of "the state of the original image and its reflection" is used here.

For in the world, even though there is a difference between the original image and its reflection in a mirror or the like, one conceives of them as non-different, thinking, "My own face has been transferred here."
Otherwise, upon seeing the reflection, the conceit "I am thin" or "I am fat" would not arise, and women would not take interest in the arrangement of ornaments and the like.
As the ancients have also said:
"That sage was marked by his girdle of muñja grass, wearing a garment of black antelope skin..."
He shone like the sun embraced by a portion of dark blue clouds.
Thus it is said.
Likewise:
"Clad in yellow garments and grasping his Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇa assumed a form both mind-born and terrifying,
like a cloud at night, streaked with lightning and a rainbow, being joined by the moon."

In this instance, although there is in reality a difference between the girdle and lightning, or between the conch and the moon, the author has spoken of their deficiency or excellence regarding the common attribute by relying solely on the intended non-difference (*abheda-vivakṣā*).

For this very reason, the author previously provided two examples here—namely, "like a Simile of Corresponding Parts" (*prativastūpamā*) and "like an Exemplification" (*dṛṣṭānta*)—in order to demonstrate the same usage previously mentioned by the ancients for a pair of objects that stand in the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding entities).
Thus, those two examples were indeed given.
And in this context, the very life [of the expression] consists in the intention to convey non-difference;
and this is indeed very abundant in actual usage (lakṣya),
as for example—
"Where palaces—possessing lightning, with lovely women; accompanied by Indra’s bow, with colorful paintings; with drums beaten for music, and emitting a smooth, deep resonance;
containing water within, with floors made of jewels, lofty, and with peaks scraping the clouds—are able to rival you through various such characteristics."
In this case, lightning, women, and so forth are employed as attributes (*dharma*) precisely because they impart distinctiveness to the cloud-palaces;
for this very reason, it is said, "by those various particularities. Since these are not mentioned simultaneously, there is no *anugāmitā* (concomitance).

Because there is an absence of identity of meaning (*ekārthatva*), it cannot be of the nature of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānya*); therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is precisely the relationship of original and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*). Furthermore, their commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) arises from their being perceived as non-different.
This should be understood to apply to necklaces and other such objects as well.
And here, the perception of non-difference is based on similarity;
yet one should not, on this account alone, designate these as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*),
because there is no intention to express them as such.
Furthermore, the cause of similarity is the possession of qualities such as whiteness;
thus, through the perception of non-difference, the necklace and so forth possess common attributes here.
In some cases, the perception of non-difference occurs even by means of another cause.
As it is said:

"Even if he were disliked, a learned man who was well-disposed toward him should be cherished like medicine for one who is afflicted; but a wicked man, even if dear, should be abandoned like a finger bitten by a snake."

Here, in the latter half [of this discussion], the fact that the bitten and the biter perform a single action—such as causing pain—is the cause of their non-difference; enough with further elaboration.
And this [figure] occurs when there is a comparison between two subjects, whether both are contextual (*prakṛta*) or both are non-contextual (*aprakṛta*). Examples in order:
When she spoke with a voice as if distilling nectar, her speech being so noble, even the cuckoo—
whose song is otherwise discordant to the listener— seemed like a lute with broken strings being struck.
In this case, with respect to the Blessed One, the two non-contextual elements— the cuckoo and the lute— are combined because they possess an incompatible sound.
This [type of paronomasia] is also found in the "partial transformation" (ekadeśavivartin) variety,
as for example:
"The lotus plants shine like faces:
their petals like lips, their filaments like teeth, and their circles of bees like locks of hair."

In this instance, because the *nāyikā* (heroine) is not employed as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for the lotuses (*nalinī*), there is the quality of being "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*).
Furthermore, this [type of simile] is conceived when a common property (*sādharmya*) is imagined through the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*) for the sake of strengthening the resemblance.

And since that [common property] is sometimes imagined as residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) and sometimes by means of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it possesses a twofold nature.
As it has been stated:
"In some cases, there is the distinction of either the object of comparison (upameya) or the standard of comparison (upamāna).
Furthermore, a third variety of this [simile], wherein similarity exists even through dissimilarity (vaidharmyeṇa), need not be mentioned.
Because this [simile] occurs only within a simile itself, and because it conveys a sense of firmness [of the comparison].
For example, in sequence:
"Bow down to that navel-lotus of Hari, which is the sovereign of the sky's center."
"Where even a sixfold body becomes like a spot on the moon."
"Know that to be the lotus-navel of Hara, who is as delightful as the courtyard of the sky,
wherein Brahmā resides like a blemish upon the moon, his body covered by bees."
Here, the state of being covered by bees is attributed to the object of comparison (the woman):
"She, slightly bent by her breasts as if turning away, wearing a garment with the hue of the rising sun,
was like a moving, leafy creeper bowed down by clusters of blossoms."
"In this case, the status of being a transitory emotion (*saṃcārībhāva*) is attributed because it resides within the object of comparison;
nor should a separate definition for it be stated,
since both [the subject and the object] are perceived as a simile."
Because the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is also present here; and if it is argued that there is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) here, we say no, for in that case,
it would follow that a definition must be formulated for every individual distinction.
This is because it includes other specific varieties such as *samuccita* (cumulative).

Now, if it is argued that this [type of simile] constitutes a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) because its fruit is the cognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*) as qualified by the qualities of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and because its purpose is the absence of any other object that could serve as a rival, we say no.
