For in this case, there is no difference in the result, since the object of comparison is perceived precisely as being qualified by the qualities of the standard of comparison.

For instance, in the passage beginning with "āvarjitā" (drawn forth), lest the absence of similarity between the Blessed Lady and the creeper—as a transitory state—should result in a logical flaw, the poet has imagined the creeper to possess that very transitory state in order to firmly establish the commonality (*sādharmya*) between the two. Now, one might object: does this not imply that there is no other point of comparison for the Blessed Lady here?
[Objection: This is not so, because the negation of other objects of comparison—just like [the negation of] non-connection (*ananvaya*) and so forth—is the meaning of the sentence.
[Reply: It is not thus;
for if one likewise postulates a distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) in the object of comparison (*upameya*), then it must be stated that the result is the negation of other objects of comparison.
Because the principle is the same.
Just as in a firm representation (rūpaka) one imagines the loss or increase of some attribute merely to reinforce the non-difference between the object and the subject,
so too here, the state of being imagined should be understood as being for the very purpose of strengthening the generality (sāmānya).
In this case as well, it should not be asserted that the figure called "non-difference" (abhedālaṅkāra) is a distinct figure [from metaphor],
because its aesthetic charm is already subsumed by metaphor (rūpaka) alone;
for the identity between the object and the subject of comparison is indeed the very essence of metaphor.
And since that very [identity] is perceived here with firmness, what indeed is its distinction from *rūpaka*?

If it is argued that *rūpaka* consists in the perception of mere non-difference, whereas *abheda* consists in the perception of non-difference from everything else even when specific attributes are omitted— thus there is a difference in the mode of cognition— that is not so.
For in this way, there is indeed a continuous perception of non-difference here;

as for the specific distinction, let that be the determinant of their separate classification as distinct figures (*alaṅkāra*), but not of their being separate [from the category of] figures altogether.
For by the mere fact of being a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow), one does not become designated as a horse despite possessing the nature of a cow.
And thus:
"Kāma, having assumed a physical form, and the ever-present Spring;
the lover, and the eternally full Moon—these have stolen my heart."
In such cases, even when there is an excess of fixed attributes such as "having assumed a body," there would follow the contingency of other figures of speech.
Furthermore, this [figure] has infinite varieties based on its being a "garland" (mālā) and so forth; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, they have not been elaborated upon here.
When a single entity functions as both the standard of comparison and the object compared, it is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence).
According to the intended meaning of what is expressed, there is a conformity with the prior form;
however, the association of contradictory properties in one [subject] is for the purpose of excluding a second companion (*savratacārin*).
For this very reason, the application of the term *ananvaya* (non-concomitance) is also possible here.
"Just as Arjuna, whose prowess was celebrated like that of Arjuna himself, and Bhīma, whose deeds were terrifying toward enemies like Bhīma himself,
both proceeded with great care to the lord residing at Nyagrodha for the purpose of intimidating the Kurus."

"Of one alone," and so forth. Now, an objection might be raised: since the task at hand is to define the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) that rely upon similarity (*sādṛśya*), and since similarity can only exist as residing in two things, how can there be a mention here of this [figure] which does not rely on that [similarity], given that it cannot exist in only one? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "With reference to the expressed meaning," and so forth.
"Prior form" means the state of being the substratum for similarity.
For indeed, in this case, there is a verbal cognition of similarity.

This is because, as in the case of "the face is like the moon," the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is here established as something directly expressed (vācya).
For this very reason, he says: "with reference to what is expressed" (vācyābhiprāyeṇa);
the meaning is that it is not, however, with reference to the actual state of things (vastu).

In reality, since it is impossible for a single entity to possess the nature of both the property to be established (*sādhya*) and the means of establishment (*sādhana*), there would be a contradiction even in its status as the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, the definition here is based solely on the verbal apprehension of similarity. Now, one might object: "If the status of being both the standard and the object of comparison is contradictory for a single thing, then why employ this [figure], which is both logically inconsistent and fruitless? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of a single [thing]," and so forth.
And thus, for him, the very absence of a second fellow-celibate (sabrahmacārin) is the proof that establishes its status as an ornament;
otherwise, however, it would not possess the nature of an ornament.
For example:
"By his very command, while I have been protecting my subjects, this old age has made its gray hairs reach the vicinity of my ears.
That he still instructs me as if I were a mere infant—even now—is the profound partiality of the teacher toward me."

In this case, just as my preceptor instructed me when I was an infant, he instructs me even now; thus, although there is a single entity serving as both the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya), this is not that particular alaṅkāra (the figure of speech known as *dṛṣṭānta*), because there is no cessation of the understanding of a second fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*).

Furthermore, since a single entity can possess both an accomplished and a goal-to-be-accomplished attribute through a difference in temporal states, there is no conjunction of contradictory attributes in the form of being simultaneously the standard and the object of comparison.
"For this very reason" [is the concluding phrase].
Because of the conjunction with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃyoga*),

that in which there is a connection (*anvaya*)— that is, a relation— in which a single entity alone appears as both the established and the thing to be established, by way of being the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, is so described.

Here, the exclusion of any second rival (*dvitīyasabrahmacārinivṛtti*)— to the effect that "there is no one other than Arjuna whose prowess is celebrated in battle"— is indeed perceived as being as vital as life itself.
For this very reason, since the two objects of comparison— Kārtavīrya and the predatory beast— are not perceived [as being similar], this is indeed an example of *śuddha* (pure) *anugāmin*.
"In this world, which is filled with thousands of beautiful women, there is only one who resembles her."
The left half [is the cause] of the right half.
"Even though this world is filled with thousands of beautiful women,
only her left half resembles her right half."
In such cases, one should not claim that this is an example of *ananvaya* (non-correspondence).
For here, since another object is presented as the object of comparison (*upamīyamāna*), a simile (*upamā*) is being expressed.

Indeed, the very nature of this [simile] consists in the fact that a single entity functions as both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), with the result that all other possible standards of comparison are excluded.

And it should not be argued that "this [suggested meaning] is not expressed here by the word, but rather manifested; therefore, its status as *pratīyamāna* (the suggested) is logical, and it does not possess the status of being the *vācya* (the expressed).
For if this were so, the domain of the *alaṅkāradhvani* (suggestive figure of speech) would be deprived of its object.
Thus—
"O elephant, preeminent in bearing the scent of ichor, even Airāvaṇa and others have not been taught such friendliness toward the face [of the enemy].
Therefore, you possess the status of a leader of the herd among the reflections of your own form upon the jeweled walls of the mountains that are the eyes of the lightning-haired one (Śiva)."
In this case as well, *ananvaya* (non-connection) should not be mentioned;
for since the perception of similarity occurs through its own reflections alone, there is not even a scent of it [the non-connection].
Even if this were indeed perceived, its status would be that of something perceived (*pratīyamānatva*), not that of something to be explicitly stated (*vācyatva*).

According to the reasoning already stated, you should have formulated the definition of *ananvaya* simply as "similarity with that very [object] imagined as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), setting aside the notions of 'a part thereof' or 'distinguished by a portion thereof'. For example:
"Swallowing, as it were, the splendors of those praised by the assembly..."
He whose name even his enemies rejoice to utter—that man is truly a man.
Regarding this, what others have stated— that there is a "metaphor of non-connection" (*ananvaya-rūpaka*) due to the superimposition of masculinity upon the masculine— is incorrect;
for since the single entity itself exists in the relationship of subject and predicate (*vidhi-anuvāda-bhāva*), there is no superimposition (*āropa*).
When two things are compared to each other by turns, that is upameyopamā (comparison of the object of comparison with the standard of comparison).
By the word "that" (tat), there is a reflective reference to the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.
"Succession" (paryāya) is the absence of simultaneity;
for this very reason, there is a syntactical split (vākyabheda) here.
And this [type of simile] is twofold: in the case of the commonality of attributes (*dharmasādhāraṇya*) and in the case of the indication of the object and its counterpart (*vastuprativastunirdeśa*).
Regarding the first, for example:
"The water is like the sky, and the sky is like the water; the swan is like the moon, and the moon is like the swan."
The stars have the appearance of water-lilies, and the water-lilies have the appearance of stars.
In the second [type], for example:
"Where the ponds, possessing lotus-faces with beautiful reflections, appear like women; and the women, possessing faces as beautiful as lotuses with their own reflections, appear like ponds."
"Of two," and so forth; "two" refers to the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, but not to the number two.
"Therefore, between the lovely face, the lotus, and the moon, there formerly existed a state of mutual comparison;
but now, suddenly struck by old age, frost, and Rāhu respectively, a different, discordant relationship has arisen between them."
In this case, all three possess the status of both the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya), and they constitute the very limb (aṅga) of this [figure].
By the word "tat" (in the phrase "tasmin"), it refers to that [object].
The absence of simultaneity exists because it takes the form of a sequence.
"Therefore" means because of the absence of simultaneity.
And that syntactical split (vākyabheda) is both verbal and logical.
Among these, the verbal is as follows:
Making the sky appear like the surface of the earth with the dust raised by his chariots, and making the surface of the earth appear like the sky with his elephants resembling clouds.

In this case, because the sentence is completed by the phrase "making the surface of the earth like the sky," the syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is clearly verbal (*śābda*). An example of the semantic [split] (*ārtha*) is as follows:
"Only by taking refuge at Your feet do the Gaṅgā and eternal devotion [arise]."
"Let her be praised as she approaches, beautiful with her mutual resemblance [to you]."

In this case, although there is clearly a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) expressed by words, there is nonetheless a division of meaning (*vākyabheda*), because devotion is like the Ganges and the Ganges is like devotion, which is worthy of worship. And the sole fruit of this [simile] is precisely the setting aside of other points of comparison.
For this very reason, its name "the simile by means of the object compared" (*upameyenopamā*) is etymologically significant.

Furthermore, where the exclusion of another comparison is not perceived, this is not an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). For example: "The sun acts like the moon, and the moon likewise acts like the sun; likewise, the nights act like days."
When the mind is mastered by pleasure or pain, it makes the days into nights and the nights into days.

For here, it is not intended to exclude other points of comparison such as the moon or the sun; rather, it is meant to show that for those whose minds are dominated by pleasure and pain, things appear in this distorted manner.
Regarding the term "commonality" (*sādhāraṇya*):
this has been stated because it serves to exclude both alternatives—namely, the explicit mention or non-mention of the common attribute (*dharma*).

In that regard, although there is commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) in the case of the "indicative" (*nirdeśa*) position, the point here is that because it is followed by a single indication, its apprehension is clear.
However, in the case of the "non-indicative" (*anirdeśa*) position, the commonality is indeed real;
following which, examples such as "like water in the sky" and so forth have been cited.
Regarding the quality of conformity with righteousness (*dharmānugāmitva*), as it is said:

"His intellect shines constantly like a lotus, and his lotus-like intellect like his body; his splendor is like his body, and his body like his splendor; his fortitude is like the earth, and the earth like his fortitude."
Here, the phrase "it shines forth" (vibhāti) is mentioned once.

Furthermore, the indication of the *vastu* and *prativastu* is, as before, twofold here as well: by way of pure universality (*sāmānya-rūpa*) and by way of the relationship between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
Among these, the relationship between the original image and its reflection has been illustrated by the author himself.
For in that case, there is the relationship of original and reflection between the two faces, which are like water and a mirror.
An example of the nature of pure generality (*śuddhasāmānyarūpatva*) is as follows:
"By those two beautiful [eyes] opening simultaneously, they immediately attained the status of being mutual counterparts."
Your eye, with its pupil shimmering and soft, throbbing within, and the lotus, with a bee hovering inside—[the two are alike].
(Here,) due to the state of being tremulous and swaying, there is the nature of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānya*);
furthermore, between the *tāraka* and the *bhramara*, there is the relation of original image and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*).
And because it follows through the intention of manifestation (*unmeṣa*), this is an illustration of all three types of difference as well.
START Sūtra 15:
Memory is the recollection of another object resulting from a similar experience. // RuAss_15 //
Another entity that is similar [to the subject] is not a basis for inference because it lacks an inseparable connection (avinābhāva),
as for example:

Beholding this child, whose splendor surpasses that of gods and asuras and who is equal to me in form, I recall the joy of the Raghus wielding his bow for the destruction of those who opposed the sacrifice of Kuśika’s son.
Without similarity, however, there is no memory, and this is not an ornament (alaṅkāra). As it is said:
"Here, having desisted from hunting along the Godāvarī and having his fatigue dispelled by the breeze from the waves..."
I remember you, my son, with your head resting in secret upon my lap within the reed-huts.

And in this context, regarding the qualifiers of the agent, it is incorrect [to claim] that they exist at the time of the rememberer when they actually exist at the time of the object to be remembered. [Regarding the term] "similar":
"A different object" refers to that which is being remembered;
"only similar" is said because similarity resides in both [the perceived and the remembered].

Therefore, this is the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) consisting in the conceptualization of similarity between that which is being remembered and that which is being experienced, or between that which is being experienced and that which is being remembered.
As it has been said:
"Just as the cognition of similarity produced by the perceived object resides in the remembered one,
so too this [cognition] which pertains to the perceived object is produced by the remembered one."
Thus [it is said].
Among these, the first type is exemplified by the author himself; for in that instance, the intended similarity is between the child and Raghunandana alone. The second type, however, is as follows—

"O friend, on its bank stands a pleasure-mound with peaks fashioned of exquisite sapphires, beautiful to behold with its enclosure of golden plantain trees; seeing you with lightning flashing at your edge, my heart, distressed by the thought 'He is the beloved of my beloved,' remembers that very mountain."
Here, there is the conceptualization of a similarity between the cloud being experienced and the pleasure-mountain being remembered.

Thus, it should be understood that although the similarity is related to both [the perceived and the remembered], the cognition of the remembered object occurs again solely through that which is being experienced. Now, one might object: "If this is so, since the understanding of one thing arises from another, why is this not inference (*anumāna*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the absence of invariable concomitance," and so forth.
They say that non-separation arises from identity and constant concomitance;
however, such [identity] is absent between what is being experienced and what is being remembered.

Furthermore, when establishing the similarity between the child and the descendant of Raghu, the attribute of "being the lord of the city" (purabhāvatva) and so forth is indicated as a recurring feature, because it is exceedingly well-known.
This [comparison] of the dharma also occurs by way of the relationship between the object and its counterpart (*vastuprativastubhāva*).
In that regard, by virtue of having the nature of a pure universal form (*śuddhasāmānyarūpa*), it is as follows:
"May the Nandaka [sword] bestow upon you thick joy, containing within it the reflection of the splendor of exultation."
"Constantly performing the playful remembrance of Rādhā within the flow of the Yamunā, [he is] Murāri."
In this case, there is an identity between "exhilaration" (*ullāsa*) and "gracefulness" (*salīlatva*).
An example by way of the relation of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) is as follows:
"O beautiful one, beholding the sky sealed by the full moon marked with a digit of the crescent..."
I remember you, your cheeks touched by the streaks of smoke from the fire of the wedding sacrifice.
In this instance, there is a relationship of original and reflection between the cloud, the young woman, the line of smoke, and so forth.
To further solidify this fact that similarity is the cause [of the figure], he provides a counter-example with the words beginning "sādṛśya" (similarity):
because there is no experience of something similar, the resulting memory cannot have similarity as its cause.
Regarding the phrase "being produced in the state of being remembered":
the meaning is that "being produced in the state of being remembered" is the object to be expressed (*vācya*), yet it is not perceived;
for this very reason, there is no expression of the object to be expressed.
The statement "being brought about by the state of the rememberer" is a description of that which was previously inexpressible.

Although, because it belongs to the state of the rememberer, the qualities of the agent— such as his abstinence from hunting— are also delimited by past time and thus brought about by that state, nevertheless, because they are presented as qualifiers of the rememberer who is delimited by the present time, [they are understood as such].

Since it is precisely that which is delimited by it (the object) which is perceived, the two aforementioned objections remain valid; thus, the connoisseurs alone are the authority [on this matter]. However, the scope of the *preyas* ornament is memory evoked by a cause other than similarity (*sādṛśya*).
For example:
"Ah, even in anger, her face is lovely!

In this case as well, because the factors such as the *vibhāvas* are already suggested (*āgūrita*), it is not something conveyed by its own words alone, as in the example beginning with "atrānugādam."
"Those who once beheld you in battle— your forehead struck by the blow of a spear, the front of the field made crimson by the flow of abundant blood as you struck down your enemies—
their curiosity has now vanished before the fire of Smara, blazing with the mass of flames from the fires of their eyes that have flared up to burn the unbearable body of Kāma."
In such passages, when there is the experience of another similar object, there is the figure of speech *viśeṣālaṅkāra*, which consists in the production of an impossible thing,
because its occurrence is possible even when the cause is shown to be of the nature of a general action (*kriyāsāmānya*).
According to another school of thought, this is *kāvyaliṅga*.
Thus, these figures of speech have been determined on the basis of similarity, through the equivalence of difference and non-difference.
[The author] also shows another counter-example with the words "of the *preya* figure," etc.;
the word *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and).
The cause, such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), is distinct from similarity.
"Even there" means even when this is the case.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: when the *vibhāvas* and so forth are suggested (*āgūritatve*), the object of the figure of speech *preyas* is a recollection (*smṛti*) evoked by a cause other than similarity.
In that regard, an example of recollection when the *vibhāvas* and so forth are suggested is: "Oh, how lovely her face is even in anger!
An example of [recollection] when expressed solely by its own word is as cited in the passage beginning with "atrānugodam," and so on.
And here, we shall explain later on how the figure *preyas* and this *bhāvadhvani* have distinct spheres of application;
thus, the purpose of both counter-examples is also due to their having different scopes.

Furthermore, he says "By those by whom you were seen," etc., to show that even when remembrance is caused by similarity, it does not culminate in this [type of suggestion] because it does not constitute the meaning of the sentence (*avākyārthatvāt*).
In this context, the primary object (*vastu*) is the sight of Jayāpīḍa;
however, another object (*vastvantara*) is the sight of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*).

For those people who longed for the sight of you, not only was their thirst for seeing you quenched, but they even attained the sight of the Blessed One, which was otherwise impossible for them. This is an instance of the production of an impossible secondary object (*aśakyavastvantarakaraṇa*).

For the nature of the figure *viśeṣālaṅkāra* (the "peculiar") consists in the production of another object that is impossible [to produce], whereas here there exists the perception of another object that is impossible [to perceive]; thus, raising the doubt as to how this can be considered *viśeṣālaṅkāra*, he says: "Of the production," and so forth.

Furthermore, he says: "In other opinions," and so forth, in order to show that this very same thing has been accepted by others as the figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), based on the relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*).
"Etad" (this) refers to recollection.
"In another opinion" refers to the view of Udbhaṭa,
as it has been stated:
"When that which has been heard in one place serves as the cause for a recollection or an experience elsewhere, that is called *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication)."
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, because here there exists the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*), even the conventional usage involving what is being experienced and what is being remembered is distinguished; thus, this has been stated as a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
Concluding this, he introduces another [topic] with the words "Therefore, these... and so forth.
"These" refers to the four figures of speech beginning with simile (*upamā*).
START Sūtra 16:
Metaphor (rūpaka) occurs when there is a superimposition (āropa) characterized by the predominance of non-difference, provided that the object of the superimposition is not denied. RuAss_16 //
Because non-difference is predominant, there is the actual existence of difference. Superimposition (*āropa*) is the imposition of one thing upon another;
since it is held between the object and the subject, when the object is denied, that is *apahnuti* (concealment).
Otherwise, however, it is a *rūpaka* (metaphor) because the subject (*viṣayin*) effects the form of the object (*viṣaya*), which possesses that form;
whereas similarity (*sādharmya*) is indeed already included [within this].
As they say:

"Metaphor (*rūpaka*) is held to be simile itself when its distinction has become intensified. Thus, because the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is intensified through superimposition (*āropa*) such that there is non-difference, the subsequent classification of figures based on that [superimposition] follows.
Regarding the word "now" (*saṃprati*):

it means that immediately after the figures based on the equality of difference and non-difference, it is appropriate to define those in which non-difference is predominant; thus, it has reached its proper occasion.
Therein, first, he defines *rūpaka* (metaphor) with the words "when non-difference is predominant," and so forth.
"In reality" means not merely from the standpoint of conventional cognition.
"Existence" (sadbhāva) [is used] because the terms "primary" and "secondary" are relative;
elsewhere, "superimposition" (āropa) means the introduction of something else.
"In another" refers here to the face and so forth, which are the subjects under discussion (*prakṛta*).
"Of another" refers to the moon and so forth, which are not the subjects under discussion (*aprakṛta*).
And this [identification] occurs through indication either by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or by grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
But that is not merely a designation by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For if it were so, there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), since in cases such as "some have reached the state of Kaṇāda," even though there is the presence of superimposition (*āropa*), there is no coreferentiality.
If it is argued that there is a "noble" (*ārya*) coreferentiality and thus there is no under-extension, we say no.
The indication of two distinct things through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed the characteristic of superimposition (*āropa*);
however, that is not indicated here,
because they are indicated through grammatical separation (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), and its meaning is to be understood from that.
The determination of the object and its designation do not have a single form,
because they are contradictory; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the superimposition of blue, which would result in over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, since it is not said that two distinct things are designated as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) within a superimposition (*āropa*), this [position] is also impossible;
thus, this [explanation] is faultless only up to this point.
If it is asked, "If that is so, then is another word superimposed upon a word, or another object upon an object? we reply: [it is both].
In that case, there is no superimposition of one word upon another word,
because— as you yourselves have stated— it is not perceived that words such as "face" take on the form of words such as "moon," since each is apprehended in its own distinct internal form.
Rather, it is the superimposition of one object upon another object.
And that [superimposition] is taught in such a manner because it is directed toward a specific purpose, not out of delusion.

For this very reason, there is a superimposition of silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell, but no superimposition of the moon upon the face; for the latter arises quite naturally and thus possesses the nature of a delusion.
For this very reason, in that case [of poetic identification], there is a cognition of the object of superimposition as being concealed by that which is superimposed.
Here, however, someone who knows the face to be distinct from the moon nevertheless superimposes the meaning of "moon" upon it for a specific purpose.
It is for this reason that it has been stated: "there is no denial of the object of superimposition."
With this very intention, you also stated: "This is a confusion of presentation; it is not a confused cognition," and so forth.
Of that [superimposition], the object (*viṣaya*) is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), while the superimposed entity (*viṣayin*) is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*).
Being "seized" by these two constitutes its logical consistency (*yuktatva*).
As it has been said: "But another [type] is sāropā (superimposition), where both the object and the subject are stated as such.
[The word] "otherwise" means:
when there is no concealment.
Thus, by this [statement], the distinction between *apahnuti* (concealment) and *rūpaka* (metaphor) has also been stated.
"They say" refers to Daṇḍin and others.
And therefore, because of the existence of similarity (*sādharmya*), it should be understood that this [figure] is also vitalized by the three types of distinctions that follow from it.
"Just as:

'Behold this lunar orb, the companion of nectar, marked by a stain— the pillow for Rati's cheek, blackened like a mass of applied collyrium by the ichor-drops from the ears of the elephant of Kandarpa, its surface being covered by swarms of bees like clusters of flowers from the trees of heaven.'"

Here, the reflection (*pratibimbana*) of the stain (*kalaṅka*) occurs through the water of the gift and so forth; the states of being "stained" (*lāñchita*) and "marked" (*aṅkita*) possess the nature of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānyarūpatva*); and because the state of "moving in the nectar-ray" (*sudhāraśmicara*) is pervasive (*anugata*), it is "pervasive" (*anugāmin*). Thus, there is an animation by these three varieties [of *śleṣa*].
By this, it is stated that metaphor (*rūpaka*) is indeed a superimposition (*āropa*) based solely on similarity.
However, some hold the view that even a superimposition caused by another type of relation is merely a constituent part of metaphor.

As the author of the *Alaṅkārabhāṣya* says, beginning with "The nature of metaphor consists in the ultimate sense of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)," and continuing, "It is either superimposition (*sāropā*) or something else [superimposition of identity], and it arises either from similarity or from another type of relation," and so forth.
As it has been said:

"A mouthful of nectar, a mass of splendor, a fountain of the essence of joy, a wagon of whiteness, a pool of moonlight, a grindstone of frost, a cushion for the Mind-born [God of Love], a celestial chariot of the beauty of erotic passion—oh, how wonderful! For one who has seen him, the one whose banner is the deer becomes a vessel for boundless faith in happiness."
In this case, there is the superimposition of the effect, faith, upon the cause, which is the form of the moon.

The author of the *Alaṅkāra* [Vidyādhara], following the *Anusāriṇī*, stated here: "Because it is the cause of faith, it is 'faith'"; by further declaring that "this is a 'garland-metaphor' (*mālārūpaka*) because multiple objects are superimposed upon a single qualificand," he has indicated this very position.

Now, one might object: "Since even those figures of speech (alaṅkāra) that contain a process of determination (adhyavasāya) possess a predominance of non-difference, why are only those figures whose essence is initial superimposition (āropa) defined? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of superimposition," and so forth. This [superimposition] is of three kinds: the partless (niravayava), the with-parts (sāvayava), and the transitive (paramparita). The first is twofold: the simple (kevala) and the metaphorical (māvarūpaka).
The second [type] is of two kinds only: that which has all things as its subject (*samastavastuviṣaya*) and that which is partially manifest (*ekadeśavivartin*).

The third [type], being based on the use of punning words (*śliṣṭaśabda*), is twofold; each of these, in turn, being either a simple metaphor (*kevalarūpaka*) or a series of metaphors (*mālārūpaka*), is fourfold.
Thus, there are eight varieties of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
However, other individual subdivisions—such as those stated by way of sentence (*vākya*) or compound (*samāsa*)—are possible; these should be sought elsewhere.
The word *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the subdivisions in relation to other figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*), while the word *tu* (but/however) indicates the specific subject matter.
That in which [an object] is superimposed after having emerged from its constituent parts is so described.

That in which [an object] exists while being superimposed together with its constituent parts is so described. That in which, through a succession [of superimpositions], the state of being superimposed upon another arises due to the greatness of one [element] is so described.
"Initial" means partless (*niravayava*).
A "garland" (*mālā*) arises from the superimposition of many [metaphors] upon one or many [objects].
Thus, the "garland-metaphor" (*mālārūpaka*) is to be understood as being formed through a succession [of such superimpositions].

"Second" means possessing parts (*sāvayava*). That is so described as that in which the object is the referent of the expression denoting the entire thing consisting of the superimposed nature. "In one part" refers to the objects of the superimposition.

The object itself, being of that very nature, unfolds or transforms into the form of that which is superimposed for the purpose of conveying its intended meaning; where this occurs, it is so described.
This is the third [type], namely *paramparita* (transferred).

Although in this case, which is based on *śleṣa* (punning), a similarity based on attributes consisting of qualities or actions is indeed impossible, nevertheless, there is a similarity produced by words alone through the process of identifying [the two objects] as non-different.
"Grāhyam" (is to be understood).
"Others" refers to those distinct from these eight varieties.
"Are found" means they exist only in the ancient treatises on poetics (*alaṅkāra*).
The sense is that they are not perceived [as distinct].
For even though their essence is the same in that regard, it is precisely this eightfold division that is perceived as the source of their diversity.
And as follows:

"O Lord of Men, the lamp of Your majesty blazes forth: the foot of the world is its base, the Tortoise is its stand, the Lord of Serpents is its wick-holder, the Earth is the vessel, the oceans are the reservoirs of oil, the Golden Mountain is the growth of the rounded wick, the fierce-rayed Sun is the flame, the darkness of the high sky is the soot, and the host of enemies being consumed are the moths."
In this instance, although the meaning of the sentence is already expressed, the striking peculiarity (*vaicitrya*) arises solely from the fact that all the objects [of the comparison] are unified.
For example, in sequence:
"O beautiful one, when a servant has committed an offense, it is only fitting for masters to strike him with their feet; therefore, I am not pained."
That your foot is pained by the tips of the thorns of the rising, hard sprouts of horripilation—surely that very pain is mine.

A fresh handful of nectar for the gods, a sickle for the cutting away of darkness, a lotus-stalk vine that has become a source of distraction for the faces of the *kokila* birds in the celestial Ganges,

and a certain double manifestation of the god of love’s bow— such is the slender body of the moon rising on the first day of the lunar fortnight, acting as a thread of hope for those who have offended their beloveds.

"O King, O ear of the Kali age, I have eaten a meal consisting of a vast heap of food as bright as jasmine, served upon the leaf-plate of the expansive sky, and drenched in the thick milk of the buffalo-like waves of the Ganges."
"O Lord of the Earth, this line of Tamāla forest, thick with your sword, shines like the moonlight;
for there your youthful valor delights, having forcibly brought away the fame of your enemies from the splendor of the moon."
In the phrase "kṣitibhṛtaḥ" (mountains/king), there is a pun (*śliṣṭa*).
As for the "metaphor by succession" (*paramparita*):
"Does it not destroy the luster of the lotus? Does it not bestow joy upon the eyes? Does it not increase the fortune of the fish-bannered god [Kāma] merely by its sight?"
That another cool-rayed moon has risen in the moon of your face is indeed true; yet, if there were pride in this matter, it surely exists here in your bimba-red lip, which is [itself] nectar.

In this instance, there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) of the nectar of the lower lip with the celestial ambrosia (*pīyūṣa*), based on the metaphorical identification of the moon in the form of the face; here, the words are linked through their identical phonetic form.
"O Swan of the minds of the wise! O Sun that causes the lotuses of the faces of enemies to close! O Blue-Throated One (Śiva) to the enemies who are mountains! O Fire that accepts the fuel of battle!

O Expert in bestowing affection for the Truth! O Terrible One in the vanguard of victory! O Lord, O Excellent Hero, may you perform the imperial sovereignty of Brahmā for a hundred years! [In this verse, the various epithets are metaphorically identified with the attributes of a swan, the sun, Śiva, and fire.]

In this case, there is first the superimposition "you alone are the *haṃsa* (swan)," followed by the superimposition "the mind itself is the *mānasa* (lake)," and so forth; thus, this is a *śliṣṭa-śabda-mālā-paramparita* (a series of metaphorical identifications based on punning words).
"I go for refuge with my mind, speech, and body to the compassionate Lord of the World, the pair of feet of Hara, which is a boat for crossing the ocean of birth, old age, and death."

"The sword of the Indra of Mālava triumphs in battle— a couch for the Fortune of Kingship, a wave of the ocean of manly prowess, a banner of fierce victory that has shattered the lineages of his enemies, a silken stream of the water of his generosity, a dark blue cloud for the swan-like fame of the Lord of the Muralas who was fainting from the terror of war, and a personal attendant to the Earth."
Here, "the chamberlain of the earth" (*kṣmāsauvidalla*) is a *paramparita* (successive) type of *ekadeśavivartin* (partial metaphor).
Other varieties such as these have also been indicated at least briefly.
[The phrase] "in order" (*krameṇa*) means according to the sequence of their enumeration.

And in the phrase "the doubling of the bow of Smara," upon a thorough consideration of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), there is the cognition of an imposition (*āropa*) of the moon being the bow of Smara; since the relationship [of this imposition] is based solely on similarity (*sādṛśya*) caused by numerous attributes such as crookedness (*kuṭilatva*) and so forth, and since there are multiple impositions upon the single moon, this is a *mālārūpaka* (garland metaphor). As for an example of multiple [objects]: [Example follows: The moon is the face of the night, the lotus is her eye, The swan is her laughter, and the white water-lily is her smile; The moonstone is her cheek, the jasmine is her breath, The sandalwood tree is her body, and the musk-deer is her heart. In this case, the face and other parts are imposed upon the moon and other objects, which are themselves the subjects of the description. This is a *mālārūpaka* because it consists of many impositions. Furthermore, this is not a case of *samastarūpaka* (compound metaphor), because the words "face" (*mukha*) and so forth are used in their primary sense (*mukhyārtha*) with respect to the moon and other objects, and thus do not denote the night and other things through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor is it a case of *pariṇāmālaṅkāra* (transformation metaphor), because the night and other things are not intended to be treated as the actual face and so forth. Nor is it a case of *bhrāntimān* (illusion), because there is no cognition of error (*bhrānti*) regarding the night and other things. Nor is it a case of *ullekha* (multiple perspectives), because there is no mention of different perceivers (*pratipattr*). Nor is it a case of *saṃdeha* (doubt), because there is no uncertainty (*saṃśaya*) regarding the identity of the moon and other objects. Nor is it a case of *apahnuti* (concealment), because there is no negation of the moon and other things. Nor is it a case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because there is no expression of a possibility (*utprekṣā*). Nor is it a case of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because there is no sublation (*bādha*) of the literal meaning. Nor is it a case of *rūpaka* (metaphor) in its simple form, because the word "face" (*mukha*) and so forth are not used in a secondary sense (*gauṇārtha*) with respect to the night and other things. Therefore, this is indeed a *mālārūpaka*. Moreover, in this instance, the *rūpaka* is established by means of a *samāsokti* (speech of ellipsis), because the qualities of the night and other things—such as being the beloved (*kāminī*)—are suggested (*vyajyate*) by the qualities of the face and other parts, such as being the face itself. Thus, the *rūpaka* is the primary figure (*aṅgin*), while the *samāsokti* is subordinate (*aṅga*). This is because the qualities of the face and other parts are expressed directly (*vācyatvena*), whereas the qualities of the night and other things are merely suggested (*pratīyamānatvena*). However, in cases where the qualities of the face and other parts are suggested, and the qualities of the night and other things are expressed, the *samāsokti* would be the primary figure and the *rūpaka* subordinate. For example: The face is the moon, the eyes are the lotuses, The teeth are the jasmine flowers, and the smile is the moonlight; The body is the sandalwood tree, and the musk-deer is the heart, Of that woman who is the very embodiment of the spring season. In this case, the *samāsokti* is the primary figure, because the qualities of the woman—such as being the embodiment of the spring season—are suggested by the qualities of the face and other parts, such as being the moon and so forth. This is because the qualities of the face and other parts are expressed directly, whereas the qualities of the woman are merely suggested. Furthermore, in this instance, the *rū

Her arms are like young lotus stalks, her waist is the palace of ruby for Rati, the slope of her hips is a slab of pearl-stone, her smile is a cascade of nectar, her speech is the warbling of cuckoos, and her hair is the chowrie of the God of Love; what in this world is not extraordinary about that girl whose eyes are like those of a startled fawn?
Here, because many superimpositions are applied to many [objects], there is a "garland of metaphors" (rūpakamālā).
And this is also seen to be based on paronomasia (śleṣa),
as for example:
"His eyes are like the Puṣkara lotuses, his speech is the Madhumatī river, his intellect is the Vipāśā, his mind possesses the humility of a river, and his lower lip has the redness of the Śoṇa;
indeed, his conduct is the Pāpasūdana—oh, this king, taking refuge in such sacred sites, desires to bathe! Thus, as it were, he wears hot water upon his garment."
Here, because there are multiple puns (*śliṣṭa*) and multiple superimpositions (*āropita*), this is a "garland of metaphors with punned meanings" (*śliṣṭārtharūpakamālā*).
Others consider that in the word *ābhāti*, there is also "suggestion by compounding" (*samāsokti*); thus, another example is cited.

"Just as one might gather the incomparable beauty of the flowers of your consciousness, sweet with its fragrance, which has blossomed in the forest-rows beyond the realm of sense-objects— so may I, accompanied by my dear friend discernment and with devotion that shines with excellence, be intent on wandering within the garden of worldly existence."
Because the superimposition of the heroine upon devotion is not expressed by words, it constitutes a metaphorical transformation (*vivarta*) based on location.
It should be understood that the reading "the description of the word *pūyūṣa* (nectar) as being linked with the nectar of the lips" is a corrupt reading fabricated by the scribe.
For here, the description is established by means of the nectar (*pīyūṣa*) of the lower lip;
therefore, the reading "śliṣṭaśabdanirūpaṃ adharāmṛtasya pīyūṣeṇa" should be accepted.
In this context, others consider that the word *amṛta* (nectar), like the word *pīyūṣa*, does not denote the taste of the lips; therefore, another example is cited:
"O you who have illuminated the three worlds with a supermundane, great light..."
O Lord, by whom is Your jewel-like pearl from a noble lineage not praised?

Here, the superimposition of the lineage (*vaṃśa*) itself upon the pearl-jewel (*muktāratna*)—preceded by the superimposition of the string (*sūtra*)—is a case of *śliṣṭa-śabda* (punning) *kevala-paramparita*.

In the passage beginning with "learned" (*vidvat*), there is a *paramparita* [superimposition] based on the identification of the swan (*haṃsa*) with its majesty, and the identification of the mind (*mānasa*) with the lake.
Likewise, the identification of the ocean (*arṇava*) serves as the cause for the superimposition of the boat (*taraṇḍa*); thus, it is *paramparita*.
In the example beginning with "paryaṅka," there are many superimpositions upon a single object; thus, this is *mālā-paramparita* (garland-like successive metaphor).
An example of many [superimpositions] is as follows:
"Śrī is the digit of the moon upon the chest of Śrīdhara; Gaurī is the lightning upon the cloud that is the neck of Śrīkaṇṭha."
May Śakra, Akṣipā, Śvākarā, Rājahaṃsī, and Śacī grant you auspicious blessings.

In this case, because there are many superimpositions upon various [bases], it is a "garland of metaphors" (*mālāparamparita*). The phrase "and so forth" indicates that even a metaphorical metaphor (*paramparita*) can be of this type, namely, one that is partial (*ekadeśavivartin*).
"Indicated" means precisely by this demonstration.
Consequently, both types of *śliṣṭa* (pun) are seen to possess constituent parts.
Among these, an example concerning the entirety of objects (*samastavastuviṣaya*) is as follows:
"Splitting its petal-lips, with a mass of filaments in a shimmering form,
the night-lotus laughed, emitting a fragrant scent under the moonlight of joy."

[Setubandha 416]: "The smile, with its petals of lips not yet parted and the thick mass of filaments in the form of quivering teeth, emits a fragrant scent like a night-lotus at the rising of the moon of joy."
In this instance, *kumuda* possesses a double meaning (*śliṣṭatva*).
An example of *ekadeśavivarti* (partially developed) is as follows:
"That sky-liṅga, which is thrilled by the scattered pearls of the stars, smeared with the sandalwood paste of moonlight, and washed by the water-pots held in the hands of the gods."
When the lotus—the discarded offering of the sun’s reflection—fell from the water-vessel of the western quarter, Time quickly placed the moon upon its head as a fresh white lotus for its worship.

In this matter of time (*kāla*), since the worshipper and so forth being superimposed are not expressed by words (*aśābda*), there is "partial manifestation" (*ekadeśavivarti*). Because the term *toyādhāra* (receptacle of water) denotes both the ocean and the vessel for ritual water-offerings (*nirmālya*), there is "paronomasia" (*śleṣa*). Furthermore, in some cases, this [metaphor] also functions as a "firm superimposition" (*dṛḍhāropa*) by first negating the subject (*viṣayiṇa*) in order to strengthen the non-difference [between the subject and the object], or by the removal or the addition of a quality that constitutes the cause of difference between them.
It is seen in sequence as follows:
"Fond of strife, constantly disregarding her elders and kinsmen, showing contempt..."
Surely one's own wife is indeed a *kṛtyā* (sorceress); yet for the upright and righteous man, she is not a *kṛtyā*.
In this case, the *kṛtyā* (sorcery) is superimposed upon the wife preceded by a negation.
For, through that negation, the firm similarity between the wife and the *kṛtyā* is perceived.
The meaning of the sentence here is: "The *kṛtyā* does not apply itself to its own task in the same way as she [the wife] applies herself to her task."
And in this regard, that which others call the figure of speech *viśeṣālaṅkāra* has already been refuted by the very refutation of the figure of speech *abheda*, so no further effort is made here.
An example of *hāni* (loss) is as follows:
"The glories of forest-dwellers accompanied by their wives, resting within the laps of cave-dwellings..."
There, at night, the medicinal herbs become lamps for lovemaking that require no oil.
In this case, there is the conceptualization of a decrease due to the filling with oil;
by way of excess, for example:
"For this is the fourth sacred fire, or even the fifth, which is the Veda."
Or rather, he is a moving sacred ford, or dharma incarnate.
In this case, there is an excess of attributes such as being the fourth state (*turyatva*) and so forth.
"Between the miserly sword and the miserly man— who has his fist tightly clenched, who dwells in a sheath, who is naturally dark, and who is stingy— the only difference lies in their outward form."

In this case as well, the metaphor (*rūpaka*) should be understood as one involving firm superimposition (*dṛḍhāropa*). For here, because the sword (*kṛpāṇa*) is mentioned as being conjoined [with other attributes], a verbal superimposition (*śābda-āropa*) is not perceived; nevertheless, due to the mention of a difference in mere form, and through the power of reflecting upon the meaning of the sentence, there is at the final conclusion an admission of the existence of all other specific attributes.
Through firmness, there is the realization of the non-difference between the object and the subject;
and it has already been stated previously that this very [realization] is the true nature of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Other varieties as well should be inferred and illustrated by oneself.
This is also seen by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*):

"She is a desert for the waters of goodness, a sky-wall for the paintings of good conduct, a dark fourteenth day of the waning moon for the moonlight of virtue, and a stroke of a horse's tail for the quality of straightforwardness."

For those who have served even this lineage of kings in the Kali age with such evil intent, how much skill is there in their service toward the Wielder of the Trident, who is accessible through devotion alone?

And here, although that which is being superimposed possesses gender and number because it functions as the subject (*dharmin*), in some cases—even where the connection with number is inherently impossible—it takes on the number of the object (*viṣaya*), because the superimposition occurs distributively (*pratyekam*).
For example: "In one place, the cheeks of the sage, wearing matted hair and bark garments, are like forest fires," and so forth.
For there is no plurality in the sage Kapila.

The poison born of the cloud-serpent forcibly brings about dizziness, restlessness, mental dullness, dissolution, fainting, darkness, physical exhaustion, and even death for women separated from their lovers.
In this instance, there is indeed *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the word *viṣa*, which is influenced by the meaning of "poison" as evoked by a specific effect of a fixed number [of syllables].

Since the phrase *jaladabhujagajam* ("born from the cloud-serpent") serves as the proof for the *rūpaka* (metaphor), and because that [proof] was not established previously, they say that the word *viṣa* is not a case of *śliṣṭaśabdaparamparita-rūpaka*; rather, there is *śleṣa* alone here.
[The author adds: "Even by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*)."
The meaning is that it is not only by way of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*).
And in order to show another specific variety of its charm (*vicchitti*), he says "here," and so forth.

By the phrase "even though the gender is fixed" (*āviṣṭaliṅgatve 'pi*), it is indicated that even when the subject (*dharmin*) is restricted to its own essential nature alone, there is still the acceptance of another property (*dharmāntara*) consisting of number which is related to another subject.
Regarding the phrase "because it is impossible for it to be joined with number":

although, according to the principle that number is the cause for the linguistic usage of "one" and so forth, its connection is possible even in a single substance, this was stated with the intention of referring to [number] as residing in multiple substances.
"By superimposition upon each" means by means of such forms as "this fire is tawny" and "this fire is tawny."
Therefore, because the superimposed object, the sage Kapila, cannot possess plurality, it possesses the number of the substratum (*viṣaya*).

To highlight the distinction between this type of *paramparita* (transferred) metaphor, which is based on *śliṣṭatā* (punning), and the *śleṣa* (pun) itself, he says: "the delusion," and "manifested."
The meaning is that it has been made the object of cognition from the very beginning.
[This is] because of the absence of prior establishedness;
for the metaphor (*rūpaka*) is caused by the pun (*śleṣa*).
The phrase "tannibandhanam" means "based upon that [śleṣa].
The word "iti" indicates a reason.
Therefore, the intended meaning here is that the figure of speech is *śleṣa* alone, and not *paramparita-rūpaka*.
This point requires consideration:
for *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs between two things that are both contextual (*prakṛta*), both non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), or one contextual and one non-contextual;
yet here, there is neither contextuality nor non-contextuality for both.
Because, during the rainy season, the water of the cloud is worthy of description;

and since *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs only when there is a similarity of adjectives between the contextual (*prakṛta*) and non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) subjects, whereas here there is a similarity even of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), this is the domain of *dhvani* arising from the power of words, not of *śleṣa*.
Therefore, the figure of speech *śleṣa* does not exist here.

Nor is it *dhvani* (suggestion), because the meaning of "poison" (*garala*) is expressed through the power of the word itself by virtue of the majesty of the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "born from the cloud-serpent.

Thus, in this case, the ornament is indeed the metaphor based on the use of punning words (*śliṣṭa-śabda*). It has been stated that if the meaning of "poison" were to be perceived even through another metaphor, such as "born from the cloud-serpent," then that would be the province of *dhvani*.

In the presence of the metaphor "born from the cloud-serpent" (*jaladabhujagaja*), the metaphor based on the use of a pun (*śliṣṭaśabdanibandhana*) occurs precisely through the majesty of that [first metaphor] regarding the word "poison" (*viṣa*).
Otherwise, the metaphor "born from the cloud-serpent" would be redundant; for without it, the meaning of "venom" (*garala*) would be understood [directly]. Enough with this prolixity.
START Sūtra 17:
When that which is being superimposed is useful for the subject at hand, it is *pariṇāma* (transformation). RuAss_17 //

In *rūpaka* (metaphor), because that which is being superimposed lacks utility for the subject at hand, it enters into a relationship solely as a mere embellisher (*uparañjaka*) of the subject; however, in *pariṇāma* (transformation), since the thing being superimposed is useful by virtue of becoming the very self of the subject, the subject transforms into the form of the thing being superimposed. Because there is no manifestation of coming, following, or departing [as in the case of actual transformation], it differs from the Sāṃkhya concept of *pariṇāma*.
It is of two kinds due to its usage in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
The first is as follows:

"Having crossed the celestial river that serves as a garland upon the head of the Lord of Beings, he, as the third [person], offered to the ferryman a fare consisting of his friendship for the son of Sumitrā."
Followed with difficulty by Śabara maidens whose breasts were grasped within the span of their arms, his eyes upturned in curiosity, he departed swiftly for that mountain, Citrakūṭa.
Here, the friendship with the son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa), which is the subject at hand, is transformed into the nature of another form— the state of being a co-locus with that which is superimposed—
because the boat serves a purpose in the context by taking on the form of friendship.

Thus, in this case, just as in *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), the thing superimposed is useful for the subject at hand and remains there by virtue of being identical with the locus of the superimposition.

For this very reason, there is the superimposition of that conventional usage upon it; the same should be understood here as well, with the only difference being that in that case the object itself is explicitly employed, because the subject is already implied.
In this case, however, both are explicitly mentioned; yet, because of their identity, both possess the quality of being subject to transformation.
An example of the second type is as follows:
Then, first he approached the lord of the earth with eloquent words, full of maturity and employing figurative paths of speech; only after that did he present the horse and other gifts.
In the case of a royal assembly, however, a gift is appropriate;
and since that [gift] here takes the form of speech, there is a transformation of words into the nature of a gift through their being in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
— [This refers to the passage beginning with] "of that which is being superimposed," and so forth.

Demonstrating the distinction from *rūpaka* (metaphor) despite the similarity in the state of being the object of superimposition (*āropa*) and the act of superimposing (*āropya*), he explains this very point with the words beginning "that which is being superimposed" (*āropyamāṇam*).
Regarding the phrase "by way of coloring the subject at hand" (*prakṛtoparañjakatvena*):
it refers to what was stated—that it is called *rūpaka* because the subject (*viṣayin*) possesses the form of the object (*viṣaya*).
"By way of being the inherent nature" means by way of being an integral part of the context.
"Utility" refers to its functional application.
Because without that, the subject matter at hand cannot be established.
"It transforms" means it persists by being distinguished from the discourse concerning what is not the subject matter.

Because the purpose of the context would not be accomplished if [the word] were to abide merely in its own primary sense (*prakṛtasvarūpa*), it follows that here, due to the absence of utility for the context, the utility belongs to that which is superimposed (*āropyamāṇa*). Thus, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), the unique (*asādhāraṇa*) nature of the utility for the subject at hand is demonstrated. For a property (*dharma*) that is unique is a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because it establishes the specific identity of that thing.
Therefore, there is no connection with the subject matter (*prakṛta*) in other figures of speech either. Thus: "Any other blessing would be redundant for you who have attained all auspicious things."
"Obtain a son who is worthy of your own virtues, one who will be as venerable to you as you were to your father."
In this context, [the figure] is *upamā* (simile), as in:

"In the meantime, the sun descended to the middle world, as if to announce the news of Sarasvatī’s descent. In the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), as in: "The lake, agitated by the churning of Mount Mandara... [and so forth].
Let the multitude of fish,
turtles, and water-snakes emerge from the deep waters of the lake, rising up with great speed.

In this regard, in the case of *rūpaka* (metaphor) and other such figures of speech, there is propriety (*aucitya*) alone, not utility (*upayoga*). For propriety serves to bring about the comprehension of the contextual meaning once [the figure] is established; utility, however, functions as the cause for the contextual meaning precisely because it is already established. Thus, there is a great difference between these two.
For it has been said:
"In the case of *ananvaya* (self-comparison), the repetition of words occurs only as a secondary consequence due to propriety;
however, in this *lāṭānuprāsa*, it is the direct cause [of the figure]."
In this regard, the distinction between the two has been stated based on their respective fitness (*aucitya*) and application (*upayoga*).
Consequently, the claim made by others—that because they share the distinction of fitness and application, both are applicable everywhere to the subject at hand—is incorrect.
Therefore, *pariṇāma* (transformation) is indeed distinct from *rūpaka* (metaphor).

In this case, however, since the non-contextual object cannot be established at all without the superimposition of the contextual object, its very life consists solely in its utility for the subject at hand:
"Burning is water; spreading heat is steam; the throbbing is perceived through the nostrils; the sighs are flickering, blazing lamp-flames; her body is submerged in pallor.
Or what else shall I say? Throughout the entire night, she remains by the window facing your mansion, her moonlight blocked by the parasol of her hand."
For here, since the obstruction of the moonlight cannot occur without the superimposition of the hearer, that [obstruction] serves as a means for the subject at hand (*prakṛta*).
And because the subject at hand thus transforms into something not originally present, it is called *pariṇāma* (transformation).
Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, then what is the distinction between this and the Sāṃkhya notion of transformation? he says: "By tradition," and so forth.
"When this substratum (dharmī), without falling away from its true nature (tattva), first abandons one attribute and takes up another, that is called transformation (pariṇāma)."
Thus is the definition of transformation according to the Sāṃkhya school.
"By way of having friendliness as its nature" means by way of having friendliness as its essence.
"Because of its utility": because crossing is impossible without a boat.

Therefore, since the boat is utilized in the context at hand, and since it performs the function of that [crossing] belonging to the actual friendliness (*maitrī*) under discussion, the designation of that [friendliness] is metaphorically attributed to it.
He establishes this very point by means of an illustration as well, with the words "tad atra" and so forth.
Here, "atra" refers to the case of *pariṇāma* (transformation) and *samāsokti* (brief expression); in both, that which is superimposed must be useful for the subject at hand.
Because the non-contextual [element] is implied solely for the sake of establishing the contextual [element];
even though it is being superimposed, it stands there as a qualifier (*avacchedaka*) of the contextual, and not as a concealer (*ācchādaka*). Thus he says, "And that," etc.
"Precisely for this reason."
Precisely because it consists of the nature of the object of superimposition;
"therein" means in the case of *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
He applies this very principle to the subject at hand with the words beginning with "evam" (thus), and so forth.
If this is so, then one might ask: what is the distinction between *samāsokti* (synecdoche) and *pariṇāma* (transference)? Anticipating this doubt, he says "only," and so forth.
"Of those two" refers to the two being designated.
"Appropriate" means...
The word "by way of being useful" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
When there is doubt regarding the object, that is doubt (saṃśaya). (Sūtra 18)
When non-difference is predominant, there is simply a superimposition (āropa).
The subject (viṣaya) is the contextual object, upon which the non-contextual object is superimposed and thus becomes the basis for doubt.
When there is doubt regarding the non-contextual (aprakṛta), the object itself is indeed doubted as well.

Therefore, when a doubt is evoked by the poet's imagination through its application to both the contextual (prakṛta) and the non-contextual (aprakṛta), it constitutes the figure of speech *saṃdeha* (doubt).
[Regarding the phrase] "of the object" (*viṣayasya*), etc.:

Since "object" (*viṣaya*) and "subject" (*viṣayin*) are correlative terms, the mention of the object implies the subject as well; therefore, both are included here. Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is that both the object and the subject are the objects of the cognition of doubt. If it is objected: "Even if the term for the subject is implied by the term for the object due to their being correlative terms, how can the state of being doubted be obtained for the subject through mere implication alone, without its being explicitly stated? We reply: no.

Because doubt consists of a deliberation that rests upon both indefinite alternatives, and because such doubt is impossible when residing in the object alone, the subject must necessarily be connected with it; thus, the very definition provided [in the Sūtra] is superior. He explains this very point by analyzing it in detail, beginning with the words "In the object," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "as the basis" (*yadbhittitvena*):
the sense is that otherwise, there would either be a lack of subject matter for what is not the primary topic, or the fault of mentioning something irrelevant (*apraṅkṛtābhidhāna*).

Therefore, suspecting that it might be thought that the objects themselves (*viṣayiṇām*) possess such a state by virtue of having the [unmanifested] as their basis (*viṣayabhittitayā*), he says "not the primary topic," and so forth.
The word "also" (*api*) signifies that it is not only the subject (*viṣayin*) that is subject to doubt, but the object (*viṣaya*) as well. Consequently,
this figure of speech may occur in some cases where only the subjects are in doubt, and in others where both the object and the subject are in doubt.
In both cases, there is a conformity with a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
For doubt is a deliberation that relies upon two indefinite aspects,
and it occurs only among those who possess the object.

Because it is precisely the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) that are being doubted; for this very reason, the phrase "by way of pertaining to the relevant and the irrelevant" should be applied according to the circumstances. [The term] "evoked by creative intuition" (*pratibhotyāpita*) means:
It does not, however, arise spontaneously, such as in the form "Is this a post or a person? and so forth;
that [doubt] is of three kinds.
It is pure, contains certainty within, and concludes with certainty.
It is "pure" when the very doubt reaches its final resolution,
as for example:

"Is she a fresh sprout bursting forth from the abundance of sap of the tree of youth? Is she a wave splashing out from the play of the ocean of beauty? Or is she perhaps the very staff of instruction for the God of Love himself, who, filled with intense longing, confidently imparts his teachings at the proper time?"
That which has certainty as its core, begins with doubt, has certainty in the middle, and ends with doubt—for example:
"Is this the sun? No, for it is surely accompanied by seven horses. Is it fire? No, for it does not certainly spread through all directions."
Having gazed at you for a long time in battle, your enemies entertain doubts as to whether this is Kṛtānta himself, borne by his buffalo mount.
The *niścayānta* (conclusion with certainty) is where there is doubt at the outset and certainty at the conclusion. For example:
"Is it the moon? Where is the spot? Is this a lotus? Where has the water gone?"
"O deer-eyed one, by your playful and charming words, it is certain that this face is something other [than what it appears]."
Sometimes, that which is being superimposed is seen as having a different locus [from the substratum], as for example:
"Are the various trees and mountains colored, or is the sky bent down? Or is it spread out?"
Has the earth been filled with unevenness, or have the quarters of the sky been withdrawn by the darkness?
In this case, regarding the object of superimposition (*āropa-viṣaya*), which is the darkness (*timira*), passion and so forth are superimposed as having a locus distinct from trees and the like.
Some, however, say that this is a form of doubt (*saṃdeha*) based on the locus of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*).
Others, on the other hand, because the particle *nu* indicates possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), declare this to be a form of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Explaining these three varieties, he provides an illustration with the verse beginning "pure" (*śuddha*), and so forth.

Here, because the slender woman who is the subject (*viṣaya*) is not the object of the doubt, the doubt belongs only to the mango blossoms and other things which are the superimposed subjects (*viṣayin*).
An example of both the subject and the superimposed subject being involved is as follows:
"Is this a lotus, or the orb of the moon, or perhaps the face of the intoxicating-eyed woman which removes all fatigue?
For that blackness seen in its center imitates the pair of eyes of a deer, beautiful as bees."
In this instance, the common property of "removing fatigue" and so forth is presented as a pervasive attribute (*anugāmitva*).
In some cases, it also occurs through the relation of "thing and counter-thing" (*vastu-prativastubhāva*), as for example:
"Is this a lotus entwined with black bees, or is it a face with beautiful dark hair?"
Thus the world suspects you, O fair-limbed one, when you have descended into the Sarayū.
In this context, the states of being "not black" (*asitatva*) and "deep blue" (*sunīlatva*) constitute the nature of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānyarūpa*).
Furthermore, there exists a relationship of original image and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) among the lotus petals.
Thus, because this [simile] is based on similarity, its twofold division—based on common attributes (*samānadharmanimitta*) and multiple attributes (*anekadharmanimitta*)—need not be explained.
For its inclusion is established solely on the basis of similarity as the cause;
furthermore, it lacks aesthetic charm (*cārutva*), unlike other causes such as contradiction (*vipratipatti*) and the like.
The phrase "by having different substrata" means by way of grammatical non-co-ordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
He states another alternative view, beginning with "some" (*kecit*).
By this, the author himself has also stated that doubt is rooted in conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Therefore, this [doubt] also rests upon conceptual determination and becomes threefold, according to whether its own nature, its cause, or its result is being doubted.
In that regard, an example of doubt concerning the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is as follows: "rañjitā" and so forth; or likewise:

"Consider this: when the cool-rayed moon—remover of the fatigue of night-lotuses, preceptor for initiation into the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), mirror for the faces of the quarters, friend of the *cakora* birds, and full-blown—is present..."
Was the body of heaven and earth filled with camphor, smeared with sandalwood paste, washed with mercury, or fashioned from crystal stones?
In this instance, because the whiteness of the moonlight is identified with a flood of camphor through poetic identification (*adhyavasāya*), it is rooted in such identification.
An example of doubt regarding the cause (*hetu-saṃdeha*) is as follows:
"In heaven, for those fortunate ones who touch upon the practice of remembering Your lotus-feet with intense concentration, there flow continuously streams of tears..."

Is it from the momentum of the activity of questioning concerning existence, cultivated over a long period of time, or is it from the joy of beholding the moon-like face of Liberation that has been attained?
In this case, two causes for the tears—namely, joy at being separated from worldly existence and the imminence of liberation—are determined.
An example of doubt regarding the result is as follows:

"At the end of the dance, was it to uproot the Pārijāta tree, or perhaps to touch the celestial Gaṅgā, or was it to split the moon and sun, that he approached with the perception that they were red lotuses?"

May that hand of yours, held aloft by the Lord of the Gaṇas for the sake of our well-being—whether to grasp the weight of the garland of stars as an ornament or to strike down those born of heaven—be auspicious to you all.
In this case, the result of the production of elephants—such as their dispersal—is intended.
Since the particle *nu* here, like the word *ādi*, indicates possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), he says "others," etc., in order to show another alternative view;
thus, the meaning is "as if colored [by passion]."
In the preceding sense, however, the word *nu* should be explained as referring merely to a conjecture.
Sūtra 19:
The cognition of another object due to similarity is error (*bhrāntimān*).
Because it shares the common characteristic of being non-correct knowledge (*asamyagjñāna*), its definition follows immediately after that of doubt.
Error (*bhrānti*) is a property of the mind;
that mode of expression in which it exists is "erroneous" (*bhrāntimān*).
And the object of this [superimposition] is an error induced by similarity,
as for example:
"With the expectation that her lips were bimba fruits, with the notion that her curls were ripe jambu fruits, and with the delusion that her red cheeks were pomegranate seeds..."
O King, by its very completion, it instantly caused those with eyes like lotus petals—who were already exhausted in the desert—to faint from thirst within the cages of the Gurjara king’s parrots.
However, delusion caused by a severe blow to a vital organ (*marmaprahāra*) and the like is not the province of this poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
For example:
"By him whose entire chest was pulverized by the blow of Dāmodara..."
And the wrestler Cāṇūra beheld the sky filled with a hundred moons.
Even an error caused by similarity is accepted only when it is evoked by the poet's creative intuition for the sake of artistic embellishment (*vicchitti*),
as has been illustrated;
it is not one that arises spontaneously, such as the [error of perceiving] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
In this way, it should also be understood that [this definition] applies even to doubt, such as "it might be a post or it might be a person.
The point is that [error] is characterized by its commonality with incorrect knowledge (*asamyagjñāna*), and not by its similarity to being "pregnant with superimposition" (*āropagarbha*).
For superimposition occurs only when the object and the subject are simultaneously made the objects of a single cognizer; therefore, an error pregnant with superimposition is not possible anywhere.
Because when mother-of-pearl and the like are perceived in their true form as mother-of-pearl and so forth, there is no misconception of them as silver and the like.

Now, one might object: "Error is a property of the mind; it is logical to say that 'one who possesses it' is 'possessed of error' (bhrāntimān). Therefore, how can this term be applied to a poetic figure (alaṅkāra)? Anticipating this doubt, he says "Error," etc.
The meaning is that "he" refers to a particular mode of expression; therefore, the word *bhrāntimat* is used figuratively (*upacarita*) for this poetic figure.
Regarding the phrase "employed through similarity":
it is not as in [the following verse]:
"She is in the palace, she is on every path, she is behind, she is in front, she is on the couch, and she is in every direction—for one afflicted by separation from her."
O mind! There is no other nature for you whatsoever; that, that, that, that, that, that—what is this doctrine of non-duality in the entire world?

In this passage, the simultaneous perception [of the woman] in multiple locations, such as the palace and elsewhere, is caused by the contemplation of identity (*tanmayatā*) resulting from intense passion for a single, though limited, woman; thus, there is the figure of speech *bhrāntimān* (Error), for that would occur if the palace and so forth were perceived as having the form of the beloved.
However, since one thing is perceived as being another beloved, this is clearly the domain of the figure of speech *viśeṣa* (Particularity).
If it is argued that this is merely an illusion (*bhrānti*) arising from the sight of a beloved who does not actually exist in the palace and so forth, we say: no.
For in that case, there would be mere illusion and not a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).

Rather, by the power of the cause consisting of intense passion, there occurs a spontaneous manifestation of the perception of a young woman, even though she is unreal, within the palace and such places.
Because it is not produced by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*),

even in such passages as: "King Harṣa too, overwhelmed by grief for his father, regarded Fortune as a curse, the earth as a great sin, sovereignty as a disease, enjoyments as serpents, and his residence as hell," and so forth, there is no figure of speech known as *bhrāntimān* (the mistaken).
