In that case, as was stated immediately prior, because the misconception (*abhimāna*) of silver does not arise when one perceives [an object] in its true form as mother-of-pearl and so forth;

here, however, although Śrīharṣa perceived Fortune (*Śrī*) in the form of his object, he perceived her as a curse because he was overwhelmed by grief for his father—thus the ornament of the "Uneven" (*Viṣama*) is more appropriate. "The left hand desires to apply collyrium even to the right eye, and the arm desires to fasten the serpent-bracelet even on the left arm."
May that face, marked by a shared smile as the two of them behold their respective untrained halves of the Blessed One’s body, grant us our heart's desire.
In this case as well, the figure of speech is *saṃskāra* (impression) alone, not *bhrāntimān* (illusion).

For here, due to the constant practice of applying collyrium to both eyes of the Blessed Lady, immediately after the application of collyrium to the left eye, there arises a compliance with the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for applying collyrium to the right eye; thus, it is indeed *saṃskāra*.
Furthermore, in the absence of the awakening of that impression, such an application of collyrium would not occur.
On the contrary, since the nature of the Lord's half is understood here exactly as it is, the impression of the collyrium has not taken root;
thus, because the very act [of perception] proceeds without faltering, the production of an error regarding that object is impossible, and there is no room for one who is deluded.
For a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that has fully taken root is indeed an error (*bhrama*);
however, one that remains as its own essence alone is an ornament of latent impressions (*saṃskārālaṅkāra*).
For this very reason, it is said that "one is able to give through speech."

Thus, in this context, it is understood that there is only a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) caused by the constant practice of giving lotus-like eyes, and not even the highest delusion (*bhrama*) based upon it;
for the half-body of the Supreme Lord is perceived as being exactly so, and there is not even a trace of [delusion] therein.
For this very reason, it is said to be "untrained" and "marked by a smile."
The specific distinction between these two has already been stated in the *Alaṅkārabhāṣya*; therefore, it should be followed from that very source.

Thus, since error (*bhrānti*)—which is the domain of this figure of speech—is caused solely by similarity and not produced by any other cause, one should not allege that the definition is under-extended (*avyāpaka*).
Likewise, because this [figure] is caused by similarity, there are three possible ways for the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) to function.
In that regard, "concomitance" (*anugāmitā*) is as follows: "O lovely-eyed one, look! This deluded bee, mistaking your blossoming eyes for blue lotuses, is chasing after them."
In this instance, the property (dharma) indicated is that of "expanding" as a pervasive characteristic (*anugāmin*).
However, its nature as a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānyarūpatva*) is as follows: "This sun, approaching the western quarter, has become like the bimba-fruit from the mouth of an angry female serpent."
He is instantly gazed upon by the sea-monsters of the ocean out of greed for the mass of flesh, as red as fresh blood.
In this case, the states of being copper-colored and reddish possess the nature of pure universals (*śuddhasāmānya*).
An example of the relationship between the original object and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) is as follows:
"The rays of the moon, though struck by the dark-blue luster of the ear-ornaments worn by women, [shine forth]."
In the face of the proud woman, which was smeared with collyrium, her husband, out of great apprehension, [did not look].
"The moonbeams, drawn away by the sapphire rays of her ear-ornaments,
were wiped away by her lover from the face of the indignant woman, fearing they were tears mixed with collyrium."

In this instance, there is a relationship of archetypal correspondence (*bimbabhāva*) between the state of being smeared with collyrium and the state of being struck by the rays of Indra’s [Indra’s] weapon.
To further solidify the fact that this [error] is caused solely by similarity, he provides a counter-example beginning with "gāḍha" (deep).

Even though it is caused by similarity, he states—beginning with "sādṛśya"—that this error is exclusively the domain of an illusion evoked by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*), and not a real, objective one.
"It has been illustrated" refers to the passage beginning with "on her lips, which have the appearance of bimba fruit," and so forth.
He applies this very same principle even to cases of doubt, starting with the words "in this way," and so on.
Regarding the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*): by implication, it necessarily contains a superimposition (*āropa*). For in that very case, its cause is similarity (*sādṛśya*).

For when doubt is rooted in a mental determination (*adhyavasāya*), the state of being doubted regarding the object and the subject would arise either from similarity or from another type of relationship, as was illustrated previously.
Thus, it should be understood that this figure of speech does not exist at all unless it is characterized by superimposition (*āropa*) even in the absence of similarity.
Therefore, one must not claim that this is not a poetic figure simply because there is no common property (*sādharmya*), provided that another cause [for the doubt] is present without distinction.
Even when there is similarity, only that which is brought forth by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*) constitutes a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), and not that which arises naturally.
Sūtra 20:
*Ullekha* (the act of delineation) is the apprehension of even a single object in multiple ways due to a particular cause.
Where a single object is perceived in multiple ways, that is *ullekha* (multiple description), because it involves the delineation of a plurality of forms.
And this is not a mere *ullekha* without a cause;
rather, it is produced by virtue of the cause known as the possession of various attributes (*nānāvidhadharmayogitva*).
In this regard, inclination, desire, and proficiency are the respective motivating factors.
As it has been said:
"It differs according to inclination, according to desire, and according to proficiency."
Even the appearance [of an object] is a single entity when established through synthesis.
Thus [it is said].

For example, as in the *Harṣacarita*, in the description of the district named Śrīkaṇṭha: "It is a grove of asceticism by the sages, a seat of love by the courtesans, and a hall of music by the dancers," and so forth.
For here, the single district named Śrīkaṇṭha is described in its manifold forms—such as a grove of asceticism and the like—due to its association with those respective qualities.
Furthermore, the [three] factors of taste (*ruci*), purpose (*arthatva*), and linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) can generally be applied both collectively and individually.

Now, one might object: "In this context, in passages such as *'avajravañjaram' (like a diamond fortress) by the Śaraṇāgatas, or *'asuravivaram' (the cave of the Asuras) by the Vātikas*, there is an employment of the poetic figure of metaphor (*rūpaka*); how then can this be considered the domain of the figure of *ullekha*?
This is true.
First of all, there exists a domain for this [figure] distinct from metaphor (rūpaka), such as in the example "the penance-grove," where its nature is possible in reality. However,
where a metaphor is established, if this mode [of expression] is also possible there, let there be a commingling (saṃkara) of the two.
However, its non-existence cannot be asserted on this basis alone;
therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
For in that case, let it be the poetic figure *bhrāntimat* (the presence of error), since it is based on the perception of something possessing the form of what it does not actually possess.
This is not so;
for there is no such unprecedented excellence (atiśaya) known as "perception in various ways," and this ornament is caused by that very excellence.
If you accept that the perception of confusion is indeed admitted, then let there be the poetic figure *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of "difference within non-difference.
This is not a fault.

The conclusion is that because it is delineated through multiple *dhātus* (verbal roots) by way of a division of objects known as the difference among perceivers—and because that [division] consists of distinct modes of expression—it is in no way possible to effect its inclusion [within other categories].
For example: "By the elderly women he was perceived as ‘Nārāyaṇa’; by the young women as ‘Śrīvallabha’;
but by the children, out of curiosity, he was seen thus [as a mere boy]."
"He is called Nārāyaṇa by those of advanced age, Śrīvallabha by young women,
and by children, moreover, he is confirmed as such out of mere curiosity. In this same way,
[the application of names] is to be understood in cases such as "Pṛthu in speech, Arjuna in the chest," and so forth.
However, this is the distinction: in the former case, there was a depiction of multiple meanings through different perceivers, whereas here it is through different objects.
[Objection: But if there is a depiction of multiple meanings by way of the forms of the teacher and so forth, that is *śleṣa* (paronomasia); why then is it established here as a separate ornament?
True;

however, since another form of interruption (*vicchitti*) is observed here due to the various elements (*dhātu*) and their phonetic figures (*nimitta*), *śleṣa* (paranomasia) would be the cause for the emergence of that impression.
It is not, however, entirely absent.

Therefore, this is a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) because, in such a case, there is a presence of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) even in the absence of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Consequently, in instances such as these, *ullekha* alone is superior. Furthermore, this figure of speech should be illustrated by relying on the charm of other figures of speech as well.
Regarding the phrase "even of one":
it refers to apprehending [it] in many ways,
not, however, to conceptualizing it as manifold.
For apprehension occurs when comprehension has been produced either spontaneously or through effort, but not when it is merely spontaneous.
As they say:
"Therefore, that [apprehension] is either devoid of the association with words or accompanied by them."
Everything that apprehends objects such as genus and so forth is accepted as perception.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, since conceptualization (kalpanā) and the like lead exclusively toward comprehension, they cannot occur within spontaneous comprehension; thus, because they pervade both cases, it is appropriate to follow exactly what was stated in the sūtra.
Regarding the phrase "due to the abundance of forms" (rūpabāhulya):
for this very reason, there is indeed an initial perception of another object.
Otherwise, there would not even be the apprehension of a single thing in multiple ways. For this very reason, its definition follows immediately after [the discussion of] error;
for a single thing is not apprehended in multiple ways independently.
However, he says "na cedam" and so forth, [meaning] "but this is not so," because it is due to the force of that specific purpose.
Regarding the word "etad" (this):

since a single entity, which possesses various kinds of properties, becomes the object of cognition as an undivided whole, how is it logical for there to be a manifold apprehension whose objects are each individual property? Having raised this doubt, he says "tatra" and so forth.
In this context, "therein" refers to the grasping [of objects] in many ways.
"Interest" (ruci) is conceptualization by way of independence.
"Desire" (arthitva) is the state of being intent upon the longing for purposeful action (arthakriyā).
Mastery consists in taking recourse to the linguistic usage of the elders.
This has been stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"Through the connection with various qualities" means through the association with manifold attributes such as distinctness (*viviktatva*) and so forth.

The pursuit of gems is directed toward the forest hermitages; the pursuit of courtesans is directed toward the temple of love. Likewise, the training and the pursuit of dancers are directed toward the concert hall.

By the word "mostly" (*prāyaśas*), it is indicated that there is no particular delight [in this]. Now, one might object: "In this fragment of a text describing the region called Śrīkaṇṭha, which was cited as an example, there is indeed a connection with other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*); how then can you say that it falls exclusively within the scope of this [figure]? To this, he says "Now... (*nanu*) and so forth.
Having conceded this very point, he provides a rebuttal with the words "Granted" (*satyam*) and so forth.
The word "tāvat" (firstly/in this case) is intended to indicate the misconception regarding the absence of *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Regarding the phrase "of that form," it means of the form of the penance grove (*tapovana*) and so forth.

Here too, the claim made by others—that because of the connection with the existence of a whole (*avayavin*), there is the presence of *sāropā* indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus one might suspect the figure of speech to be *rūpaka*, and therefore the necessity of considering its distinctness (*viviktatva*)—is incorrect.
Because there is no relationship of part and whole (*avayava-avayavin*), metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) itself is non-existent [in this case].
For a "penance grove" does not exist as a part within any single portion of the region named Śrīkaṇṭha, such that it could be superimposed by sages upon that whole.

Rather, for the sages and others, there arises such an appearance based on their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*), their specific needs, and so forth, through the qualities of Śrīkaṇṭha—who possesses those very qualities—viewed under the aspect of qualities such as seclusion and the like which characterize a penance grove.
Furthermore, even if there is an intention to express the relationship between parts and the whole, that alone does not constitute *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Although its definition is ultimately based on figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is still considered an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) because it brings about a form for the object;
otherwise, it would be merely figurative indication itself.
For even metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not have the ultimate nature of a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
And here, by means of the superimposition of [the forest] of asceticism and so forth, there is no excellence whatsoever in the object of superimposition,
because its being of that very nature is possible in reality itself.
Therefore, it is established that its scope here is indeed distinct from *rūpaka* (metaphor);

not only is this [figure] distinct from other ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), but it is shown to be possible even where there is a presence of the *rūpaka* ornament. To demonstrate this, he says "where," etc.
This "mode" (*bhaṅgi*) also consists in the apprehension of one thing in multiple ways.
"By this much" means by the mere employment of the metaphor (*rūpaka*).
"And from that" means because of the commingling (*saṃkara*) of the metaphor and the poetic delineation (*ullekha*).
[The opponent objects: "But surely, where there is no application of metaphor, there may be the application of another ornament. To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of that which does not have that form":
even though it does not possess the form of a penance grove (*tapovana*), it is so designated because it is associated with the appearance of being a penance grove.
For this alone is the true nature of error: the apprehension of something as being what it is not.
"Of that which is unprecedented" refers to that which is impossible for one who possesses error (*bhrāntimat*).
"Because it has that as its cause" means because it is caused by the excellence known as the apprehension of multiple forms.
If, moreover, there were even a trace of error here, then let there simply be a commingling (*saṃkara*) of this with that; thus he says: "In the case of commingling," and so forth.

"If it is so," [the opponent objects]: "Even if it is merely an illusion, let there be a confusion between the two because of that. To this he replies with the words beginning "In the case of confusion," etc.
"If it is so."

The meaning is: "the distinction of this [subject] from that which possesses error, or its confusion with it. "This" refers to the existence of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). "Therefore" refers to the division resulting from the difference between the perceivers.
Indeed, the very distinction between all figures of speech (alaṅkāras) lies in their difference in arrangement (vicchitti).
Thus, having established this very principle after first refuting various opposing views, he provides another example with the words "nārāyaṇo tti" ("He is Nārāyaṇa," etc.).

And here, because the terms "old woman" (vṛddhā) and so forth are used respectively in the sense of "one who has cast off" (vyuptatti) and "one who possesses meaning" (arthavat), there is an indication of [his] being Nārāyaṇa and the rest.
"It is the cause for the arising of that creative intuition (*pratibhā*)," because without *śleṣa* (punning condensation), the *allekhā* (the act of sketching out) cannot be accomplished here.
"In its absence," means:
There is an absence of mention;
hence the phrase "ataśca" (and therefore), because even in the absence of *śleṣa* (punning), this particular aesthetic effect (*vicchitti*) is possible.
The term "of such a kind" refers to that which consists in a distinction of objects.
For example:

"May the glance of Pārvatī, who is in love with her first union— shy before the face of her beloved, compassionate toward the elephant-hide garment, terrified of the serpent, filled with wonder at the nectar-dripping moon,
envious at the sight of the daughter of Jahnu (Gaṅgā), and distressed by the hollow of the skull— be for your welfare."
In this context, there is the delineation of the multiplicity of a single vision through the distinction of its various respective objects.

Thus, since this [vision] can occur not only by relying on *rūpaka* (metaphor) and the like, but also by relying on other poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), he says: "In the same way, with respect to other poetic figures," and so forth.

Among these, the first type is based on doubt (*saṃdehāśraya*), as for example: "Is he the sun, or is he fire? Thus do his enemies determine him. Is he the wish-fulfilling gem, or is he the tree of paradise? Thus do those who have come from afar wonder. Is he the spring season, or is he the flower-arrowed god of love? Thus do the women of Rāma’s city think. Is he Rāma, or is he the son of Jamadagni? Thus do the archers consider him."
Herein is the depiction of a single object as possessing multiple, seemingly contradictory attributes;
this very point is also the basis for hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), as in the following example:

"The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is the witness to his sovereignty; fire (*vahni*) has its great luster eclipsed by him; the spear (*śakti*) is one whose offenses have been softened; the rod of punishment (*daṇḍa*) is his sword; he is a knower of forcibly abducting the wives of his enemies; and he is a beholder of wells, ponds, and other such things."

O Lord of wondrous form, one who knows your power sees a noose in your hand; one who knows your treasury sees a banner; one who knows your self-will sees a mace; and one who knows your nature sees a trident traced upon the palm of your hand.

In this case, through the hyperbole beginning with "Thou art indeed Indra," the non-difference of the King from the World-Guardians (Lokapālas) is perceived; thus, there is a representation (*ullekhana*) of one [subject] as having multiple forms.
And an example based on metaphor (*rūpaka*) due to a difference in the objects is as follows:

"The passion of the month of Caitra upon the heads [of the quarters], the young sprout upon the trees, the mass of coral in the ocean, and the thick dust of vermilion applied to the foreheads of the elephants of the directions—"
May that expansion of rays—the light born at dawn from the redness of the sun upon the peaks of the divine mountains and within the expanse of the sky—grant you well-being.
In this case, there is a multiplicity based on the metaphorical substratum (*rūpaka*) belonging to a single [entity] alone through a difference of objects.
The reading "kārakāntara" is a corruption; for what is actually mentioned here is the basis for the distinction of the *kāraka* itself in its primary form.

This [cognition] is threefold because it consists of the delineation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), its cause (*hetu*), and its fruit (*phala*). Among these, the delineation of its own nature has just been illustrated. As for the delineation of the cause, it is as follows:
They know you as the self-born one, who is always the cause of creation, the sustainer of all beings, and the enemy who is the cause of their destruction.
In this instance, there is a depiction of the manifold nature of the causes for a single birth. As for the manifestation of the result, it is as follows:
"O King, the subjects you have protected know only the Dharma according to the scriptures; those who know the inner secrets know only wealth, which is but a portion of the treasury."
"Having attained the sense of fulfillment through desire alone, no discerning person perceives any purpose in your birth other than for liberation."
Here, there is a depiction of the manifold nature of the fruits of a single birth alone.
[Sūtra 21:
Apahnuti (Concealment) consists in the denial of an object.
This is stated by way of contrast with the denial (*apahnava*) introduced [previously], namely that there is the cognition of another object.

Because it occurs in the context of superimposition (*āropa*), when the object of superimposition is denied while the thing being superimposed is cognized, it is the figure of speech called *apahnuti* (denial). And its formal manifestation (*bandhacchāyā*) is threefold.
There is superimposition preceded by concealment, and concealment preceded by superimposition;
or rather, concealment is indicated by words such as "quibble" (*chala*) and others which establish its unreality.
In the first two aforementioned types of division, there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*);
however, in the third type of division, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).
An example of the first is as follows:
"When the moon displays the grace of a water-lily leaf within its orb, people call it a 'hare'; but that is not how I view it.
I, however, consider the moon to be one whose body is marked by the scar of a wound from the falling meteor-like side-glances of young women overcome by separation from their lovers."

When there is a denial (*apahnava*) of the hare in the moon, the superimposition (*āropa*) of the moon—which possesses a scar-like mark resembling a rabbit—is not faultless, as it does not sustain the logical connection (*anvaya-ghaṭanā*). This is as in the following example: "This orb of the full moon, whose body is lovely with its full development and which shines with vast radiance, does not rise into the expanse of the sky desiring to conquer the world. Rather, it is now the raised parasol for the burden [of the earth], possessing the splendor of white clouds, for one whose sole passion is the exertion to shatter the pride of people swollen with vanity. In this case, the "moon" is denied its identity as a lunar orb and is instead identified as a "parasol"; thus, the superimposition is not without flaw.
The second is as follows:

"May that Kumāra grant you the glory of celibacy— he who always dwells upon the peaks of Mount Saṃyama, which are like groves of blue lotuses for the eyes of the shimmering celestial nymphs, but who does not abide upon the peacock, though it possesses a beautiful plumage."

The third example is as follows: "O King-Moon, as your enemies flee through the empty desert together with your fame, the pearls from the pure pearl-necklaces— shaken by the high, trembling breasts of the Gūrjara women who have fled their homes in terror— fall like stars."
With drops of perspiration as large as jasmine buds.
In this context, it will be established that when the word *manye* ("I think") is used in place of the word *śūnya* ("empty"), it constitutes *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (metaphorical fancy with concealment).
Furthermore, it will be stated that when the word *manye* is used in a different sentence, such as "But I consider him to be the moon," it is simply *utprekṣā*.

Even though there are two varieties in this case—arising from the reversal of the sequence of application between concealment (*apahnava*) and superimposition (*āropa*)—they have not been counted as distinct types because, unlike the previous cases, they do not produce a striking poetic effect.
In that regard, an example of superimposition preceded by concealment has been cited continuously. However, as for concealment preceded by superimposition, it is as follows:
"This female Kāpālika wanders here, white with the smearing of moonlight-ashes, bearing the bones of stars, and delighting in the passion for the practice of disappearance."
She wanders from island to island, bearing upon her forehead—under the guise of the lunar mark—the fragrance of the *siddhāñjana* placed in the hollow of the moon.
Furthermore, in some cases, non-reality (*asatyatva*) is expressed through the form of words such as "body" (*vapus*), which denote the nature of another object; for example:
"In that lake of the nectar of beauty belonging to the deer-eyed one, Smara—surely scorched by Śiva—must have fallen upon her broad hips.
For this line of smoke, indicative of the extinguishing of the embers of his limbs, transforms into the form of a line of hair within the cavity of her navel."
Thus [it is said].
“Of the object,” and so forth.
“As another entity,” and so forth.
The phrase "follows those characterized by error" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

For this very reason, some— considering that such a sequence is improper according to the maxim of the frog-leap (maṇḍūkapluti)— have reversed the order of the text, defining apahnuti immediately after bhrāntimad and ullekha immediately after atiśayokti.

And this is not so; for the author has not defined *ullekha* immediately after *atiśayokti*, as he will state: "Having thus described two ornaments based on identification (*adhyavasāya*), the ornaments now based on implied comparison (*gamyamānaupamya*) are being discussed."

"Even there, although those [figures] are twofold by virtue of residing in the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) or the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), the two figures residing in the meaning of a word are stated in sequence.
Therefore, because the cognition of another object (*vastvantara-pratīti*) exists [in the case of *ullekha*], its definition was formulated by the author immediately after that of *bhrāntimad*.
For this very reason, since the cognition of another object occurs continuously even in *ullekha*, it is appropriate that its definition be given right here; thus, the text as it stands is correct.

If this is so, then why has the definition of *ullekha* (repetition) and *apahnuti* (concealment) not been formulated here by way of inversion? Anticipating this objection, he says: "prakrānta," etc. "Idam" refers to the definition of *apahnuti*.
He explains that very point with the words beginning with "āropya," etc.
The meaning is that when the object (*viṣaya*) is negated, there is the affirmation of something else that is the subject (*viṣayin*).
By this [it is said]:
"They do not call poison poison; you, O Brahmin, are called poison."
Poison kills only the individual, but the property of a Brahmin destroys one along with one's entire lineage.

In this case, because the object (*viṣaya*), poison, is first negated and then superimposed upon the object of Brahman’s own property (*brahmasvaviṣaya*), it is indeed a *rūpaka* (metaphor) characterized by a firm imposition, not *apahnuti* (concealment).
For the definition of *apahnuti* is the presentation of another thing—the subject (*viṣayin*)—precisely on the basis of the object (*viṣaya*) that is to be negated.
Here, however, there is a presentation of the very object to be negated, namely the poison, as being superimposed upon the object of Brahman’s own property. Now...
If it is argued: "In this case, since the primary poison is negated, there is the prescription of the secondary poison, namely the poison of Brahman's property" (*Alaṅkāraratnākara*, p.
42), then what is the meaning of the statement that "there is the prescription of the secondary poison, namely the poison of Brahman's property"? Does it mean "of Brahman's [property]"?
Among these, the first position is not tenable;
for, according to the logic of poison, there is no external object whatsoever that consists of both Brahman’s property and poison.
Furthermore, in that case, there could be no statement distinguishing between "this is Brahman’s property" and "this is poison."

Nor is there any figurative sense (*gauṇatā*), because [the word] functions in its own primary meaning (*svārtha*). That which applies to one thing while referring to another is called figurative. And here, the nature of Brahman does not apply anywhere else, such that it would have a figurative sense.
Thus, even in the second alternative, figurative usage is not tenable;
nor is there a dual injunction here,
because the primary meaning is sublated by the absence of the activity of possessing Brahman's property, and [the term] therefore functions with respect to secondary qualities.

Even in the third case, there is no prescription of poison as something secondary (*gauṇa*). Because the primary meaning is obstructed by the absence of the function of [consuming] Brahman’s property, it operates through secondary qualities; thus, since that which is prescribed is secondary in that context, the *rūpaka* (metaphor) is properly understood as a "firm imposition" (*dṛḍhāropa*), because poison was superimposed there preceded by a negation, with the desire to convey the firm conviction that Brahman’s property is indeed poison.
If it were stated again that "this [wealth] of Brahmā is poison," there would be a mere denial (*apahnava*).

Therefore, the definition of *apahnuti* should be formulated as follows: when the primary object has been set aside, the denial of that object constitutes *apahnuti*, which is a prescription of something else.
[The word] "of that" refers to the ornament named *apahnuti*.
By the terms "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) and "single sentence" (*ekavākya*), the definitions of the three types [of split] have been provided as applicable. It is not faultless,
because it lacks the maintenance of the sequence as previously stated.
For this very reason, he states another example, beginning with "of the full moon" (*pūrṇendoḥ*), etc.
Because of the employment of the word *manye*, which indicates probability and the like,
it is not a case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Because the conditions for *sādhyavasānā* (superimposition-based) and other types of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) are absent.
"It will be explained" refers to [the discussion] regarding *utprekṣā*.
And by that [same principle], I consider the word *manye* (I think) to be expressive [of apahnuti] just like the words *iva* and others;
however, in the absence of the full set of conditions for *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), the employment of the word *manye* expresses only *vitarka* (speculation).
Therefore, even though it is the same [in both cases], those who assert that examples such as "he drank insolence" (*avātpaḥ prāgalbhyam*) are illustrations of *apahnuti*...

The authors of the *Alaṅkāraratnākara* and others maintain that this is indeed an instance of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because by the phrase "not so for me," the position of the hare is refuted; since there is no possibility of one thing having the nature of another, the phrase "I think" establishes the certainty of the scar's identity alone.
What can we say of those who are skilled in investigating what precedes and what follows?

Thus, there are many other errors of this kind elsewhere, in the examples and so forth; however, for fear of excessive prolixity, and because our refutation of their criticisms is already well known to them, [we have not detailed them here].

We have not refuted it by means of our own position. This [example] was cited merely to demonstrate the possibility [of such a case], namely, that which is expressed by words such as "chala" (quibble) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "denoting the nature of another object":
since the word *vapuḥ* denotes the meaning of "body," here,

moreover, because the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) undergoes a transformation into the form of the object of comparison (*upameya*), it would constitute the figure of speech known as *pariṇāma* (transformation).

In this case, however, since the purpose is to suggest the fall of Madana (the God of Love) who was consumed by Śarva (Śiva), the primary intention is to deny the existence of the line of hair (*romāvalī*) and instead emphasize the crest of smoke (*dhūmaśikhā*). Therefore, this is neither *pariṇāma* nor *rūpaka*.
This is because, through the force of the word *vapuḥ*, which results in a deceptive meaning, the object being superimposed is perceived once the locus of the superimposition has been denied;
for it has already been stated previously that *rūpaka* occurs only when the locus of the superimposition is not denied.

Now, if it is argued that here too, since co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible between two distinct things, the negation must apply to one of them; and since a negation of the superimposed object is untenable, the negation is understood to terminate in the object of superimposition itself—this is not so.

For in this case, because the moon and so forth do not actually exist in the face and so forth, the literal meaning of "moon" is sublated; thus, it indicates by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) the qualities associated with its own nature, but a negation of the object—the face—is not perceived.
Since words such as "face" function primarily in their own literal sense,
what is ultimately understood here is the face and so forth as qualified by attributes such as the moon;
there is no sublation of the face and so forth.
It is not [the figure] *mukha* (face) and so forth, because there is an absence of such a reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa*). Nor is it an *udāharaṇa* (illustration),
because there is an absence of the disruption of the connection and so on.
And by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), untruth is sometimes expressed even through the instrumental case;
for example:
"O vine, abandon your dealings with my arms; O beloved, do not commit such a rash act against your own neck; your servant is still breathing."
These trees, which you yourself caused to grow with flowers until they were shedding tears, now seem to grasp a razor-blade under the guise of their swarms of bees, as if to cut the noose.
Here, the employment of the instrumental case in "kusumaiḥ" (with flowers) serves as the basis for the concealment [of the actual cause].
And because this [figure] is based on superimposition (*āropa*), it arises either from similarity (*sādṛśya*) or from another type of relation.
Even when it arises from similarity, there are three possible ways for the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) to function.
In that regard, *anugāmitā* (persistence) is as follows:
"People say that this moon possesses a dark spot as soft and black as a young *tamāla* leaf;
that is indeed a falsehood, for here the sky shines forth, revealed by the gaping wounds of the tooth-marks of the merciless Rāhu."
In this instance, the quality of being as dark as the *tamāla* tree is employed as a concomitant attribute.
An example of a pure universal form is as follows:
"This *pārijāta* tree was brought from the grove of the Lord of the Gods to the earth by Hari."
This excellent collection of *sumanas* flowers does not inspire pride in one born in the land of Kaśmīra.
In this case, the acts of removal and attainment possess the nature of pure universals (*śuddhasāmānya*).
The relationship of the original image and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) is as follows:
"The sky is not adorned with moonlight, nor is there a cloud with a streaked path of shadow; there is no appearance of stars, nor is this the orb of the nectar-rayed moon."
"Even this ocean, though consisting of the agitation of milk, is Mount Mandara with the serpent as its eye; this is a cluster of jewels, and this is a jar from which a stream of nectar flows."
Here, the state of being an ornament of moonlight is indicated by way of a reflection as consisting of the agitation of milk.
An example based on another relation is as follows:
"While the branches and creepers of the trees were agitated by the tumultuous Malaya breeze rising playfully, they indulged in a certain kind of swinging sport."
Surely the talkativeness that belonged to the cuckoos in the forest was the silence that leaped forth from the eyes of the doe-like wives of travelers.

Here, while the cause—the cuckoo’s eloquence—is negated, there is the prescription of its effect—the traveler’s silence. Thus, this [type of *apahnuti*] involving superimposition (*āropa*) has been demonstrated in detail.
Now, that which involves identification (*adhyavasāya*) is shown as follows:
"It is not because of his splendor or beauty, nor because he is the elder brother of the gods, nectar, and so forth who have made him their refuge, nor because he is the crest-jewel of the Lord;
that the young moon’s state of being worshipped thus in every direction and sub-direction has clearly arisen from his service to the lotus-face of the beloved."
In this case, having suppressed the fact that the quality of being worthy of worship is caused by [the Lord's] majesty and other such qualities, another cause is superimposed.
Or, for example:
"That the god who produces nectar rises every day with fifteen digits for the sake of satisfying the gods, ancestors, and men—this is untrue."
"Having encountered a reflection within your cheek, he wanders about by some clever device, intent on seizing the nectar of your lower lip."

Here, having swallowed (nigīrya) the cause characterized by the experience of each respective zodiac sign at the time of sunrise and so forth, another cause that is the result thereof is identified [through poetic identification].
Concluding this, he introduces another point with the words "In this way," and so on.

START Sūtra 22: Having thus defined the figures of speech based on superimposition (*āropa*) when non-difference is predominant, he now defines those based on identification (*adhyavasāya*): therein, when the predominance lies in the operation of identification, it is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
The determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the subject is the apprehension of non-difference through the swallowing up of the object. Regarding the phrase "containing superimposition" (*āropagarbhān*):

since this [type of metaphor] also contains determination, it is designated as "containing superimposition" based on its predominance—just as in the case of expressions such as "the village of wrestlers" (*mallagrāma*).
In that regard, he first defines *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) with the words "adhyavasāya" and so forth. The term "adhyavasāya" (determination) is used here, and not "saṃdeha" (doubt);
for in this context, cognitions are of two kinds, characterized by either certainty or uncertainty.
Furthermore, certainty that does not deviate from the object is correct;
it is incorrect otherwise. Thus, no distinction [between them] should be grasped.
For it is only the operation of cognition that has been undertaken for investigation here, and that is useful in the investigation of validity. Furthermore,
non-ascertainment is of two kinds, consisting of doubt and reasoning (*tarka*).
Therefore, it should not be said that what is uncertain is necessarily "doubtful" (saṃdagdha).
For even a cognition of probability (*saṃbhāvanā-pratyaya*), which is of the nature of reasoning (*tarka*), lacks the quality of being doubtful because it is not of the nature of certainty.
Since the apprehension of reasoning—denoted by terms such as *utprekṣā* and *saṃbhāvanā*—is rooted in [logical] inference, it does not have doubt as its basis.
Because that [inference] has a distinct characteristic.

Now, if it is argued that since doubt (*saṃśaya*) is non-ascertaining knowledge, and because tarka does not differ from doubt in its nature as non-ascertaining knowledge, tarka is not a separate category from doubt and thus has doubt as its root—this is not so.
For even though there is no difference between doubt and tarka in their being non-ascertaining knowledge, they possess different forms.
For instance: doubt (*saṃśaya*) is the general presentation of two alternatives, such as "Is this a post or a person?

Reasoning (*tarka*) is the sublation of one alternative through the perception of a cause favorable to one side, such as "This must be a person," by observing a reason conducive to that specific side. Certainty (*niścaya*) is the determination of one alternative without touching upon the other, such as "This is indeed a person. Thus, there exists a threefold nature of cognitions, attested by the experience of those with refined sensibilities.
If it is argued that "certainly there are indeed three types of cognition, but because there is no difference in their being non-determinative knowledge, *tarka* is a variety of doubt," we say: no.
For if that were so, then because there is no difference in their being incorrect knowledge, even error (*bhrama*) would be a variety of doubt.
If it is argued that there is a distinction between these two because one has the nature of certainty regarding the object while the other does not,
then what is the proof for this claim here?
For doubt arises by apprehending both sides in an indefinite manner.

Furthermore, there is a distinction between these two: reasoning (*tarka*) functions by subverting one alternative while relying on another, due to the appropriateness of causes conducive to seeing the horse at play and so forth;
whereas in the case of another location, the "post" alternative remains as if in competition, it does not do so on the ground where the horse is playing, but rather becomes weakened.

And because there is the possibility of negligence, it does not cease in every respect; for this very reason, the certainty [of its non-cessation] is established even in the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*).

For the certainty that "it does not cease in every respect" does not arise solely from the refutation of a contrary position (*pratipakṣa-bādhā*); rather, such certainty is possible even when no proof exists for the contrary.

Because it arises from the presence of evidence that either establishes or subverts [a position], doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a deliberation of the form "what could it be? which rests upon both sides without being fixed;
whereas *tarka* (reasoning) rests upon one side or the other.
If it is argued that doubt may still arise even by resorting to one side [of the alternatives], thinking, "What is the specific means for this result?", we say: no.
For, since one has accepted another alternative without restriction, there is no firm establishment in any single side.
Furthermore, as seen in the case of a person standing outside a wall, while specific individuals enter the path of memory, specific posts do not.

Thus, since *tarka* (ratiocination) arises from the recollection of one specific feature, it is distinguished from doubt (*saṃdeha*), which arises from the recollection of both features; this and other such extremely profound arguments for establishing the difference between these two have not been stated here as they are irrelevant to the present subject.

Therefore, one must necessarily admit that there exists an intermediate state between doubt and certainty, characterized by a sense of probability (*saṃbhāvanāpratyaya*) that hangs suspended like Triśaṅku.
Even so, since *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is rooted in a cognition consisting of a possibility that is non-definitive in nature, how can it have as its root *adhyavasāya* (identification)?
For the very essence of *adhyavasāya* consists in the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object and the definitive determination (*niścaya*) of the superimposed subject;
yet neither of these two is possible here.
"Because of the appropriation of the object and because of the absence of certainty.
To this it is replied: Here, determination (*adhyavasāya*) is of two kinds—the innate (*svārasika*) and the produced (*utpādita*).

Among these, in the case of the innate, the object is not even cognized; rather, the cause [of its appearance] is such that, by its own power, the cognition of the subject (*viṣin*) arises spontaneously.
For indeed, for a cognizer who has already ascertained the true nature of mother-of-pearl, the cognition "this is silver" could never arise.

In other cases, however, even after perceiving an object, if one conceives of it [as something else], one might produce a perception of that object through the force of a conceptual construction dependent on oneself.

For when one knows the object as distinct from the subject, such a perception—occurring naturally and directed toward a specific purpose—is merely restated by the speaker; it is not produced [by the speaker].
As they say:
"That [cognition] in which the cognition of another subject is restated as being of the nature of an error is 'the locus of error' (bhrāntimān)."
Furthermore, in this context, "naturalness" (svārasikatva) is intended precisely as that which is brought about by the poet's creative intuition (pratibhā);
for otherwise, as was stated previously, there would be mere illusion (bhrāntimātra). The other [type], however, is the object of poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
And that [superimposition] is of two kinds: established (*siddha*) and to be established (*sādhya*).
The established is that in which the primary status belongs to the object of determination (*adhyavasita*) because the subject (*viṣaya*) is swallowed up by being unexpressed;

the to-be-established is that in which the primary status belongs to the object of determination because the subject is swallowed up by being expressed through the employment of "as if" (*iva*) and so forth, since it consists of a cognition of probability.

Because the object [of comparison] consists of the cognition of possibility due to the employment of "yat" (as if), "iva" (like), and so forth, and because it is swallowed up (nigīrya), the primary importance belongs to the result of the identification (*adhyavasita*).

Since the object is being swallowed up due to the employment of "sādhya," "yatra," "iva," and so forth, and because it consists of the cognition of possibility, the primary importance belongs to the act of identification itself.
For this very reason, he says: "the primacy of the operation" (*vyāpāraprādhānya*).
For this very reason, in some cases here, the object is not mentioned;
because the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that is serviceable for the literal meaning (*vācya*) is introduced as something yet to be established (*sādhyamānatvena*).
And in other cases, even when the object is not mentioned, there is no [charge of] being already established (*siddhatva*).
Because the subject (*viṣaya*) is swallowed up by the words "like," etc., it should not be said that this [figure] contains a superimposition (*āropagarbha*).
In that [other case], there is a cognition of the subject as the superposed object (*viṣayin*);
here, however, because the subject is swallowed up, there is a cognition of the superposed object alone.

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that the definition of *adhyavasāya* (identification) is the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object? But here, since it is the object itself that is being swallowed up, how can there be *adhyavasāya* in this instance?"—this is not so.

For according to the statement, "When another [the subject] has internalized the object, that is *sādhyavasānikā* (identification with a substrate)," the defining characteristic of *adhyavasāya* is the internalization of the object by the subject.

And since that [identification] occurs either by swallowing up the object (*viṣaya*) or by making it the swallowed (*nigīryamāṇatva*), there is no distinction whatsoever. Furthermore, according to the principle stated previously, this state of being swallowed occurs whether the object is expressed (*upātta*) or unexpressed (*anupātta*); thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.

Therefore, it is established that when the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is accomplished, if the identification is to be the primary element, then the essential nature [of the object] is the primary element. Thus it is proven.
The author himself will analyze this further and explain it below; therefore, one should understand it from that very place.

That which constitutes the "determination of the probandum" (*sādhyādhyavasāya*) is precisely what constitutes its nature as "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*). For possibility arises by weakening one side and strengthening the other side; thus, it stands on an equal footing with the determination of the probandum.
For that [superimposition] also arises through the loosening of the object and the firmness of the subject;
for this very reason, even the subject possesses reality by virtue of its verbal expression and its function,
since it manifests in the form of a determination of the probandum precisely through the firmness of the subject.
As you yourselves have stated: "In the case of *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic probability), there is firmness regarding that which is being probable, not laxity regarding another.
Here, because the subject (*viṣayin*) being probable possesses firmness, it differs from doubt (*saṃśaya*).

For the definition of doubt is a deliberation of the form "what could this be? which rests upon two indefinite aspects. Furthermore, because the object of *saṃbhāvanā* lacks firmness, it is also distinguished from certainty (*niścaya*).

For in the case of a [literal] object, the establishment of an alternative position may occur either because the proof for one side is weakened due to the existence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), or because of the existence of a proving factor (*sādhaka*) for the other;
furthermore, since hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consists of a determinate cognition (*niścaya*), it is distinct from this [metaphor].

As for what the author will state later—"where there is the perception of the subject (*viṣayin*) as being unreal while it is yet to be proven"—that should be understood as referring to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*).

Thus, because the object (*viṣaya*) is swallowed up and the subject (*viṣayin*) is ascertained, it is established that this [figure] is rooted in *adhyavasāya* (imaginative identification); therefore, the definition stated previously is indeed a well-considered expression.
Consequently:
"Because there is no ascertainment [of identity] when using words such as ‘as if’ (*iva*), and because the object is [still] apprehended..."
In some cases, there is no poetic fancy (utprekṣā) due to a definitive determination, but rather due to doubt.
Thus, what has been stated above is indeed improper; enough with further elaboration.
And that [error] is of two kinds: the probandum (*sādhya*) and the established (*siddha*).
The probandum is that wherein there is a cognition of the subject as being unreal.

And the unreality (*asatyatva*) of a property residing in the substratum (*viṣayin*) [is established] when that property is perceived through its being possible in the substratum and impossible in the object (*viṣaya*).

A property consists of qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*); upon the perception of its possibility or impossibility, the unreality of the substratum is perceived therein because of its lack of ultimate reality (*aparamārthatā*), whereas the other [the object] is perceived as real because of its ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*).
When something is unreal,
the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding its cognition as real is the probandum (*sādhya*);
therefore, the predominance belongs to the cognitive operation.
Wherein there is the perception of reality even for that which is in fact unreal for the subject,
and wherein there is existence because of the absence of the previous cause of unreality—
therefore, the predominance belongs to the determined object (*adhyavasita*).

In that context, when there is a cognition of something as being the object of proof (*sādhya*) and the emphasis is on the operation [of the mind], it is expressed by such terms as "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), "conjecture" (*saṃbhāvanā*), "presumption" (*abhimāna*), "reasoning" (*tarka*), "inference" (*ūha*), and "poetic fancy" (*utprekṣā*).

Thus, poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is the conceiving of the subject at hand as something else, through its connection with the qualities or actions belonging to a non-subject, based on its status as a non-subject.
And that [fancy] is indicated as being directly expressed (*vācyā*) by means of words such as *iva* ("as if").
When [the object] is already being perceived, however, there is the employment of words such as "as it were" (*iva*).

And that [metaphor] is fourfold, according to whether the genus (*jāti*), action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), or substance (*dravya*) are superimposed as the objects of determination (*adhyavaseya*), even though they are not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*).
Although these varieties may also apply to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), no distinct poetic charm (*vaicitrya*) arises; therefore, they have not been enumerated.
Since each [of these] is twofold by way of being characterized by the conceit of existence or non-existence, there are eight varieties.
Furthermore, since each of the eight types of distinctions has the nature of either a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*), there are sixteen distinctions.
And since each of those distinctions is twofold by way of being adopted or not adopted as a cause (*nimitta*), there are thirty-two sub-varieties.
And within each of these, there are ninety-six varieties, consisting of the imagination (*utprekṣaṇa*) of cause, essential nature, and effect.
This is the scope of expressed imagination (*vācyotprekṣā*).
Even therein, since the imagination of the essential nature of a substance (*dravya*) occurs most frequently, the varieties of the imagination of cause and effect must be subtracted from that total.

Although there are this many varieties of *pratīyamānā* (suggested) [utprekṣā] from the perspective of its enumeration, nevertheless, the non-specification of the cause (*nimitta*) is not possible in that case; thus, this variety belongs to the young [poets].
For when words such as *iva* are not employed and the cause is not mentioned, the act of imagining (*utprekṣaṇa*) lacks a basis for its establishment.
Generally, in cases of *svarūpotprekṣā* (imagination of the essential form), the distinction [between figures] is indicated according to what is possible.

This [imagination], moreover, relies on the meaning (*artha*). In the domain of *dharma* (quality), it sometimes originates from the cause of a word that possesses double meaning (*śliṣṭa-śabda*), having been introduced through the expression of similarity at the time of the syntactic connection of the word-meanings (*padārtha-anvaya*). Yet, by the power of the intended purport of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-tātparya-sāmarthya*), it culminates in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) through the process of ascending to the operation of the cognizer (*abhimantṛ-vyāpāra*).
In some cases, when words such as *chala* (deception) and so forth are employed, there occurs *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (poetic fancy involving concealment).
Therefore, due to the variety of the modes already mentioned and those yet to be described, this [type of poetic fancy] is infinite.
He explains this very point with the verse beginning "viṣaya" and so forth.
"Apprehension of non-difference" [is so called] because of the internal organ being the object.

Although the determination of the probandum (*sādhyādhyavasāya*) consists of a cognition of probability (*saṃbhāvanāpratyaya*), he says "the probandum," etc., in order to demonstrate its distinction from that [cognition] with respect to the actual entity (*vastu*).

Because the cognition of probability assists the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of purifying the object, in the statement "this person must exist," the reality of the person exists according to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛttena*).

Furthermore, since that [object] is determined there as being subordinate to a purpose, it is said— "cognition as unreal"— because the object, though possible within the scope of the connection, does not possess reality in fact.
He states the reason for this very point with the words "and untruth," etc.,
[concluding with] "the binding to the object."
The meaning is that [the object] is determined as non-different from the property residing therein. By this, its lack of utility is indeed reinforced.
"Property" (dharma) refers to that which resides in the subject (viṣayin).
And that very [dharma] is the cause for the poetic fancy (utprekṣaṇa).
"Of that" refers to the dharma;
"of the locus of the possibility" refers to the subject (viṣayin).
In this context, "therein" refers to the object that is the locus of possibility;
"of the other" refers to the object that is the locus of impossibility;
and "of which" refers to the subject (the possessor of the property).
"And therefore" means:
because determination (*adhyavasāya*) is that which is being established; "even though it is unreal" means: even though it lacks objective reality.
In reality, because the subject cannot exist there,
it is the "cognition of truth";
for hyperbole (atiśayokti) has the nature of a definitive certainty (niścaya).
The phrase "due to the non-existence of the cause" refers to the concealment (*nigīraṇa*) of the movement of attributes (*dharmasaṃcāra*) and so forth.
The phrase "and for this reason" means that because the movement of attributes lacks predominance (*prādhānya*), the subject (*viṣayin*) alone possesses predominance;
the meaning is that since the object (*viṣaya*) has been swallowed up, the subject itself is predominant. This is what is called "predominance of the determined [subject]."
The nature of the states of being "to be proven" (sādhya) and "established" (siddha) has been explained immediately prior; therefore, no further effort is made here.
In that context, the word "therein" (tatra) serves to specify two things.
The connection is that [the object] is expressed by such words as "ascertainment" (adhyavasāya) and so forth.
He concludes this very point with the words "tadevam" and so forth.
As they have said: "Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is the imagining [of something] as being characterized by a particular state. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the suggested [fancy]":

Because of the initial employment of the particle *iva* and because it is not explicitly stated as a word, [the *utprekṣā*] is to be inferred rather than being suggested (*vyaṅgyā*), since the various divisions of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are what the author intends to explain, and thus the mention of divisions of the suggested would be irrelevant.
Thus, the rule is established by way of restatement: "In this manner, *utprekṣā* exists both as the expressed (*vācyā*) and as the implied (*pratīyamānā*)."
"And that" refers to "variety";
it is so called because, being swallowed up [by the primary object], it lacks predominance.
"Respectively" refers to genus and so forth;
"of the sign" refers to the phenomenon (dharma).
For it is by the power of that very [sign] that there is a connection with what is not the subject at hand, through its inclusion within the subject under discussion.

The threefold division of this [poetic figure], characterized by cause, essential nature, and result, constitutes its very lifeblood; therefore, that alone has been presented last as the locus of its final rest. Furthermore, the enumeration of divisions such as *jāti* and so forth—which, while not bringing about variety, was nonetheless performed out of deference to ancient authorities—was for this very reason not illustrated by the author in his own words.
And we shall not cite it as "this," referring to that which was just mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "even there":
although the aforementioned multitude of distinctions exists,
the word "mostly" (prāyas) indicates that the occurrence of cause and effect is possible in some instances.
For this very reason, the author of the *Alaṅkārānusāriṇī* has demonstrated the possibility of these two as well.
Thus, when there is the possibility of substance, cause, and effect, the previously stated number alone is superior;
otherwise, however, due to the absence of these sixteen varieties, there would be only eighty varieties.

And because, according to the method to be explained, it is impossible for this [consciousness] to have causes and fruits that lack a cause or an appropriation, only sixty-four varieties are possible.
"To this extent" means ninety-six;
"this manner" refers to the following.
This refers to the definition of suggested (pratīyamāna) poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
Regarding the word "mostly" (prāyaḥ):

the meaning is that this [suggested fancy] does not occur as frequently among the types of suggested figures as the expressed (vācyā) fancy of essential nature (svarūpotprekṣā) does among its respective varieties.
Furthermore, it is not that this [suggested variety] is entirely non-existent; rather, forty-eight distinct types are possible.
As it is stated in the *Alaṅkārānusāriṇī*: "There are forty-eight varieties of suggested *utprekṣā*.
This is because they also have their basis in the meaning (*artha*).

The meaning is that although the dependence on words for the sake of the sense is not useful anywhere [in this context], nevertheless, its having as its cause words that are *śliṣṭa* (possessing double meanings) brings about a certain variety in it.
The connection is that simile (*upamā*) culminates in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). "Infinite" means having many varieties.
Now, this [type of *utprekṣā*] is illustrated by the *Diṅnāga*:
therein, an *utprekṣā* based on genus (*jātyutprekṣā*) is as follows—
"May that moon protect you, which is curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk and appears placed upon the head of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), tawny with fire."
Like a sprout released from a crystal-white skull-cup, nourished day by day by the water trickling from the Mandākinī.
Here, because the word "sprout" (*aṅkura*) is a generic term (*jātiśabda*), a genus (*jāti*) is the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
An example of the poetic fancy of action (*kriyotprekṣā*) is:
"Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium."
Here, the actions of smearing and raining are poetically imagined (utprekṣyete) as being the nature of darkness and the sky respectively;
however, in the second half [of the verse], it is said: "Like service rendered to a wicked person, my sight has become fruitless."
In this case, there is only a simile (*upamā*), not a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
An example of the poetic fancy of quality (*guṇotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"This is that very spot where, while searching for you, I dropped one anklet upon the ground."
It was seen to be bound in silence, as if out of the sorrow of separation from your lotus-feet.
In this case, suffering (*duḥkha*) is the quality (*guṇa*).
An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on substance (*dravya*) is as follows:
"Having beheld this netherworld (*pātāla*)—which was empty of the moon, that festival for the eyes—"
"Here, by means of the faces of the women, a creation consisting of moonlight has been fashioned within the sky."
In this case, because the moon is a single entity, it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*).
These are examples regarding the conceit of existence (*bhāvābhimāna*). Now, the opportunity has arrived.
"By way of a mere indication" (diṅmātreṇa) implies that the distinctions such as genus (jāti) and so forth are not being fully enumerated.
"By virtue of having entered into darkness" (tamogatatvena).
The meaning is: "by swallowing up [the idea] that darkness possesses qualities such as being capable of moving.

For here, having swallowed up the fact that the subject (dharmin) "darkness" possesses one set of qualities, it is established as possessing another set of qualities; this we shall explain immediately below.
This is what is called a "poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding substance."
The poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) consists in the imagining of a substance in its own form; for that very [substance], there is the conceit of cause (*hetūtprekṣā*), as in:
"Victorious is that celestial river, the cause of coolness, falling from the crown of the Destroyer of Tripura onto the Snowy Mountain."
Born from the ocean of milk, she dwells there eternally; like the moon, she is the cause of both whiteness and coolness.
In this case, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the substance (*dravya*) as the cause.
An example of a poetic fancy regarding the effect (*phala-utprekṣā*) is as follows:
"In the midst of the water, facing the sun, [the lotuses] grey with dust..."
Day after day, the night-lotuses perform penance as it were for the sake of the moon.
And here, the moon possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*).
By the words "these," etc., he extends [the analysis] to show that these very [instances] serve as examples for the conceit of existence (*bhāvābhimāna*).
As for the conceit of non-existence (*abhāvābhimāna*), it is as follows:
"Alas! Her two cheek-bones, having become so emaciated, seem as if unable to bear one another, reaching such a state of exhaustion that they cannot even look at each other."
Here, in the phrase "not seeing," there is the misconception of the non-existence of the action.
The same should be understood for [the non-perception of] genus and so forth as well.
An example of a quality serving as the cause [of cognition] is as follows:
In the example cited as ‘navabisalatākoṭikuṭilaḥ’ (crooked like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk), [the cause] is that of crookedness;
as for an action, it is as in ‘rīdṛkṣāṃ kṣāmatāṃ gatau’ (having reached such a state of emaciation), where [the cause] is the reaching of emaciation. These are examples of the mention of a cause.

An example [of this] is: "In the absence of grasping, darkness, as it were, smears the limbs. An example of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause) is: "As if out of the pain of separation, it has become silent," and so forth.
An example of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) is: "When the sun, having transgressed the proper time, set out to go toward the quarter frequented by Kubera..."
The southern wind, bearing fragrance, she exhaled through her mouth like a sigh of resentment.

An example of *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) is as follows: "The thorny forest edges, as if wishing to see the letters [of his name], tore open the skin of the forehead of the King of Cola as he fled in fear, wondering: 'What indeed will he experience even today?'"
Thus, the direction for examples of expressed *utprekṣā* has been given.
An example of implied (*pratīyamāna*) *utprekṣā* is as follows:
"O fortunate one, she, unable to endure [your absence], dwells in your heart which is filled with many women."
Day after day, with no other occupation, she makes her already slender body even more emaciated.
"O fortunate one, she, finding no room in your heart already filled with thousands of women,
day after day, with no other occupation, makes even her slender body grow thinner."
In this case,
[the rays] are imagined as being "not remaining" (amāantīti) because they serve as the cause for attenuation;
the same should be understood regarding other varieties [of poetic figures].
"It is to be inferred" refers to the example of the conceit of non-existence (*abhāvābhimāna*).
"Of the cause and material" is because crookedness and the attainment of emaciation are directly specified.
"Without grasping" (anupādāna) is said because the grounds for concealment and so forth are being understood.
"In other distinctions" refers to those concerning essential nature, results, and so on.
Because it is perceived as something to be known (*jñeya*).
Among these, an example of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) is as follows:
"The moon, on all sides, [is like] a fountain of joy through its union with the cool breeze..."
Behold here the beauty of honey, produced by branches whose hands are trembling young shoots.
"The Fortune of Spring spreads everywhere through her branches, which have hands of trembling young shoots and are like thieves of joy at the arrival of the Malaya breeze."

Here, having suppressed (nigīrya) such qualities as "having hands that are trembling sprouts" by attributing them to Madhulakṣmī, the act of speaking is imagined (utprekṣita) in its own essential form.
Furthermore, the cause—namely, [the speaker’s] capacity to produce eagerness toward that [act]—is not explicitly stated.

As for the statement that it is impossible for a cause not to be mentioned in a suggested (pratīyamānā) utprekṣā within the enunciation (uddeśa), the reason there is generally the impossibility of imagining the essential form [of the object] itself.
The intention of the author is that for him, suggested (pratīyamāna) poetic fancy (utprekṣā) exists only in the form of cause and effect.

This has been stated with the underlying thought that, according to the principle to be explained later, it is impossible for the imagination of cause and effect to occur without the employment of a motive (nimitta).
Therefore, even suggested fancy of essential nature (svarūpotprekṣā) occurs precisely through the employment or non-employment of a motive.
In that regard, [the example] for non-appropriation of the sign has been cited;
but as for appropriation, it is as follows:
"This darkness, spreading everywhere, conceals the entire universe."
She anoints every limb of the person with thick brushes of nectar.

Here, having swallowed [the literal meanings] such as "being spread out," the act of smearing is imagined (utprekṣita) in its essential form as having arrived [there], and the cause for this is [his] quality of being a concealer and so forth.
"For he is the fourth pure fire, or even the fifth Veda;
or he is a moving sacred ford, or Dharma incarnate."

In such cases, however, according to the view of Vāmana, this is *viśeṣokti* (poetic figure of "peculiar cause"), as in the example "the earth-Kārtikeya. According to the author's own view, however, it is *rūpaka* (metaphor) with a firm superimposition (*dṛḍhāropa*).

As he will state: "That which is defined as *viśeṣokti*—namely, 'the assertion of a peculiar cause when there is a conception of the removal of one [factor] for the sake of strengthening the similarity'—is, in our system, merely a variety of *rūpaka*."
For this very reason, one should not claim that this is an example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) due to the absence of its necessary conditions here.
Similarly, in the case of "Another Indra is the king," the *rūpaka* (metaphor) consists precisely of a firm superimposition (*dṛḍhāropa*).
This has been demonstrated by the author himself in his discussion of *utprekṣā* in the *Alaṅkārānusāriṇī*.
An example of *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) is as follows:
"The horripilation emerging from his side while he was being groomed by the women skilled in auspicious arts appeared like a sigh escaping from the many wives who were being left behind."

"Behold, the horripilation has emerged on the ears of the future bride— who has had her ears filled with the names of noble lineages by those seizing upon auspicious signs— in order that she may hear them."
In this instance, the result is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as "as if to hear.

An example where the cause is expressed through punning (śliṣṭaśabda-hetu) is as follows: "He who was celebrated on the surface of the earth as a sacrificer renowned for his uniqueness, became the ultimate ground for the arrows of Cupid, which arrived with a frantic scramble of 'I first, I first!'"
In this context, regarding the subject of *dharma*, the word *mārgaṇa* is used with double meaning (*śliṣṭa*). It is "double-meaning" because it denotes both "an arrow" and "one who seeks.

An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) beginning with a simile (*upamā*) is as follows: "On the forehead-slate of the Goddess, they act as musk-paste tilakas; on her lotus-face, they act as bees; and even upon her head, they act as ornaments of fresh tamāla buds."
May those splendors of the neck of Śrīkaṇṭha—which act as blooming blue lotuses upon your ears, and as dark aloe-wood pastes upon the slope of your breasts—proclaim auspiciousness for you.

In this regard, although at first sight there is the perception of a simile due to the rule "the suffix *kvip* is added after all nominal stems" (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kvip*) when *kvip* is prescribed after a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), nevertheless, because the possibility of a literal standard of comparison is precluded in the present context, the final result is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) arising from the suggestion of a probability.
This is as in the description of separation, for example, in the verse beginning with "acting like armlets with their bracelets" (*keyūrāyitamaṅgadaiḥ*).

This [comparison] has also been illustrated in the *Sāhityamīmāṃsā* in various places within the *Harṣacarita*, even in contexts involving complete similes (*samastopamā*) and poetic reversals (*pratīpa*);
however, it is not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive length. Furthermore, this occurs at the beginning (*āmukha*), and not at the conclusion.
Regarding the phrase "the cognition of a simile":
since the elided suffix *kvip* is employed precisely for that purpose,
one should not argue that this cannot be considered *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) because of the absence of an explicit expressive word (*vācaka*) here.
Indeed, the mere possibility or impossibility of a denotative word is not the sole determinant for the existence or non-existence of figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).

For if it were so, in the case of "disguised praise" (*vyājastuti*), even though censure and the like are expressed, the cognition of the unstated praise and so forth—which results in the status of a figure—would not be established.
Therefore, the sentence-meaning itself, when fully developed, is the proof that establishes the essential nature of the figures of speech.

Furthermore, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is entirely distinct from the comprehension occurring at the time of the syntactic connection of word-meanings; this is due to the possibility [of such a distinction] and propriety (*aucitya*).

The meaning is that while the presence of the subject (the *viṣayin*, such as a musk-tilaka) on a surface like the forehead is possible and occurs according to propriety, it is not so for the object (the *viṣaya*, such as a blue throat).

Therefore, as for what others have stated—that this simile contains a *pariṇāma* (transformation) because the subject (*prakṛta*) is transformed into the form of the non-subject (*aprakṛta*), such as musk-paste and so forth—that reveals their ignorance of the true nature of *pariṇāma*.

Its essential nature is not merely "appropriateness" (*aucitya*), but rather its utility to the subject as previously described. And such appropriateness is not incompatible with poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Because that [identification] exists everywhere, it culminates in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). For, since the luster of the throat itself is perceived as the musk-tilaka and so forth, there is an apprehension of non-difference through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object by the subject; thus, there is an absence of the comprehension of similarity (*sādṛśya*).
Similarity resides in both [the subject and the object].
Furthermore, there is no cognition here of the contextual and the non-contextual as being unified.
By the phrase "as for example," its abundance in illustrative instances is shown.
That [simile], however, which is observed in the domain of expressing a complete simile (*samastopamā*),
is as follows:
"May that [deity] with feet like staffs protect you, crushing the staff-like feet of Caṇḍīkā."
The crescent moon, shimmering before him, attains a weight comparable to a fraction of the tip of a balance-beam.

In this case, although the word *tulā* (balance/simile) is present, because there is the cognition of the crescent moon alone as the "end of the balance-beam" (*tulākoṭi*), it is a case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
An example of *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (fancy with concealment) is as follows:
"When the city's playful women had hurriedly reached the bank [of the river] due to the collision with a whale..."
Where the Siprā river shines as if with loud bursts of laughter, under the guise of its shimmering garland of foam.
In this case, "possibility" (saṃbhāvanā) is understood through the greatness of the word *eva*, and "denial" (apahnava) is understood through the use of the word *chala*.
The same should be understood when words such as *chadman* are employed.
In examples such as "another Indra," where the word *apara* is not used, this is simply a simile (*upamā*).

However, when that [word *iva*] is employed, since there is the possibility of an identification (*adhyavasāya*) based on the perception of the subject at hand—the king—as Indra (*pākaśāsana*), and because its status as something to be established (*sādhyatva*) is perceived through the word *iva*, this is indeed a case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

When the word *iva* and others are not employed, because the identification is already established (*siddhatva*), it is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). But when both the words *iva* and another [such as *manye*] are not employed, it is metaphor (*rūpaka*).

Thus, within this variety of *utprekṣā* existing in its different modes, in the case of *hetūtprekṣā* (causal fancy), that property (*dharma*) belonging to the subject which one fancies as the cause is, by virtue of the process of identification (*adhyavasāya*), treated as non-different from it and adopted as the ground for the fancy.
And that [property] is necessarily expressed (*vācya*) alone.
Otherwise, with respect to what would there be a cause?
As in the example, "As if not seeing each other," and so forth;
here, the non-seeing is imagined as the cause for the emaciation—which is presented as being connected to the two cheeks, the subjects under discussion.
