The cause-and-effect relationship and the attainment of a state of exhaustion constitute the *nimitta* (ground) therein.
Thus, in the verse "It appeared as if bound in silence due to the pain of separation from your lotus-feet," the cause of the silence residing in the anklet is its state of being pained;
in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of that [silence], silence itself should be understood as the *nimitta*.
The same applies everywhere.
For example, by using the word *chadman* (disguise):
"Your forehead shines, covered by a multitude of drops of perspiration."
"By the god of love, her breast-region, though priceless, was perceived as if it had already been offered for a price."

And because there is a difference in cognition based on the employment or non-employment of various specific words, he says "the other," etc., in order to demonstrate its distinction from the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*s).
"In the employment of that" means in the employment of the word "other.
Because of the non-employment of the word *iva*, which indicates possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) and so forth, [the comparison] is established as a fact.
For this very reason, there is no mention of the object (*viṣaya*) here at all.
For it was stated immediately prior that if the object were mentioned, it would be a *rūpaka* (metaphor) involving a firm superimposition (*dṛḍhāropa*).
On the other hand, in all other cases, it is indeed proper to mention the object.

Thus, he demonstrates the nature of the cause, the essence, and the effect of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), which exists through such a variety of divisions, as appropriate, beginning with the words "tadevam" and so forth.
"That property" (*sa dharmaḥ*) refers to that very thing toward which the cause is poetically fancied.
"By virtue of identification" (*adhyavasāyavaśāt*) means by resorting to non-difference even where there is difference.
"Undifferentiated" means by way of a property not connected to the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*).
"That" refers to the property resorted to as the cause (*nimitta*).
"Necessarily" means...
The meaning is that it never becomes inexpressible again.
"Otherwise" means in the case of its being inexpressible.
"Against what [would there be] a counter-reason? means this.
Because that very [cause] is the nature of the fruit;
for it is not logical that the very thing which is conceived as the cause should itself be inexpressible,
since a means of proof (sādhana) would otherwise result in being without an object, in the absence of that which is to be proven (sādhya).
And if this [object] were merely a cause (*nimitta*), it would follow that it is both expressible and inexpressible.
Thus, it is established that a single property can be both the cause and the effect of that which is being conceptualized from the perspective of the reason.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "not seeing," and so forth.
In this context, "itihetu" refers to the imaginative conception [of a cause].
It is called the "cause" because the imaginative conception cannot be established without it.
Here, there are two kinds of emaciation: that produced by austerity and that produced by non-perception.
Due to the force of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), these two are resorted to as non-different.
For this reason, a single property alone serves as both the cause (*nimitta*) and the fruit (*phala*).
In reality, however, that which is produced by austerity (*tapas*) possesses the nature of the cause, while the other possesses the nature of the fruit.
Therefore, there is no fault of mutual dependence,
because both are distinct; thus,
it is simply silence.
The meaning is that there is nothing else whatsoever.
And for this reason, silence—whether produced by immobility and so forth or produced by suffering—is adopted without distinction.
By the word "everywhere," it is stated that the description of the nature of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the cause is not in conflict with any of the objects of characterization (lakṣya).

Having thus demonstrated the nature of the *hetūtprekṣā* (causal fancy) as far as possible, he now demonstrates the nature of the *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the essential form) as well, beginning with the words "In the *svarūpotprekṣā*...

In a *svarūpotprekṣā*, where a subject (*dharmī*) is fancied as being situated within another subject, the attribute (*dharma*) serving as the ground for that fancy is sometimes explicitly mentioned, as in the verse beginning "May that drum protect you... (*sa vaḥ pāyādunduḥ*).
In this context, qualities such as crookedness (*kuṭulatva*) are indeed explicitly mentioned;
however, in examples such as "like the shore of the ocean of passion," qualities such as being a cause of agitation are understood through implication.

Furthermore, where a quality itself is imagined as residing in the subject (*dharmī*), there too [the distinction between *sopahitam* and *nirupahitam*] depends on whether the ground (*nimitta*) is explicitly stated or not.
Regarding *upādāna* (appropriation), as it is said:
"When he was established in this [state] without having yet received consecration,
the earth— its knowledge being erased— trembled as if overwhelmed by fear."
In this instance, regarding the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) that [the darkness] is overwhelmed by fear because it has reached the ground, the cause—trembling and so forth—is explicitly stated.
As for the case where it is not stated, consider "The darkness, as if smeared, [covers] the limbs," and so on.
Here, in the poetic fancy that the darkness acts as the agent of the action of smearing because it pervades [the body], the cause—such as spreading—is merely implied.
In cases such as malice (*vyāpāda*), however, another cause would have to be sought for the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Furthermore, it is not logical for the subject (*viṣaya*) itself to be what is merely implied (*gamyamāna*); for since that subject serves as the locus of the fancied state, it is appropriate that it be explicitly expressed (*abhidhātum ucita*) as the topic at hand (*prastuta*).
Therefore, what has been stated is indeed correct.

Even though, by the mere mention [of the definition], it is understood that in the case of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature), there is both the taking up and the non-taking up of a cause (*nimitta*), nevertheless, with the intention that just as in *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the cause) the taking up of a cause is possible, so too here [in *svarūpotprekṣā*] it should not be considered possible, this has been stated again here.

And when a quality (*dharma*) is here imagined as being inherent in another substratum (*dharmyantara*), one might wonder what the nature of the cause (*nimitta*) would be in that case; anticipating this doubt, he says "where... and so forth.
"The quality itself" means it is not the substratum (*dharmī*) that is [imagined] as being inherent in another substratum.
The meaning is "by way of being the substratum for the property-possessor" (*dharmibhittitayā*).
For here, having suppressed the fact that the property-possessor possesses other properties, its status as possessing internal properties is established.
Therefore, in this case, the object [of the cognition] exists by virtue of being the substratum for the property-possessor.
Since it is impossible to establish a property (*dharma*) alone without its substratum (*dharmin*), or else, if it were being established as something distinct, it would itself become the substratum;
in reality, however, it is the property alone that is the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*),
by the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of which the non-difference of the subject (*viṣayin*) is determined.
And that swallowed attribute (dharma) is sometimes expressed and sometimes unexpressed.

In examples such as "having attained consecration" (*prāpyābhiṣekam*), others consider [the cause] to be a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of a cause); thus, it is illustrated by another example: "Like a mountain peak struck by fresh rain, firm, supportless, and compact... (*navarosadalia-ghaṇaniravalaṃba-saṃghaḍia-taḍikaḍappavva*).
The neck of the man-lion, with its tawny manes, is victorious.
Victorious is the neck-seizing grip of Narahari, whose tawny mane is like a mass of lightning flashing from clouds shattered by the wrath of men.

Here, having suppressed (nigīrya) the quality of possessing filaments in that which possesses the property of being bound at the neck, the state of being like a mass of lightning is poetically imagined (utprekṣita).
Furthermore, the cause—tawny color—is explicitly mentioned.
And the suppressed attribute is presented as residing in the substratum.
"In the case of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the agency of the act of smearing," that is to say, when such an implication is suspected;
for in this way, there would be the cognition: "as if it were the smearing of darkness."
Nor should one suspect that this is not the case here; thus he says, "because of pervading," and so forth.
"Another cause" refers to such qualities as the power of concealment.

By means of that [cause], having swallowed the contrary property (*vidharma*)—namely, the act of pervading—in relation to the subject (*dharmin*) which is darkness, the property consisting of being the agent of the action of smearing is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*). This is the meaning.
As the illustrious Mammaṭa has said:
"Pervasion and so forth are conceived in the form of smearing and so forth.

And where, by the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of another attribute, an attribute itself is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the substratum (*dharmibhittitayā*), there, because the subject (*dharmin*)—which constitutes the locus—is the very foundation, its status as being implied follows the principle just stated.
He says "it is not tenable" with the words "na ca" and so forth.

"Of the object" (viṣayasya) means of the substratum (dharmī), which serves as the basis for the two properties that are being swallowed up [in the metaphor] and being poetically imagined (utprekṣyamāṇa).
But it should not be explained as "of that which is being swallowed," for it was stated immediately prior that it is twofold by virtue of being either appropriated or non-appropriated;
and that has already been illustrated.
Or as it is said:
"That which, like a white lotus, or like the moon itself, or like a pair of blue lotuses risen upon a single stalk,
or having reached the root of a treasure of rubies— has been perfectly won by the power of my fortune for my two eyes."
Here, because the mouth and other [features] which are the objects of the poetic conceit (utprekṣā) are not explicitly mentioned, they are to be understood through implication (*gamyamānatva*).
"Of that" refers to the object in the form of a substratum (*dharmin*). "As the conceived locus" means as the basis upon which the conceit is projected.

"By way of being the imagined substratum" means by way of being the foundational basis for the imagined property of "smearing," which has been made the object of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) through the suppression of its actual properties such as "pervasion.
This is because a property cannot find its rest without a substratum.
"Of that which is under discussion" means "of that which must necessarily be expressed.

In this way, even in the cases of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a result), by suppressing (*nigīrya*) the fact that they have as their cause another property belonging to the subject itself (*dharmi*), it is determined that they have as their cause another property and as their result another property.

Therefore, that subject (dharmin) must indeed be expressed, because of the logical justification already stated. Furthermore, when it is swallowed up [in a metaphorical expression], the property (dharma) itself is twofold, depending on whether it is explicitly mentioned or not.
That is as follows: "This is a dry land," and so forth.
Here, regarding the subject (dharmin) of the anklet, its silence is caused by its immobility; this [causal] property is being suppressed (nigīryamāṇa) and is not explicitly mentioned.
However, when it is explicitly mentioned (upātta), it is as follows:
The cakravāka bird, eager for endearments with his beloved,
pulled at the lotus fiber resting on his beak as if it were the mechanical string that causes their mutual separation.

In this instance, having swallowed (nigīrya) the fact that the Cakravāka bird’s longing for amorous dalliance is the cause [of its behavior], the status of being the cause of error (bhrānti-hetutva) is superimposed (adhyavasita). Furthermore, the swallowed attribute (dharma) is explicitly mentioned (upātta);
however, when it is not explicitly mentioned (anupātta), it is as follows:
At that time, the night-lotuses, full of joy,
blossomed as if to behold the withered state of the day-lotus caused by her separation from her husband.

Here, having suppressed (nigīrya) the fact that the blooming of the night-lilies is caused by the rising of the moon, their "seeing" is imagined as the result. Furthermore, the suppressed attribute is not explicitly mentioned.

Thus, having demonstrated the nature of the cause and the essential form [of the object] as they occur, he demonstrates the poetic fancy of the result (phalotprekṣā) as well, beginning with the words "In the poetic fancy of the result... and so forth.
In the case of a poetic fancy regarding an effect (*phalotprekṣā*), that which is its cause is itself the motive (*nimitta*).
If that were not mentioned, of what could it be stated to be the effect?
Therefore, in that instance, there is simply the mention of that motive, and no other alternative.
For example:
"As if for the turning back of ancient steeds standing upon their chariots,
the sun set out toward the northern direction, the land of his own birth."
In this case, going toward the northern direction is taken as the very cause (*nimitta*)—that is, the reason—for the result of turning the horse.
The word "of that" refers to the result.

Furthermore, since this meaning is understood from the commentary on the section concerning the investigation of the poetic fancy of cause (*hetūtprekṣā*), I shall not labor over it again for fear of excessive prolixity.
Thus, casting a side-glance at his own self-praise, the author concludes this [section]:

"Therefore, although this classification of the levels of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) exists in great abundance within the objects of literary description (*lakṣya*), it has not been elaborated upon here because it is difficult to discern.
Furthermore, just like words such as *iva*, the word *manye* is also an indicator of that [fancy]."
However, in the absence of the complete set of conditions for *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), I maintain that the employment of the word *manye* (I think) expresses nothing but *vitarka* (speculation).
This is as was previously illustrated by the example beginning, "I think the moon [is] your enemy’s separation," and so forth.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "tadasau" (that one...):
And he demonstrates the formal arrangement of its expressive function with the words "of that" and so forth.
"The absence of the state of being the foremost in poetic fancy" is due to the absence of the nature of the cognitive state consisting of imaginative probability (*saṃbhāvanā*).
"Previously" refers to [the discussion on] concealment (*apahnuti*).
The particle *eva* also sometimes expresses *vitarka* (speculative doubt) alone;
for example:
"When he had fashioned her two beautiful shanks, which were rounded, tapering, and not too long..."
In the process of fashioning her remaining limbs, it was as if the Creator exerted a fresh effort to produce beauty itself.
And this [figure], consisting of various types of hyperboles (*atiśayokti*) such as "non-difference in difference," is also observed.
Among these, an example of non-difference in difference is found in the *Pṛthvīrājavijaya*:
"By those receiving a succession of *bāṇa*-lingas with supreme devotion..."
By his armies, the Narmadā was made to be without the Narmadā.
In this case, there is a distinction despite non-difference, and a lack of connection despite a connection, as follows:
"May that non-duality belong to you for the nourishment of the non-duality of consciousness; may it not belong to the two bodies of the Lord of the Daughter and the Consort of Ramā."
Wherein the Enemy of Cities, as if perceiving his own blackness through the splendors of the southern half of his body, wipes away the blackness within even others.
In this case, there is a non-connection even where a connection with blackness exists.
An example of a connection where there is no connection is as follows:
"As if the moon were washed in milk, and as if the sky were cleansed by indigo."
Like the sun scratched by a chisel, it blossomed forth like the milk of spring.
In this case, although there is no actual connection such as being washed with milk or ghee, a connection is [figuratively] established.
Regarding the simultaneity of cause and effect, for example:
"Born together with fame, he grew up together with prosperity."
"He arose together with splendor itself; he emerged together with renunciation itself."
An example of the reversal of sequence is as follows:
"The arrows seem to fly forth first, and only afterwards does he raise his bow;
the subsequent blows seem to converge, and they seem to abandon the life-breaths of the enemy beforehand."
This [causal relation] is also observed even when there is a reversal between cause and effect, as for example:

"This is the river Candraprasūti, whose banks are filled with flowers dropped by the creepers that are distracted by their one-pointed devotion to the Lord’s arrow, which has been continuously raining down since time immemorial;
through the pretext of its clusters of white lotuses, it seems to constantly produce hundreds of full-moon discs upon both its shores."
In this case, there is a reversal of cause and effect regarding the birth of the moon from the Narmadā.
This is also seen through a reversal of sequence, as for example:
"Shining with a sprout-like lower lip jagged with a smile of immense pride..."
Having arisen, he has as it were instantly drunk up the milk-white glories of his enemies.
In this case, because the drinking of fame (*yaśaḥ-pāna*), which occurs immediately after its origination, is mentioned first, there is a reversal of the sequence.
However, in the reading "drinking as it were loudly" (*pibann ivoccais*) within this very same context, the two sequential events are simultaneous.

Having thus determined that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) exists when the process of identification (*adhyavasāya*) is yet to be accomplished, he defines *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) as occurring when that identification is already established:
"But when the identified [object] is predominant, it is *atiśayokti*. (RuAss 23)

In the process of determination (*adhyavasāna*), three factors are possible: its own nature (*svarūpa*), the object (*viṣaya*), and the subject (*viṣayin*). For when the object is swallowed up within by the subject, the own-nature of the determination arises. In that regard, when [the determination] is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the own-nature is predominant.
When [the object] is established as accomplished, however, there is the predominance of what has been determined (*adhyavasita*).
The predominance of the objective referent (*viṣaya*) is simply not possible within the act of determination itself;
rather, it is when there is the predominance of what has been determined that *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) occurs.
And there are five other types:
non-difference within difference,
and difference within non-difference.
There is non-connection where there is connection; there is connection where there is no connection;
and there is the destruction of the temporal sequence between cause and effect.
Concluding this and introducing another point, he says "evam" and so forth.
To characterize that very [cognition], he says "adhyavasita" and so forth.
To explain this very point, he first shows the essential nature of determination (*adhyavasāya*) as far as possible, saying "adhyavasāne."

Anticipating the objection that since determination (*adhyavasāya*) cannot be established as residing in either [the subject or the object] mutually, what would be its relation to the object and the subject, he says: "For, of the object," and so forth.
The meaning is that without both the object and the subject, determination itself does not come into being.
He demonstrates the distinction between these very [terms] with the passage beginning "In that regard" (*tatra*).
In this context, "among the three" refers to the selection [of one].
"Primacy of the essential nature" means primacy of the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*). "Primacy of the determined object" means primacy of the objective correlate (*viṣayin*).
Furthermore, the status of being the "probandum" (sādhyatva) has already been determined in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) alone;
it is simply not possible [in *adhyavasāya*] because the very nature of *adhyavasāya* does not arise.
Thus, he says "adhyavasita," etc., to explain that when the predominance of the subject (*viṣayin*) is intended to be expressed, it constitutes a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
And it is said elsewhere:
"This [metaphor] is intended when there is the cognition that [the object] is to be accomplished through determination;
but when there is the cognition of its already being accomplished, the understanding would be that of hyperbole (atiśayokti)."
Thus [it is said].
The word "five" is for the purpose of excluding numbers both less than or greater than that;
therefore, it should not be said that the destruction of the sequence of cause and effect is included within the fourth variety [of the non-existence of the effect],
for in that case, all other varieties would likewise be included therein.

If it is argued that [the cognition] occurs because it is based on a relation even when no relation such as non-difference exists, we say: no. For although in reality there is non-difference and so forth everywhere, [the cognition does not arise].

For you yourselves have stated: "Although a relation can indeed be described as a relation within a non-relation (*asaṃbandhe saṃbandha*), nevertheless, because it has been characterized by others with a desire to express its internal subdivisions, and because a distinct relation within a non-relation has been demonstrated, it has been set forth separately.
Since this follows the same logic, how could it be reasonable for this [type of relation] to be included within the fourth subdivision?

Now, if it is maintained that a fifth variety [of *asambandha*] is intended here because of such a figurative representation— even though there is no simultaneity due to the destruction of the priority and posteriority between cause and effect— then a sixth variety must also be reckoned because of such a representation even when there is no difference in location, since there is no distinction in the relation of objects to space and time. Thus, because it lacks a valid object, there is an absence of *asambandha*.
If it is argued that [this] follows as a logical consequence (*prasajyate*), we say no;

because in *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), with the desire to convey the purpose known as "excess," the predominance of the superimposed object (*viṣayin*) is intended through the swallowing up of the original object (*viṣaya*).

In the case of non-apprehension (*asagati*), however, there is no dispute that both possess a difference in definition, namely that cause and effect exist in different locations, in order to convey their mutual contradiction.

Furthermore, when the temporal sequence of cause and effect is sublated—by concealing the priority and posteriority between the cause, which is the heart’s affliction produced by the beloved, and the effect, which is the longing produced by the god of love—the [poet] expresses it thus: "By the mere sight of you, through a turning away from other objects..."

Since it is determined that she has become intent solely on the desire for you— this being an *adhyavasita* (poetic determination) of a contrary state intended to demonstrate an excellence (*atiśaya*) of purpose—
it is logical that this is a variety of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), and not a variety of *asaṃgati* (incongruity).
For in that case [of incongruity]—
The hero tied the loosened tresses of the tremulous-eyed woman with garlands of campaka flowers;
thus, resentment took firm root in the hearts of those fawn-eyed women who were his rivals.
In such cases as "the hair-tuft is bound" and "there is steadiness of resentment in their hearts," there is a difference of locus between cause and effect;
for where the binding occurs, there alone its effect—steadiness—is logically possible, which gives rise to the cognition of contradiction.
And here, this contradiction is merely apparent.

This is because there arises a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*)—known as the actual existence of a causal relationship between the hair-knot (*dhammilla-bandha*) and steadfastness—which demonstrates that they are, in reality, related as cause and effect.

Furthermore, it is not the case that a contradiction remains unperceived even when such a subversion occurs; for, like the perception of two moons, that cognition persists only as a faltering one, being inherently untenable.
Furthermore, there is no "stumbling" (skhaladgati) in hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), because its very nature is that of certainty; thus, there is not even the possibility of suspecting its impossibility.
For what is intended here is not the subversion of the temporal sequence between cause and effect, but rather that "this is the result in such a manner."

For this very reason, because of the lack of connection (*asaṃgati*) and the presence of poetic hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), there is also a difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*). Thus, it is only as previously stated that [the definition] is correct: "The lack of connection" consists in the destruction of the temporal sequence between cause and effect, while "poetic hyperbole" consists in their being located in different places. For this same reason, it has been said: "The two sprouts of the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*) regarding cause and effect are those wherein there is either a reversal of the temporal sequence or a simultaneous arising."
Thus, what has been stated by others in such passages is indeed incorrect; therefore, there is no deficiency in the number of its varieties.
Furthermore, some maintain that because all ornaments are actually subdivisions of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), this [ornament] possesses many varieties.
For instance, even in the case of *upamā* (simile), this status of being a subdivision exists.
Since there can be no surpassing of excellence when something with inferior qualities, such as a face, is compared to something with superior qualities, such as the moon—
and since there would be no poetic ornament (alaṅkāra) in cases like "the gavaya is like a cow" without such surpassing—
it is said that "exaggeration (atiśayokti) alone is considered the sole ornament of poetry," because it is the seed of all poetic ornaments.
This is not so;

for in this context, there are two possible ways in which excellence (atiśaya) functions: either it takes the form of a universal produced by the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*), such as "difference being non-difference," or it takes the form of a particular (*viśeṣa*).
Among these, the first is accepted by all as the seed of every ornament (*alaṅkāra*);
for otherwise, even such [comparisons] as "the gavaya is like a cow" would constitute an ornament.
However, it is not tenable that all ornaments are merely subdivisions of this [first type].
For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of even *viśeṣokti*, *ullekha*, and so forth [being considered *atiśayokti*],
since all poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) possess the nature of *viśeṣokti* and *ullekha*. If it is argued on the basis of the second alternative, that too has already been refuted.
For its defining characteristic is the predominance of the determined [meaning],
and that is not possible in the case of poetic figures (alaṅkāras),
because such a state is not perceived there.
Therefore, since these [individuals] cannot possibly possess that generality (*sāmānya*), how could they be its particulars? Thus, its manifoldness is refuted.
In that regard, non-difference within difference is as follows: "The lotus is not in water; the blue lotuses are in the lotus; those [three] are on a golden creeper."
And she is so delicate and lovely—what is this succession of auspicious omens?
Here, there is a non-difference [asserted] between the face and so forth and the lotus and so forth, despite their difference.
Regarding the phrase "of the face and so forth":
it refers to the face and so forth, but not to actual beauty as compared with the lotus and so forth.

But not by means of the beauty imparted by the poet. For this very reason, we conclude that the subsequent portion of the text— from "In this case, [there is] that called *atiśaya*," etc., up to "the predominance belongs to the object of identification (*adhyavasita*)"— has been written otherwise by scribes out of their own intellectual whims, despite having been intended for that specific purpose.
It is a well-known and undisputed fact that this portion was written by certain later scholars on slips of paper (patrikā) after the author [of the original work] had passed away.

Consequently, due to their lack of attention—whether because it was a digression from another work or because it was deemed unnecessary—this fragmentary section, which is for the most part inconsistent, was written from other slips.

It is certainly not the case that at that very same time, in one and the same place, having stated that there is non-difference despite the difference of the face and so forth from the lotus and so forth, [the author] would have then said: "But not... [and so on].

The statement that "the determination of non-difference between the face and the lotus, and so forth, is to be applied" and so on, is inconsistent with its own earlier and later parts; such a thing could not be imagined from this author who possesses great learning.
An example of difference within non-difference is as follows:
"Her loveliness is of another kind, and her manner of speech is some unique charm;
that Sāmā does not merely possess the common beauty of a courtesan."
"O Lord of Beings, there exists another kind of beauty and some other sort of grace of deportment; even a mere outline of a dark-complexioned woman does not occur elsewhere."

In this case, although there is no difference between qualities such as *laḍahatva* (gracefulness) and the rest, they appear distinct because they are treated as different [qualities]. Or, for example: "When the path is gained, when it is forcibly kissed, and when it is approached by the lover—though it is but a single beloved’s mouth, the variations in flavor differ from one another."
"Even upon the single lip of a beloved— one obtained on the road, one received by force, and one offered by herself— there arise different varieties of aesthetic flavor."
Here, although the nectar of the beloved’s lip is non-different [from the speaker], it is presented as distinct through a division of objects.
An example of non-relation where there is a relation is as follows:
"The expenditure of the wealth of beauty was not reckoned; great suffering was voluntarily endured; a fever of anxiety was produced in the heart of a person wandering at will."
This poor girl too is ruined by the absence of a lover worthy of her own virtues; what purpose was placed in the mind of the Creator while he fashioned her slender form?

Here, although there is a connection between the expenditure of the wealth of loveliness and [the creation of this woman], a lack of connection (*asaṃbandha*) is established for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the slender woman’s loveliness.

Or, for example: "In the act of her creation, was the Moon the Creator, the bestower of beauty? Or was it Love himself, whose sole essence is passion? Or was it the month of spring, the source of flowers? How else could the ancient sage [Brahmā], dulled by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from sensual objects, have been able to fashion this heart-stealing form?"
In this case, although there is a connection with the creation of the ancient Prajāpati, a lack of connection is stated. An example of a connection where there is no connection is as follows:
"If a flower were placed upon a new leaf, or if a pearl were set within a bright coral..."
Then he should imitate that clear smile of hers, whose ruddy luster spread across her lips.

In this case, the connection is through possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), as for example: "Burning that cooks the streams of water; thick vapor rising from the nose; sighs that cause the bright flames of the lamps to flicker; a body submerged in pallor—what can I say while suffering? Her condition persists throughout the entire night, with her hand acting as a parasol to ward off the moonlight at the edge of the path where you travel."
In this context, although there is no actual connection between burning, the lamp, water, spreading, and so forth, a connection is stated as if it were established.
Regarding the phrase "of loveliness and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (ādi), only "turning" and "shadow" are included.
In that very case, although there is non-difference, a distinction is intended;

for in the second half [of the verse], even where there is a connection, there is a lack of connection. The observation of the purpose—that the three quarters of the verse beginning with "the expenditure of the wealth of beauty was not reckoned" are for the sake of demonstrating the excellence of the slender lady's beauty—is intended as an illustration applicable to all examples.
"By way of conventional designation," but not in reality.
Precisely because the relationship is not real, he states another example: "Fire is water," and so forth.
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction.
The destruction of the temporal sequence of cause and effect occurs either through a reversal of that sequence or through their simultaneity.
An example of such a reversal is as follows:
"O beloved of women, her heart was first occupied by the arrow of the flower-bowed god,
and only afterwards did it come within the range of your eyes."
An example of simultaneity (*tulyakālatva*) is as follows:
"The time has arrived—dense with restless clouds, and with forest breezes fragrant with *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, and *nīpa* flowers; alas, the wives of travelers have been lost!"

And here, by the phrase "the destruction of the priority and posteriority of cause and effect," three distinct varieties are stated by means of *tantra* (a single word serving multiple functions): first, the destruction or reversal of the well-known relationship between cause and effect; second, the destruction or inversion of their priority and posteriority—that is, the sequence established as occurring at earlier and later times; and third, their simultaneous occurrence (*sahabhāva*).
And thus, there are also five types of the destruction of cause and effect.
Because these are intermediate sub-types, their fivefold nature was previously explained by incorporating a restrictive rule.
Among those, the inversion of cause and effect is as follows:
"True and false, with its inner core, the essence of the moonlight—
the thousand-petaled [lotus]— the Sarasvatī declares the cause of the Lord of Aris."
"Such a brilliant, yet shrinking,
cause for the moonbeams and the thousand-petaled lotus of the lake."
Here, in the contraction of the moon’s beauty, the hundred-petaled lotus is determined to be the cause by way of inversion.

In this case, there exists a *hetu* (cause) consisting of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) in the form of "non-difference where there is difference. In the latter half, however, that same [hyperbole] is the cause, based on the use of words with double meanings (*śliṣṭa-śabda*).
And here, the connection with such a state is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the speaker’s beauty.
An example of the reversal of sequence is as follows:
"First, O angry one, knowledge becomes darkened; then, the frown."
In the beginning, passion assails the senses;
last of all, the eye;
first, ascetic heat ebbs away, and afterwards the water of perspiration.
"First, infamy spreads; immediately after, the lower lip [quivers].
Here, regarding the effects of anger—such as the knitting of the eyebrows and so forth—the sequence of their becoming darkened and so on is swallowed up (negated), and their reversal is superimposed.
An example of that same [reversal] occurring in simultaneity is as follows:
In the palaces of the moon-faced women, the attendants emerge from their mouths, the jeweled girdles from their hips,
and modesty from their hearts.
"From the pleasure-houses the attendants depart, from the hips the smooth jeweled girdles, and from the hearts shame— all these flee together at once from the moon-faced women."
In this case, although the departure of the attendants and others occurs sequentially, simultaneity is superimposed [upon it].
Thus, in order to show that all these varieties have as their object that which transcends worldly possibility, he says:
"Among these five varieties, the statement of non-difference and so forth regarding difference has as its scope that which transcends the world."

Therefore, in this context, there is an identification of non-difference regarding that result called "excellence" (*atiśaya*), which serves as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) because it is the motivator. For instance, in such examples as "A lotus in what is not water," although there is a factual difference between the face and the lotus, the actual beauty of the face is identified with the beauty imparted by the poet; this identification of non-difference is the cause for speaking of them as non-different despite their difference.
And since the determination (*adhyavasāya*) is established therein, the primacy belongs to that which is determined.

However, one should not apply the determination of non-difference (*abheda-adhyavasāya*) of speech and so forth with lotuses and so forth, because this would fail to encompass cases such as "difference within non-difference" (*abhede bheda*).

For in that instance, in the passage beginning with "another charmingness" (*aṇṇaṃ laḍahattaṇaaṃ*), an excellence of charm is identified with [the object] through a distinction that serves as the cause for the identification (*adhyavasita*).
This should be understood similarly in other cases as well.
It is precisely with this intention that the predominance of the identified [object] is asserted.

Among the five types [of causal relation], that type which exists by way of the relationship between cause and effect will be defined for the sake of detailed exposition in the section on figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) based on causality.
Regarding the phrase "among these" (*eṣu*) and so forth:
"among these" (*eṣu*) is the locative case denoting the sphere of objects (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
And this is the definition of its components:
"transcending the world.
The meaning is that their object is exclusively a superior entity fashioned by the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) of the poet.
Regarding the phrase "herein" (atra), it refers to this fivefold division.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of collecting other objects of cognition (prameya).
"The fruit" (phala) [is as follows].
Because it is precisely that [beauty] which is intended to be expressed;
"therein" means in the statement of non-difference between the beauty of one who has vomited out [his own] beauty and the beauty bestowed by the poet.

One might object: "But here, the superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) of the lotus and so forth upon the face and so forth is perceived; how then can this [definition] be stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But not... and so forth.
Furthermore, one might ask: "And why is there no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in those cases? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For in that case... and so forth.

For in the verse "The lotus is not in the water," if the application of the superimposition of non-difference were made with respect to the subjects (*dharmin*), such as the face and so forth, then because that [superimposition] is intended to reside precisely in the subject, there would be no lack of pervasion here with respect to the attributes (*dharma*).

Therefore, the intended meaning is that in the preceding [definition], the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the properties (*dharma*) must be applied so that there may be only one single position (*pakṣa*) throughout;
and this is merely an illustration,
for its defining characteristic is the predominance of the determined object.
And whether that [non-difference] belongs to the substrata (*dharmin*) or to the attributes (*dharma*), what distinction is there by which there would be non-pervasion?
On the contrary, if one accepts the determination of non-difference between two attributes, it would follow that even similes (*upamā*) and the like would be cases of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*),
because in those cases as well, there is an intended expression of non-difference despite the difference between the attributes themselves.

And thus, if there were a distinction based on being of a different class (*vijātīya*), it would follow that even two properties (*dharma*) would be distinct; therefore, enough with expounding upon the meaning of this incoherent text.
[The phrase] "for the sake of elaboration" (*prapañcārtham*) means for the sake of detailed exposition, but not for the sake of definitive determination (*nirṇaya*).
Because this has already been determined right here,
and the elaboration (*prapañca*) will be shown in that very place.
Concluding this, he introduces another point:
START Sūtra 24:
Having thus explained the two figures of speech based on *adhyavasāya* (poetic identification), the figures of speech based on implied comparison (*gamyamānaupamya*) are now stated.

Since these too are twofold—pertaining to the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) and pertaining to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*)—the two figures of speech pertaining to the meaning of a word are stated in succession:

When a comparison is implied, *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) occurs when there is a connection with a common attribute between the subjects under discussion and those not under discussion, by virtue of being inherent in the meanings of the words.
For when there is no explicit statement at the outset, the state of being understood [by implication] arises.

In that case, *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) occurs when contextual and non-contextual meanings are connected through common qualities or actions; it is one in which the meaning is already established.
For example:

The days, adorned with various kinds of fresh foliage and possessing a vivid crimson hue, attained their full growth; and the lotuses, blooming by the power of the sun’s rays, likewise reached their maturity.
Here, because the description of the season has been introduced, and because both the days and the lotuses are the subject matter (*prakṛta*), the action of "attaining growth" [is common to both].
The same applies to a quality (*guṇa*). For example:
"The yogic belt, the mass of matted hair, the bark of the *tāra* tree, and the deer-skin—
since these are appropriate for your limbs, let it now be said [what you seek]."
Appropriateness (*ucitatva*) is a poetic merit (*guṇa*). An example of [the use of] non-contextual elements is as follows:
"The army of your horses, rushing forward, fell into his mouth—[he whose body was as tender as the petals of a blue lotus]."
The dust of the defeated Gūrjara king was wiped away by some slender woman, and your fame was wiped away by your sword-blade.
In this instance, with respect to the Gūrjara king, the heroine and the sword are non-contextual (aprākaraṇika), while the act of wiping is the common action (kriyā).
An example of a common quality (guṇa) is as follows:
"In whose mind does the softness of your limbs not appear when seen?"
The hardness of the *mālatī* flower, the crescent moon, and the plantain tree!
Harshness is a merit.
Thus, this [figure of speech] has been explained as fourfold. [Sūtra:

If similarity is understood [rather than expressed by words], and there is a connection with a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) between two things—whether both are the subject (*prastuta*), both are the non-subject (*aprastuta*), or one is the subject and the other the non-subject—[it is *Dīpaka*].
[The figure] *tulyayogitā* occurs [in this case].
By the words "evam" and so forth, it is indicated that the basis for comparison is understood, because words such as "iva" (like) are not employed.
"Regarding the word *padārtham* (the meaning of a word): because the cognition of the meaning of a word is more immediate (*antaraṅga*) than the cognition of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*).
In that regard, he first states the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) with the words beginning *aupamya*."
He explains this very point with the words beginning with "iva" (like) and so forth.
In that context, "tatra" (therein) refers to when the comparison is implied.

Regarding the term "of the contextual [subjects]" (*prākaraṇikānām*), since the connection of a common property between two [subjects] is established by its very possibility, the use of the plural number is intended to include many subjects.
For this very reason, it should not be said that [the figure of speech] is for the purpose of grasping the comparison of many things;
because in the examples to be mentioned, the comparison of only two things is manifested. The same should be understood regarding *dīpaka* as well.
Regarding the term *anvitārthā* (having a connected meaning): this is because here there is a connection with things possessing common attributes (*samānadharmasaṃbandhin*).

By this very [definition], its fourfold nature through two types has been stated, owing to the connection of the subjects under discussion (*prakṛta*) and those not under discussion (*aprakṛta*) with a single attribute consisting of either a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*).
Nor should hyperbole (atiśayokti) be mentioned as its vitalizing element (*anuprāṇaka*),
because this figure occurs even without it in the examples to be cited later.
Furthermore, although there is an absence of comparison (*aupamya*) here, the author has cited two examples of "equality of qualities" (*guṇasāmya*) because they were cited by earlier writers.
Furthermore, where a comparison is perceived, that is illustrated as follows:
"O beloved, at this moment of emotional agitation caused by jealousy, it is fitting for you that there be a faltering in your gait, in your speech, and in your graceful movements."
Harshness (*ātrōcitattva*) is a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
An example of this when it concerns two things that are not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*) is as follows:
"While you remain for a very long time, unwearied in bearing the burden of the earth..."
O King, today the foremost of the serpents and the Tortoise are exceedingly happy.
In this instance, happiness is the quality (*guṇa*). Furthermore, some consider both the heroine and her lover to be contextual (*prākaraṇika*); thus, it is illustrated by another example as follows:

"By the rays from the nails of Śambhu, who was bowing down, Gaṅgā and the digit of the moon were established as his crest-jewels, thereby bringing about the state of being worthy of worship for all the worlds."

How can this pair of Umā’s feet—which bestow supreme bliss upon the virtuous and remove the calamities of those who are unfortunate—be attained by the fathers of daughters, for whom the Himalaya must be left far behind?
In this case, since only the two feet of the Blessed Lady are the objects of description, the Gaṅgā and the digit of the moon are non-contextual (aprakṛta).
And "bringing about" (āpādana) is an action.
This [figure] also occurs by way of the relationship between the original image and its reflection (bimba-pratibimba-bhāva).
For example:

"Where Śāradā delights in the thousand-petaled lotuses that are the mouths of the lords of poets, and where Ramā likewise takes pleasure in them; and where Sarasvatī, having mounted her own royal swans, stands playfully casting forth inconceivable words."
Here, there is the relationship of original and reflection between the two lotus-faces;
and with this very intention, the author has demonstrated its distinctiveness in the *Alaṃkāravārtika*:
as an example of its nature as a pure universal—
"Let there be two nurses near the palm tree for its growth:
one who yields milk, and the other, the mother of all prosperity."

Here, by the words "in this way" and so forth, [the author] concludes this point and introduces another. [He states that] in this case, the *prasravaṇa* (flowing forth) has the nature of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānyarūpatva*).
By the words "in this way" and so forth, [the author], while concluding this, introduces another [topic].
START Sūtra 25:

Having established *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) when the relevant (*prastuta*) and irrelevant (*aprastuta*) subjects are treated separately, *dīpaka* (illumination) is now described for when they are combined: "But *dīpaka* [occurs] when there are both relevant and irrelevant subjects. (RuAss 25)
The phrase "the understandability of the comparison" and so forth continues [from the previous definition].

Among the contextual (*prākaraṇika*) and non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika* [objects]), a common attribute (*samāno dharmaḥ*) mentioned in one of them serves—by its incidental application (*prasaṅgāt*)—to assist (*upakārāt*) the other; because it thus illuminates (*dīpanāt*), it gives rise to the figure of speech called *dīpaka*, which is similar to a lamp (*dīpa-sādṛśyena*).

In that case, since terms such as *iva* are not employed, the relationship of subject of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is to be understood through implication (*gamyamāna*).
And that [relation] is indeed real;
whereas in the former case, it is merely intentional— whether based on pure topicality or pure non-topicality—
since the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is brought about by topicality itself.
The designation "object" (*padārtha*) is used because of the connection of many [objects] with a single action and for the sake of propriety;

however, in reality, since it pertains to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), there are three varieties of this [figure], known as *ādidīpaka*, *madhyadīpaka*, and *antadīpaka*, according to whether the attribute occurs at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence.
Regarding the phrase "of those that are relevant and irrelevant":

"In one place" means in either the contextual or the non-contextual [subject]. "In another place" refers to the contextual subject and so forth; the suffix *-ka* (forming *dīpaka*) is applied here according to the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.97), because there is no name (*saṃjñā*) for the whole that is understood through similarity.

In this context, "dīpaka" (the illuminator) refers to the following: it is called "factual" (*vāstava*) because the subject at hand and the subject not at hand function respectively as the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
The phrase "in the previous [case]" refers to *tulyayogitā*.
By this, it is also shown that there is only this much difference between *dīpaka* and *tulyayogitā*;
however, on this account alone, it is not proper to establish separate definitions for these two.
Because the commonality known as "containing a simile" (aupamyagarbha) follows both [the subject and the object],
a separate definition would likewise be required for "combined simile" (samucitopamā) and other such figures; however,
the author has nonetheless provided them [separately] out of deference to the ancients.

Regarding the term *vaivakṣika* (dependent on the speaker's intention): the meaning is that wherever it is intended by the speaker to express either the state of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the state of being the object of comparison (*upameya*), that very point must be accepted based on the force of the context and other such factors.

Consequently, the underlying sense is that the relationship of standard and object of comparison does not arise solely on the basis of whether something is "unintroduced" (*aprastuta*) or "introduced" (*prastuta*), according to the principle: "For there is no observation of deviation [in the application] of what is already introduced by means of anything else."

Thus, according to the view that "simile (upamā) is considered the similarity of the unknown with the known," the relationship of the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) cannot be based solely on the distinction between being known and unknown. This is because, in instances such as "the water is like the sky, the sky is like the water," the relationship of upamāna and upameya is accepted even though both are equal and lack well-known qualities; thus, the proposed rule is shown to have exceptions. Now, one might object: "In this case, the common property (sādharmya) is perceived as residing in the meaning of the sentence as a whole; how then can it be said to reside in the meaning of the individual words? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "anekasya," etc.
The same should be understood for the preceding cases as well.
An example in sequence: "The sky shines with the sun, poetry with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), youth with vigor, the Lord of the Earth with nectar, and this world, O King, with you."
The sky is illuminated by the sun; poetry by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); youth by the god of love (*smara*); the lord of rivers by nectar; and this world by you, O Mother of Men.
Having purified the quarters of the sky with her wandering, at the end of the day,
the radiance of the sun— copper-red like the hue of a young leaf— and the sage’s cow both set out to go to their respective dwellings.
The wealth of misers, the crest-jewels of serpents, the manes of lions, and the breasts of noble women— how could these belong to those who are not immortal?
The wealth of the miserly, the crest-jewel of serpents, the manes of lions, the breasts of noble maidens, and the nectar of the immortals— from where can these be touched?

Thus, the three types of *dīpaka* involving a single action have been determined. And here, just as *dīpaka* occurs when a single action pertains to multiple factors (*kāraka*s), so too does *dīpaka* occur when a single factor pertains to multiple actions. For example:
Whose mind is not curious to assist the virtuous, to sustain prosperity, to travel through the sky, and to hear the life-stories of the great-souled ones?
Here, the mind is indicated as being distinguished by curiosity due to its agency in various actions such as providing assistance and so forth.
However, the *mālādīpaka* (garland-like illuminator) will be defined in another context by means of an illustration.
Since both the cow and the twilight are the subjects under discussion (*prakṛta*), others consider this to be *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing); therefore, it is illustrated with another example:
"For some it is spent through the pursuit of dharma, for some through the pursuit of wealth, and for some through the pursuit of pleasure; such indeed is the cycle of existence."
"For some, the cycle of existence passes away through the pursuit of dharma; for others, through the pursuit of wealth;
and for yet others, likewise, through the pursuit of sensual pleasure."
By the phrase "a single action" (*ekakriyam*), it is indicated that the *dīpaka* (illuminator) possessing a single quality (*ekaguṇa*) should also be illustrated by oneself;
for example: "Bearing a thousand hoods below and a thousand eyes in heaven..."
And you alone on earth bear a thousand names.
Non-duality (*advitīyatva*) is its quality.

Thus, having explained a single action or quality as residing in multiple factors of action (*kāraka*), and taking that very instance as an illustration, he states "here," etc., to show how even a single factor of action becomes a *dīpaka* by residing in multiple actions.
And here, that which is to be described—the exhalation—is the subject at hand, characterized by specific auxiliary causes such as the influence of Bhairavācārya and others.
This praise of general, irrelevant qualities—such as the poet’s performance of beneficial acts for others—is intended to enlighten the audience.
Since these general qualities are perceived as being mutually comparable by virtue of residing in a single agent, this is an instance of *kāraka-tulyayogitā* (similarity of agents).
Consequently, this is not an example of *kāraka-dīpaka* (illumination by agent).
For instance:
"To embrace the moon-faced woman, to drink nectar, to achieve fame, to acquire wealth,
and to instill in the heart a devotion to you that possesses the most excellent flavor— I consider a person who lacks zeal for these things to be nothing but a beast."
Here, a single person alone is indicated as the agent of various actions such as embracing and so forth;
the distinction between the relevant (prastuta) and the irrelevant (aprastuta) is quite evident.
She perspires, contracts, trembles, turns away, closes her eyes, and casts sidelong glances.
The newlywed bride rejoices within and desires to kiss [her husband] upon the bed.

In this instance, however, because the actions under discussion—such as tasting and so forth—are unified by virtue of residing in a single substratum, the figure of speech is *samuccaya* (conjunction), and not *kārakadīpaka* (the illuminator of the case-factor).
For the latter occurs when there is a presence of similarity (*aupamya*) between actions that are both relevant and irrelevant.
Likewise, even though all the actions are relevant here, the distinction from *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) arises precisely because conjunction lacks such similarity.
Even when a comparison is present, it is merely *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing). For example:
"He who practiced forbearance toward the weak and even toward those who were difficult to endure..."
And he who [acts] against those who are powerful, even though they are innocent, for years.
In this instance, both "taking" (karaṇa) and "seizing" (haraṇa) are the subjects under discussion,
as both are described as residing in the king.
This [type of comparison] also occurs through the relationship of the original image and its reflection (bimbapratibimbabhāva).
For example:
"A gem polished on a whetstone, a victor in battle slain by a weapon, the moon reflected in a water-jar, a young woman worn out by lovemaking,
an elephant whose rut has faded, a river in autumn with its sandy banks dried up— these shine with a beauty born of emaciation, as do men whose wealth has been exhausted for the sake of supplicants."
In this instance, there is a relationship of "original" (bimba) and "reflection" (pratibimba) between the qualities such as being licked by sandpaper and so forth.
An example of the nature of a pure universal (śuddhasāmānyarūpatva) is as follows:
"The Lord of Serpents, whose body is adorned with the jewels of his hoods, supports the earth."
O Lord, your arm-staff is adorned with the nails that have destroyed the pride of Rāvaṇa.

In this instance, "being radiant" (*rājitatva*) and "being beautiful" (*śobhitatva*) possess the nature of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānyarūpa*). Now, one might object: "Since 'cascading lamp' (*mālādīpaka*) has been defined by others immediately following this very [definition], why is it not also identified here? Anticipating this doubt, he says "chāyāntareṇa," etc.
"By another shadow" means by way of a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*).
"In another context" means because its form is augmented by a continuous chain of connections.
When a commonality existing as the meaning of the sentence is mentioned separately in two sentences, it is *prativastūpamā*.

Since the meaning of a sentence is composed of the meanings of its constituent words, the discussion of figures of speech pertaining to the sentence-meaning follows immediately after those pertaining to the word-meanings.

Among these, when a common attribute is expressed once through the employment of words such as *iva* and the like, it is a simile (*upamā*). It is likewise a simile even when the common attribute is expressed more than once through the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (the thing and its counterpart).
When there is a single mention without the use of "iva" and so forth, it is a simile (*upamā*).

However, when there is a non-single mention through the relationship of "thing and its counterpart" (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*), there is either the state of pure generality or the relationship of image and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*).
The first type is the simile by way of counterparts (*prativastūpamā*).

If the word *vastu* (thing) signifies the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), then simile (*upamā*) is its "similarity" (*sāmya*) with respect to each respective sentence-meaning; this is because the term is used according to its etymological derivation (*anvartha*). However, it is merely due to poetic convention (*kāvyasamaya*) that it is designated separately by means of another synonym.
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) will be discussed by resorting to the second type [of *vastu*].
Thus, based precisely on this reliance upon comparison, there is the *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence),
as in:
"Only the *cakorī* birds are clever in the act of drinking the moonlight."
Only those from Avanti are skillful in the art of love-play with beautiful women.

In this case, cleverness (caturatva) is indicated by the word "skillful" (nipuṇa) in the sentence concerning the object of comparison, whereas it is common to both in the sentence concerning the standard of comparison.
Furthermore, this [figure] occurs not only through similarity (sādharmya), but also through dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
As in this very same *Uttara-sthāna*, in the reading: "The women of Avanti are not skilled in the playful arts of love.
[Regarding the phrase] "the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*), etc.:
in order to explain this very point, he demonstrates its distinction from other figures of speech (alaṅkāras) with the words beginning "therein" (*tatra*).
In the example "By her he was both purified and adorned," there is a single mention [of the common property] within the simile;
whereas in examples such as "This Pāṇḍya king has a long necklace resting upon his shoulders," there is a non-single (repeated) mention.

Having thus examined the nature of the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) as it occurs when terms like *iva* are employed, the author now examines it even when such terms are not employed, starting with the words "When *iva* and so forth... and so on.

Although the repeated mention of a common attribute is also possible in the case of Illumination (dīpaka) and Equal Pairing (tulyayogitā), nevertheless, since those two do not arise without a single mention, that alone is stated here as the primary factor.
He says "repeatedly," etc., to show that the repeated mention occurs in two ways.

"The first type" refers to the nature of pure generality (*sāmānya*). If the generality here possesses only a single form, then why is it designated separately by another synonym? Anticipating this objection, he says "merely," and so forth. As it has been stated: "Generally, a single word should not be used twice."
The second mode is the relationship between an object and its reflection.
Concluding this point in such a manner, he establishes the very subject at hand with the words "Thus, in this way," and so forth.
[He does so] by means of a basis for comparison.
By stating this, the author demonstrates that *prativastūpamā* is not distinct from *dṛṣṭānta*;
for in this [figure], another unrelated matter (*arthāntara*) is introduced for the sake of similarity in order to express a specific quality of the subject at hand (*prakṛtārtha*),
and it is precisely for this reason that there exists a relationship of *upamāna* (standard of comparison) and *upameya* (object of comparison) between the relevant and the irrelevant matters here.

In the example, since such an occurrence exists elsewhere as well, the apprehension of the subject matter at hand might not be clear; therefore, another matter (arthāntara) is introduced for the purpose of clarifying that apprehension.

For this very reason, the introduction of another matter here is not useful for the subject matter itself in any way, but rather serves to eliminate the lack of clarity in the cognizer’s apprehension of the subject matter at hand.
Furthermore, some say there is no difference between these two (the example and the subject matter) because they stand in the relationship of the supported and the supporter within the example.
That is incorrect,
because the relationship of capacity and the capacitated does not exist between two specific intrinsic natures;
for it is impossible for one entity to be established by means of another distinct entity.
For that [relation] occurs only between the general and the particular,
because the general is invariably grounded in the particular, and the particular is invariably dependent upon the general.
Furthermore, if there were a relationship of capacity and capacitation (*samartha-samarthaka-bhāva*) here, this would not constitute a distinct poetic figure from *arthāntaranyāsa*.
Because the universal, which consists of the relationship between the capacity and the possessor of capacity, persists in both cases;

others, however, relying on the metaphorical sense of "similarity" (aupamya) in both instances, claim a distinction between these two based on the universal being established as either a pure universal or through the relationship of the original image and its reflection.
That too is incorrect.

Since the general definition known as "comparison" (aupamya) is followed by this much alone, it is untenable for these two to be distinct figures of speech, just as in the case of the varieties of simile (*upamā*).
Thus, even when independent of the sentence structure, the distinction between these two is established solely through the differences between the speaker and the listener.
This also applies by way of contrast (*vaidharmya*).
The word "it becomes" is to be supplied as the remainder. The illustration for that [subject] is the explanation by way of the relationship between an original object and its reflection. (Sūtra 27)
In the phrase "thirst also," the common property (*sāmānyadharma*) is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*), not only for the object of comparison and the standard of comparison;
this [type of simile] is also twofold, according to similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
The first example is as follows:
"The ocean was indeed crossed by the monkey warriors; however, only Mount Mandara, its massive body submerged in the depths of the netherworld, knows its profoundity."
"Many indeed worship speech as a goddess; however, Murāri, that poet who has undergone the hardships of dwelling in the teacher's house, knows the essence within the essence."
In this context, although a single property called "possessing a nose" (*ñcāna*) is mentioned, it is not intended as the basis for the metaphorical identification (*aupamya*).
Regarding that which is intended as the basis, there is indeed a reflection [of the subject] through such means as divine speech and worship, as in the case of "crossing the ocean" and so forth.
An example of the second type is as follows:
"You have already turned your mind toward pride; what else remains? Thus have our enemies been struck down.
For darkness persists only so long as the sun has not reached the crest of the mountain of sunrise."
In this case, there is a reflection through contrast (vaidharmya) by means of the location and so forth of the "being slain" and other such qualities.

Regarding the phrase "of that too" (*tasyāpi*), it means "even of the common attribute. Regarding the phrase "of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison," it means "of the two subjects, both the contextual and the non-contextual."

Therefore, this is the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) known as the relation of the original image and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) between the properties (*dharmas*) and the subjects (*dharmins*).
As it has been stated elsewhere: "The simile (*dṛṣṭānta*), moreover, is the reflection of all these.
However, the phrase "of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison" (*upamānopameyayoḥ*) should not be explained as having its own independent meaning [in this context].
Because another matter is introduced for the sake of strengthening the subject at hand, and because similarity is not intended [as the primary focus],
it is called "the first" by way of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*).
Or, for example:
"Knowledge, when imparted by a multitude of disciples in the proper places, indeed makes the teacher appear even more virtuous;
for the ocean, having received the waters scattered from the clouds upon the oyster shells, becomes a mine of jewels."
In this case, there is the reflection of the location and other factors upon the mother-of-pearl shell and so forth;
since this is the basis [of the comparison],
it constitutes a figure of sense (arthālaṅkāra) and not a figure of simile (aupamya).
And because that [reflection] is impossible according to the reasoning just stated,
*nidarśanā* (illustration) is the production of a reflection understood through a connection with a real entity, whether by way of possibility or impossibility. (Sūtra 28)
In the context of producing a reflection, its definition is as follows:

in some cases, a relationship with a real object, being possible, brings about the state of being an original and its reflection through its own inherent capacity; in other cases, however, because of the contradiction of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the impossibility [of such a relationship] implies that there is no reflection based on a relationship with a real object.
Among these, an example of a connection based on the possibility of things is:
"He who places the god Sun upon the position of his crest-jewel,
thereby making known to householders that hospitality must be shown to the virtuous."
In this context, because the causative suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of performing an action conducive to that [awakening], a connection with a real entity (*vastu*) is possible.
An example where a connection with a real entity is impossible is as follows:
"May that Yama protect you, whose naturally curved [bow] touches the play of the strung bow of Smara."
The moon, whose two extremities are licked by the rays of the jewels of the great serpent kings entwined in his matted locks.

In this context, the contact with the moon—which is a distinct entity—with the play associated with the bow of Love is impossible; therefore, it brings about an understanding of a play similar to that [original] play. Thus, because there is no great distance [between them], it is called "the conception of a reflection" (*pratibimbakalpana*), as expressed by the words "it is possible" and so forth.
The phrase "the state of being a prototype and its reflection" (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) means the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Because of the assertion of the non-difference between the property and the property-bearer;
and thus, in this instance of illustration, there is an inseparable connection with similarity.
By that—
At dawn, when her companions ask about their secret nocturnal activities, this newlywed bride does not speak, her face closed with shame;
yet the hidden nail-marks upon her breasts, revealed by the wonder of the leaf-designs they are incessantly drawing, proclaim the truth to them.
In such cases, even though a connection between the things (*vastu-sambandha*) is possible, because there is no manifestation of a comparison (*aupamya*), there is no *nidarśanā* ornament.
By this very [criterion], the two varieties of this [ornament] have been stated according to the possibility or impossibility of the connection between the things.
He illustrates that very point with the words beginning "by being a crest-jewel" (*cūḍāmaṇitvādinā*).

This is because [the causative suffix] is used in the sense of performing an action conducive to that [result], as in "He causes the fire of dried cow-dung (*kārīṣa*) to teach" (*kārīṣo ’dhyāpayati*).
Holding the mountain with its head for the sake of the approaching sun is such an action conducive to that result.

Therefore, since the causative suffix in the word *bodhayan* ("causing to perceive") is used here in the sense of performing an action conducive to that result, there is a simile based on a possible connection: "Just as I must perform hospitality toward a guest, so too must you."

And thus, since it is impossible for the mountain to be the agent of the act of awakening, there is no superimposition of the activity of one who considers himself a god; therefore, there is no suggested *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) here.

Nor is it the figure of speech known as *smṛti* (recollection), because the mountain’s capacity to awaken householders to the hospitality due to the virtuous is merely the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
For in that case, the recollection of another object arises from the perception of something similar;
however, householders do not possess agency in the recollection of a guest upon seeing the sun,
because they are merely being informed of their constant duty to offer hospitality.
Nor is it intended here to express a similarity between the sun and the guest, or between the guest and the sun;
rather, it is meant that hospitality toward the virtuous must be performed even by householders, just as by me.
For this very reason, the figure of speech called *viśeṣālaṅkāra*—which consists in the production of a different object—is not present here either.
Because there is an absence of such a cognition as "upon the comprehension of the heat, the comprehension of the impossible [presence] of the guest and so forth has arisen," therefore,
whether a relation exists or not, it must be said that there is no such indication;
thus, there would be only the two types of difference already described.
"Because it is impossible":
because a property belonging to one substratum cannot, at another time, belong to a different substratum.
"Because there is no remoteness": because there is no spatial or temporal distance.

Because similarity [is established] through the medium of a quality (*dharma*), there is a certain degree of proximity. For example: "A thrill on the limbs, a face full of smiles, speech accompanied by cooing..."
"Everything that ought to be done has been accomplished by my beloved with coolness."

In this case, since the cause of the beloved’s action—such as the physical sign of horripilation—is impossible [to exist] in the winter, which is a distinct entity, it brings about an understanding of its similarity [to that action]; thus, because the winter is perceived as being equal to the beloved, there is a simile (*aupamya*).

Therefore, one should not say that this is the ornament of "Illustration" (*nidarśanā*) simply because of the non-connection of the attributes (*dharma*), nor should its status as a separate ornament called "Reflection" (*pratimā*) be asserted;
for it is perfectly clear that in other examples of such "intuition" (*pratibhā*), it is never dissociated from another ornament, and thus it should not be designated as a distinct figure of speech.

In this way, it is certainly possible for other complete new ornaments to be joined with one another; however, for fear of excessive prolixity in the text, and because our intention was solely to refute and remove the criticisms directed at our own system, we have not refuted them individually.
Furthermore, one should not consider that these also constitute distinct figures of speech merely on the grounds that an opponent's view is not refuted is necessarily accepted;

rather, this [figure] is twofold, based on its occurrence with respect to the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) or the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). The occurrence with respect to the meaning of a word has just been illustrated. An example of its occurrence with respect to the meaning of a sentence is as follows:
"The cleansing of the jewels of your toenails with red lac is like the whitening of the moon with an application of sandalwood paste."
Some, however, say that this is the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), but that is incorrect;
for an *dṛṣṭānta* consists in the relationship between an original (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) between two sentence-meanings that are independent of one another.

But where another sentence-meaning is superposed upon the contextual sentence-meaning through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there the figure of *nidarśanā* (exemplification) alone is appropriate, as it is rooted in the impossibility of a literal connection.
This is not an illustration;
and thus:
"If this body, so difficult to find even in the inner apartments of a king, belongs to people dwelling in a hermitage..."
Indeed, the garden creepers have been surpassed by the forest creepers through their superior qualities.
In this case, one should not conceive of it as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*),
because according to the stated reasoning, it does not qualify as an example (*nidarśana*).
This [illustration] is based on a connection between things that is impossible.
The meaning of the word "also" (api) is that this division is not only [illustrated by] *nidarśanā*, but its sub-classification is likewise twofold.
It has been exemplified by the verse beginning with "May he protect you... (*avyātsa vaḥ*).
"Some" refers to the venerable Mammaṭa and others.

18a. *sa.* The word "that" (*tad*) refers to the statement regarding the ornament of illustration (*dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāra*). He applies this to other cases as well with the words beginning with "in this way" (*evam*); [this is done] by the aforementioned method.
Because another sentence-meaning is superimposed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) upon the meaning of the contextual sentence;

therefore, let alone that which has been stated by others— that there is a "metaphor of sentence-meaning" (*vākyārtharūpaka*) due to the existence of a literal superimposition based on the indication of coreferentiality between two sentence-meanings— that which was stated [by them] regarding the son being an example of *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) is indeed improper.
