When two sentence-meanings are independent and the common property (*dharma*) exists in the form of a pure universal (*śuddhasāmānyarūpa*), there is *prativastūpamā*.
However, not even one of these conditions is possible here;
because the two sentence-meanings are dependent upon each other and lack the nature of a pure universal, it is also incorrect to consider this an example of *arthāpatti* (presumption).
"It is indeed marvelous that he seized Lakṣmī from the lotus while it was still awake;
but what praise can there be for his theft of the gait of a rutting elephant from the pair of [Viṣṇu’s] feet?"
In this case, however, its status as an example of *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) is even more flawed than [the previous instance].
For here there is not even a mere mutual similarity between the two sentence-meanings; so what talk can there be of *prativastūpamā*?
This same kind of inconsistency, though possible, has been demonstrated in other examples of all the poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) due to the two reasons just mentioned.
And so it is said:
"Where the five-arrowed god of love obeys her command, where nectar is the servant of her face,
and where even the moon is a captive to the excellence of her beauty— that is the state of those lotus-eyed women."

In this case, because both the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) are mentioned, although the figure of speech is clearly a *rūpaka* (metaphor), it has been stated as an example of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
However, since *atiśayokti* itself does not even exist there, what is the use of citing the presence of a causal relationship? Enough of this prolixity.
Furthermore, although for that which is based on a connection between impossible things, the possibility of such a connection exists without distinction—

Even though this has been stated, in the examples just mentioned, just as the attribute connected with the standard of comparison (upamāna) exists only as residing in the object of comparison (upameya), so too an attribute connected with the object of comparison may exist in the standard of comparison as well; thus he says "this" and so forth.

This [type of simile] was previously explained by earlier authorities as occurring when that which resides in the standard of comparison is impossible in the object of comparison; however, in reality, it also occurs when that which resides in the object of comparison is impossible in the standard of comparison.
Because in both cases there exists the disruption of the connection [between cause and effect].
For example: "The paleness on the surface of the cheeks of women from Gauḍa, which was observed during their separation, was seen in the pollen within the clusters of the date-palm blossoms."
Here, the surface of the cheek is the subject under discussion;
since the quality of that [cheek], namely its paleness, cannot possibly exist in dates, a comparison is implied.
And this type [of figure] also occurs by way of a chain (śṛṅkhalā).
For example:
"O you with the shaven head, you hold a wood-apple firmly upon another wood-apple;
out of disgust for yourself, those deceived by the trickery of the reed-stalk are being led astray."
"In both cases" means either in the object of comparison (*upameya*) or in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Since the description of spring has been introduced, although both are equally contextual (*prakṛta*), the surface of the cheek is the object of comparison;
this is because it is precisely through its connection with that [spring] that the paleness is intended to be established.
The very state of being a property that is both established and to be established constitutes the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison.
For example:
"O deer-eyed one, this loveliness of your face is perceived even by the Lord of the Night."
But how has this been brought by him today; for what indeed is impossible for those possessed of skill?
In these flattering words (*cāṭu*), since the heroine is the subject under discussion, her face is the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Furthermore, the quality of that [face], namely its *lāvaṇya* (translucent beauty), cannot possibly exist in the moon, which serves as the point of comparison (*upamāna*).
Thus, this [comparison] is either based on a connection with an impossible thing, or it is the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
This [metaphor] is also seen in some cases as being formed by a string of words (*mālā*), as for example:
"Weeping was performed in the forest; a corpse was anointed with unguents; a lotus was planted on dry land; and rain was poured for a long time upon barren soil."
"A dog's tail was bent down, whispered prayers were made into the ear of a deaf man, and a mirror was held before the face of a blind man—this is what happens when one serves a foolish person."

Furthermore, the earth, with frost accumulated like dense darkness, reveals its paleness. Seeing such a sight again and again in the deep gloom, O friend, how can one live? Here, the singular number is used for the subjects because the speaker intends to convey the unity of their collective state. This is not a case of *bahuvacana-vivakṣā* (intentional use of the plural). Thus, there is no contradiction in using the singular number for the subject when the intention is to express a single unified state. Therefore, the objection raised is invalid. Consequently, the definition of *samuccaya* (conjunction) remains unrefuted. Furthermore, since the conjunction of two or more actions is possible even when the agents are different, the definition of *samuccaya* is not overly broad (*ativyāpti*). For example: "Having first drunk the wine of the moon, the bees now drink the honey of the lotuses. In this instance, the agent is different, yet the conjunction of the two drinking-actions is clearly perceived. Therefore, the definition is established. As stated: "Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the simultaneous occurrence of two or more actions belonging to the same agent, or the occurrence of two or more actions belonging to different agents at the same time. Thus, the definition of *samuccaya* is free from faults. However, some maintain that *samuccaya* consists in the conjunction of two or more actions belonging to the same agent, while others hold that it is the conjunction of two or more actions belonging to different agents. But this is incorrect, for both types of conjunction are observed in practice. Therefore, the definition should be formulated as follows: "Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the simultaneous occurrence of two or more actions belonging to the same agent, or the occurrence of two or more actions belonging to different agents at the same time. This concludes the discussion on *samuccaya*. Now, the figure *vikalpa* (option/alternative) is defined: **Vikalpa (Option):** When two or more mutually exclusive things are presented as alternatives, it is *vikalpa*. For example: "Shall I go to the forest, or shall I enter the fire? Or shall I take poison? Alas, my life is difficult to sustain! Here, the three actions—going to the forest, entering the fire, and taking poison—are mutually exclusive, and they are presented as alternatives. Therefore, this is *vikalpa*. It is not a case of *samuccaya*, because the actions cannot occur simultaneously. Nor is it *sasaṃdeha* (doubt), because there is no uncertainty regarding the primary action. Nor is it *ullekha* (poetic conceit), because there is no attribution of multiple identities to a single object. Nor is it *bhrāntimān* (error), because there is no mistaken cognition of one thing for another. Nor is it *apahnuti* (denial), because there is no concealment of the true nature of a thing. Nor is it *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because there is no exaggeration. Nor is it *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), because there is no presentation of a thing as something else. Nor is it *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because there is no imaginative attribution of a non-existent quality. Nor is it *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), because there is no depiction of the inherent nature of an object. Nor is it *smaraṇa* (remembrance), because there is no recollection of a past experience. Nor is it *bhrānti* (delusion), because there is no actual error. Nor is it *saṃśaya* (doubt), because there is no indecision. Nor is it *ullekha*, because there is no attribution of multiple forms. Nor is it *anyathākhyāti*, because there
In this case, because *samāsokti* exists even in the absence of a plurality of qualifiers,
the phrase "due to the similarity of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānāṃ sāmyāt*) should not be formulated as a rule;
for that [definition] would fail to cover cases where there is no plurality.
Anticipating the objection as to why the similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*) also functions as a cause here, he says "by means of the qualifier" (*viśeṣeṇa*), etc.
[The phrase] "the irrelevant" (*aprastuta*) does not mean that only the attributes of the irrelevant subject are intended;
for attributes belonging to one substratum cannot reside elsewhere without their own substratum.

For it is not logical that there be a continuity (*anvaya*) of the properties of a leader in one who is not a leader, because a continuity of properties belonging to something else is impossible in another.

Therefore, since the application of the designation of one thing to another—when superimposed upon that other—is impossible, it implies the subject (*dharmin*) that possesses its own designation due to an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with it; thus, by the very subject under discussion, which is implied though not explicitly mentioned...
That which is delimited by a property (*dharmin*) is not, in turn, delimited [by another];

for if that were the case, because the relevant subject would be represented as the form of the irrelevant one, there would be a superimposition of form (*rūpasamāropa*), not a superimposition of conventional usage (*vyavahārasamāropa*).
Therefore, he says: "Because the relevant subject is represented as the form [of the other], there would be a superimposition of form, not a superimposition of conventional usage."
For this very reason, he says: "by way of being the qualifier of the subject at hand.
For this same reason, it is formulated in the aphorism as: "when the non-contextual [object] is what is implied.

Thus, in *samāsokti* (synthetic expression), because of the superimposition of behavior, the state of being a qualifier—characterized by the distinction of the contextual [object] through the non-contextual—is established.

In a metaphor (*rūpaka*), however, because there is a superimposition of form (*rūpa-samāropa*), there is a capacity for concealment known as "being made to appear as that form"; thus, there is no distinction [between the two].

Therefore, having set aside the definition "Metaphor (*samāsokti*) is the delimitation of the unmentioned subject through the similarity of adjectives," one should instead formulate the rule in accordance with our own definition: "Metaphor (*samāsokti*) is the delimitation of the unmentioned subject through the similarity of adjectives.
Furthermore, any suspicion of its being a case of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) here is entirely without foundation.

Because the object (*viṣaya*) is mentioned while the subject (*viṣayin*) is not, and because that similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*) occurs in three ways—through wordplay (*śliṣṭatā*), through commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), and by containing a comparison (*aupamyagarbhatva*)—it is of three types.
Among these, an example of wordplay is as follows: "By the moon, whose passion was aroused, the face of night was so seized that its pupils trembled."
Just as she did not perceive the entire dark garment fallen before her due to passion, so too [she did not perceive the truth].
In this instance, the apprehension of the behavior of the hero and heroine occurs through the power of the double-meaning adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇa*);
for there is the cognition of the night and the moon as being characterized by the property called "heroism" and "heroinehood," without their having abandoned their own essential natures.
An example of [the same] through commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) is as follows: "The slender, charming young woman, with tremulous eyes, smiling like a flower..."
"O fortunate one, it attains full bloom merely by the sight of you."

Here, due to the similarity of qualifiers such as "slender" (*tanvī*) and so forth, there arises the cognition of the behavior (*vyavahāra*) of a creeper (*latā*) attributed to the tremulous-eyed woman (*lolākṣī*). In that case, the cause is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the property called "blossoming," which belongs exclusively to a creeper; otherwise, the specific behavior of a creeper would not be cognized through the mere similarity of qualifiers alone.
Furthermore, "expansion" (vikāsa) should be understood as used figuratively with respect to the primary subject (prakṛta).
In this way, it should also be understood when there is a superimposition of the effect (kāryasamāropa).
And this *samāsokti* is less distinct than the former [type].
The word "tat" (that) is the cause for the implied understanding of the irrelevant subject;
"tatra" (therein) is used in the sense of selection;
and "nāyaka" (hero) is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of two identical forms.
"Of those two which have not abandoned their own nature":
for if there were the state of being form and that which possesses form, their own respective natures would indeed be abandoned.
"Therein" means:

Regarding the cognition of the conventional usage of the term "creeper": one might object, "If the property called 'blooming' is accessible only through the creeper, how does it apply in the present context? Anticipating this doubt, he says "blooming," etc.
He applies this very same principle elsewhere as well with the words "in this way," etc.

Thus, it is established that although there is a commonality of attributes in a concise statement (*samāsokti*), the cognition of the behavior associated with the non-contextual object does not occur without the superimposition (*samāropa*) of its properties and activities; this being so by virtue of containing a comparison, as in:
"Adorned with the flowers of the luster of her teeth, beautiful with the sprouts of her hands..."
The deer-eyed woman was beautifully adorned with a mass of hair like a swarm of bees.

In this case, by first forming a compound based on the presence of a simile—namely, "the radiance of her teeth is like flowers" due to her exquisite beauty—and subsequently adopting another compound, "strewn with flowers resembling the radiance of her teeth," the conventional status of a *latā* (creeper) is perceived through the power of the shared adjectives. In the very same verse, if the reading were "parītā hariṇekṣaṇā" (surrounded by deer-eyed women), since there would be neither a prover nor a refuter of either the simile (*upamā*) nor the metaphor (*rūpaka*), one might initially resort to a combination (*saṃkara*). However, as before, through the power of a subsequent compound, the cognition of the *latā* arises.

However, although there may be a state of having common qualifiers due to resorting to another compound by virtue of being a "garbha" (interior) metaphor, this is not the cause for the occurrence of *samāsokti* (speech of compounding).
This is because the apprehension of another meaning occurs precisely through the medium of a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartin*), rendering [the presence of common qualifiers] redundant.
Furthermore, this principle does not apply to cases of the previously shown commixture (*saṃkara*) with simile (*upamā*).

Because there is no occurrence of *upamā* (simile) and *saṃkara* (commixture) that exist only partially (*ekadeśavivartin*), and because that partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka*) occurs through both *aśleṣa* (non-pun) and *śleṣa* (pun), it is of two kinds. An example of the non-punned (*aśliṣṭa*) variety is as follows:
Having gazed upon the face of the woman going to meet her lover in the night with eyes of lightning, the cloud,
as if crying out "Is this the moon being vomited forth along with the falling showers?", roared most piteously.

Here, in accordance with the act of gazing, the metaphor "with eyes like lightning" serves as the basis for the suggested poetic fancy (*pratīyamānotprekṣā*) found in the phrase "the cloud roared most piteously," which characterizes the cloud as a beholding person. An example of this using a pun (*śliṣṭa*) is as follows:
"Displaying an elaborate array of writing in the place for counting love’s [countless] moments, by means of the ink-like bees resting upon the broad petals of the *vicikila* flowers..."

"By means of its crooked scripts, who indeed did Spring not unsettle that scribe (kāyastha) by making him keep track of the income and expenditure regarding the lives of those separated from their lovers? (Śrī-Caitanya-caritāmṛta 6.70).
For here, among the words "leaf," "writing," and "scribe" which contain a *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the phrase "the bees as ink-sticks" serves as the cause for that metaphor;
and since its scope of application is extensive, one should not conceive of it as *samāsokti* (speech of compression).
Furthermore, the state of being well-attired is conducive only to the contextual meaning, and thus it is a support for the simile (*upamā*); therefore, it is based upon that [simile].

Regarding the phrase "by resorting to another compound": although here the compound remains strictly an *upamāna-samāsa* (simile compound), it is nevertheless described as a different type of compound precisely because of the reversal of the roles of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).
This is due to its distinct nature when compared to the preceding [type].
"In this very [instance]" refers to the passage beginning with "the luster of the teeth" (*dantaprabhā*) and so forth.
It is because there is an absence of both proof and refutation for [the presence of] simile (*upamā*) or metaphor (*rūpaka*).

For, since the quality of being pervasive (*parītatva*) is not thus compatible with both the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) and that which is not at hand (*aprakṛta*), there is an absence of proof [for either figure].
And thus, since there is no deficiency [in the constituent parts], there is an absence of sublation (*bādhakatva*).
Consequently, because there is no basis for choosing one side over the other, there is a commixture (*saṃkara*) of simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) through doubt (*saṃdeha*).
The basis for that [commixture] is the inclusion of both types of compounds.

And since that [simultaneous occurrence] is not possible within a single sentence, they are grasped by means of the term *kāmakṣāra* (the "desire-alkali"). Having raised the question—given that both simile and compound are produced through reliance on commingling (*saṃkara*), just as this very ornament [simile] occurs there, so too when a compound containing a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is joined, is it this very same ornament or a different ornament?—he says "rūpaka," etc. And this should also be applied directly to a compound whose core is a metaphor.

Because the logic is the same. If this is so, then one might object: "In the case of a simile (*upamā*) based on a common substratum as well, since the understanding of another meaning occurs through the medium of a partial metaphorical simile (*ekadeśavivartin*), why does this [designation of *dhvani*] not apply? Anticipating this doubt, he says "And not," and so forth.
"This" refers to what was stated regarding metaphor (*rūpaka*).
The phrase "due to the absence [of such]" is according to the opinion of Udbhaṭa.
As they say:
"Unlike Rudraṭa, for Udbhaṭa, there are no partial [metaphors] or mixed similes that function as partial [metaphors]. Therefore, this was stated with the intention of his view.
For, according to the author’s own view, the occurrence of those two [simile and metaphor] is possible by the method that will be explained below.

Now, if their occurrence is indeed possible according to the author’s view, then a variety of *samāsokti* (speech of compression) produced by an adjective containing a simile (*aupamya*) would not be possible;

for, as in the case of a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartin*), the cognition of another meaning is established through a mere commixture of simile (*upamā-saṃkara*) with partial similes, rendering such a figure redundant.
This is not so;
for there certainly exists the quality of having a cause consisting of a qualification containing a simile (*aupamya*) in *samāsokti*.
However, this [quality] functions as its cause only when accompanied by another distinct variety [of *samāsokti*], and not by itself alone.

For if the qualifiers were to contain a comparison within them, there would arise the possibility of a "partial metaphor" (ekadeśavivartinī upamā). In that regard, an example accompanied by *śleṣa* (punning) is as follows:
"Whom do these dense, captivating [clouds], which have turned the dark sky a deep orange, not enchant?"
Ah, in this evening, these quarters of the sky possess clouds for breasts and stars that shimmer like pupils.
In this context, regarding the reading "sphuṭasaṃdhyātapakuṅkumaiḥ," the phrase "saṃdhyātapakuṅkumaiḥ" is an epithet containing a simile within it.
An example accompanied by commonality [of attributes] is as follows:
"The slender girl is beautiful, with tremulous eyes and breasts like flower-clusters."
"O fortunate one, it attains full bloom merely by the sight of you."
Here, the epithet "having breasts in the form of flower-clusters" contains a simile within it.
An example accompanied by the superimposition of a pure effect is as follows: "He climbed upon the tops of the trees; he rolled about in the heaps of pollen from the mass of flowers."
What did Caitra not do while sporting in the forest, pulling at the garments of the flowers of the creepers?
In this case, "having flowers for its garment" (*prasūnāṃśukam*) is a qualifying attribute of the *aupamyagarbha* (the simile-embryo).
However, when these [attributes] are used alone, it is merely a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartinī upamā*), as in:
"It shone, with teeth like filaments shimmering upon the moving petal of the lower lip."
The face of the beautiful woman is charming, with its play of eyebrows like a circle of bees.
In this case, the quality of *lalitatva* (gracefulness) is what establishes the simile.
Although there is a state of having common adjectives due to recourse to another compound, this is not the cause for the presence of *samāsokti* (condensed expression).
This is because the apprehension of a different meaning occurs precisely through the medium of a *ekadeśavivartinī* (partially manifesting) simile, which constitutes its distinctiveness.
The same should be understood regarding the verse beginning with *dantaprabhā* and so forth.

Once the compound *dantaprabhāḥ puṣpāṇīvā* (the luster of her teeth like flowers) is formed, the comprehension of the creeper—which serves as the standard of comparison—is established; therefore, it is redundant to resort to another type of compound to achieve that same comprehension. For the poet’s effort is directed toward suggesting something not explicitly stated (*aprakṛta*), and since that is already accomplished by this [simple compound], what is the use of employing *samāsokti*?
Furthermore, the author has stated here that this is "condensed expression" (*samāsokti*) out of deference to the ancients.

As for what he will say later— that "wherein, in a case of simile expressed through condensed expression, it is possible to apply the similarity of qualifiers by means of another compound, there the condensed expression is said to be brought about by qualifiers containing a simile within them"—
that too is intended solely as a concession to the ancients.

Otherwise, since the same logic applies, why has it not been stated that *samāsokti* (synecdoche) also occurs in a *rūpaka* (metaphor) where a partial transformation exists and it is possible to apply identical adjectives?
That it was not so stated is incorrect;

for by the power of *rūpaka*, the cognition of that [unexpressed subject] is established from the very beginning, and it would be redundant to convey the unexpressed subject subsequently through the medium of *samāsokti*.
"The vault of the sky shines, with its moon-like face full of delight, its shimmering starry pearls, and its braided hair of dense darkness."

In such cases, however, since there is no evidence for a simile (*upamā*), it is indeed a "partially manifest" metaphor (*ekadeśavivarti rūpaka*); thus, one should not fall into the error of mistaking it for "suggested speech" (*samāsokti*).
Nor is it proper to maintain a "blend through doubt" (*saṃdehasaṃkara*) between simile and metaphor in such instances, as that has been rejected by the author of the *Alaṅkārasāra* and others.
Fearing that the definition of *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) might be rendered redundant by the discussion of *rūpaka* (metaphor),
he says "of this" (*asyāśca*), etc., and summarizes its divisions as they have been explained above with the words "thus, in this way" (*tadevam*), etc.
Thus, one [variety] is produced by means of punning adjectives (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇa*).
However, when produced by common qualifiers (*sādhāraṇaviśeṣaṇa*), it is divided into two types through superimposition (*samāropa*) and attribution of function (*kāryasamāropa*).

When produced by qualifiers containing a simile (*aupamyagarbhaviśeṣaṇa*), it is divided into two types through the mixture of similes (*upamāsaṃkara*) and compounds (*samāsa*). But the two varieties based on metaphor (*rūpaka*) are not within its scope.

Thus, there are five types of *samāsokti* (synecdoche). This *samāsokti* is first divided into three kinds: by the superimposition of a pure effect, by similarity of adjectives, and by being composed of both. Furthermore, the fivefold nature of the similarity of adjectives has been determined.
In all these cases, the very lifeblood is the superimposition of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-samāropa*).
That [superimposition] consists in the superimposition of the conventional usage of a worldly object upon a worldly thing,
and the superimposition of the conventional usage of a technical (treatise-based) object upon a technical thing.

Alternatively, there is the superimposition of the conventional usage of scriptural entities upon worldly ones, or the superimposition of the conventional usage of worldly entities upon scriptural ones; thus, it is fourfold. In this way, *samāsokti* (concise expression) is of many varieties.
"The two divisions" refers either to being directly suspected [of being one or the other] or to not being the object [of doubt], because,
due to the aforementioned reasoning, it finds its rest solely in the metaphor (*rūpaka*).
"First" means that these three divisions constitute its fundamental nature;
furthermore, the fivefold variety mentioned constitutes its intermediate subdivisions.
This is because it is a sub-variety of the "similarity of qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*).

Although there is indeed a similarity of qualifiers even in the superimposition of a pure effect (*śuddhakāryasamāropa*), nevertheless, in this case, the superimposition of the effect alone is perceived as being prominent; thus, its status as a distinct variety has been stated [in the section] on the sixfold division.
"Everywhere" refers to the group of six varieties.
"Of many kinds" means because worldly transactions and so forth are infinite. In that regard, by way of superimposing a pure effect, for example:

"O King, in the desert land, the Khadira tree scratches deeply at the breasts, firmly seizes the hair, and draws strange leaf-patterns upon the lovely faces of your enemies' deer-eyed wives as they flee in terror, while it forcibly drags their garments from their rounded hips."

In this instance, through the superimposition of pure actions such as the drawing of leaf-designs (*pattrāvalī*) and so forth, the perception of the *khadira* tree as a forceful lover (*haṭhakāmuka*) is illustrated by means of the similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*). [The word] "illustrated" refers to the verse beginning with "upoḍharāgeṇa" and so on. An example of [superimposition] consisting of both [the object and the action] is as follows:
Their tresses were torn out, their chests ripped open, their lips entirely severed, pain was inflicted upon their ears, and wounds were made upon their eyes, lovely as blue lotuses;
as they fled with steps faltering from excessive agitation, what did not the thorny trees in the waterless desert do to the wives of your enemies?

Here, there is a similarity of qualifiers in the words "sapless" (*nīrasaiḥ*) and "thorny" (*kaṇṭakibhiḥ*). In the phrases "with their side-locks (*alaka*) cut off," and so forth, there is the superimposition of an effect.
These are the four types of superimposition of behavior (*vyavahāra*), with examples given in sequence.
For example:

"What did the youth not do out of excessive torment— the fire of his eyes, which embraced the sky, kissed the faces of the quarters, and with the tips of its rays inscribed the digit of the moon that had obstructed the heavens— having submerged the flower-arrows within?"
And worldly objects, through the distinctions of taste and so forth, possess manifold varieties that one may discern for oneself:
"By those who perceive You as having a single form even amidst all Your manifestations, proceeding in countless ways through Your glory,
it is surely my conviction that they have composed Your definition by omitting the case-endings associated with the nominative."
In this matter, there is the superimposition of a thing well-known in grammar upon a thing well-known in the scriptures and treatises:

"That which has never reached the limit of the eyes, nor been joined with anything else, nor ever touched by speech; that for which no comparison has been seen, that which has not arisen from [external] objects, and that which is not nothing at all—that indescribable loveliness (*lāvaṇya*) of gazelle-eyed women, devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), triumphs as a marvel to the heart."
Here, in the case of beauty, which is a worldly object, there is the superimposition of an object well-known in the Mīmāṃsā system of philosophy.
In this same way, the superimposition of objects well-known in the systems of logic (tarka), medicine (āyurveda), and astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra) should be understood.
For example:

As Smara displayed his superiority by means of the charming play of his own side once the cause had been established, the unbroken expertise of the cuckoo served to bring about the pride of all young men, which was intended to destroy their humiliation.
In this context, there is a superimposition of a thing well-known from the treatises on logic (*tarkaśāstra*).
The word "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship) should be explained here through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the subject at hand.
"The sun-stone became dull and sweet-warmed, and the darkness displayed its swelling."
In the absence of the Lord of Herbs, the eyes resorted to the defect born of cataracts.
Here, there is a superimposition of things well-known from Āyurveda:

"As you strike at the temples of rutting elephants, as you perform protection during the *vaidhṛta* yoga upon the circle of the earth, and as you always institute the festival of processions among the Lāṭas;
since you do not abandon your auspicious former position and remain attended [by us], your glories of victory increase—what indeed is not an auspicious omen for those who possess merit?"
In this case, there is a superimposition of objects well-known in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*).

O best of teachers, you who have abandoned the state of having a limited course—even by those whose intentions are directed toward you, and even by those whose sole delight is in sound inference—you remain unknowable;
your activity is unprecedented.
"The multitude of your virtues, O connoisseur, has been determined by the wise as being neither expressible nor even definable."
In this case, there is the superimposition of a subject matter well-known from the *Bharata-śāstra* and other treatises;

for here, the designation of "rasa" such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others is perceived as being inherent in a collection of qualities (*guṇa*). This is because rasa is not to be understood through the power of implied meaning (*tātparya-śakti*).
Nor is it an object of inference;
nor is it made expressible by words through the function of denotation;
nor is it within the scope of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

However, because its internal objects of cognition have dissolved, it is free from limitation; having been made the object of the unprecedented operation characterized as *vyañjana* (suggestion), and having abandoned its status of residing in either the imitated or the imitator, it resides in the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*). Thus, by means of words such as "with spreading implications" (*prasarpattātparyaiḥ*), it is *rasa* itself that is perceived.
It is understood in this way;
other cases should also be known accordingly.
"In sequence" means according to the order in which they were listed.
By the word *mīmāṃsā*, the Uttaramīmāṃsā is intended here.
In that [Uttaramīmāṃsā], the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), has been demonstrated;
herein, the superimposition (*samāropa*) of its conventional usage has been made.
"Not by intentionality" (na tātparyeṇa).
As it has been said:
"Neither is it denotation, nor is it intentionality, nor is it indication, nor is it inference."
"Capable of being included within *dhvani* because they exist as distinct objects."
Thus it is said.
Rāma and others are the objects of imitation;
the actors and others are the imitators;
and rasa is not perceived as residing within them.
As it has been said: "The rasa does not exist in the object of imitation such as Rāma, nor in the imitator such as the actor; rather, [it exists] in those possessed of sensitivity.
This is what is meant by "something else."

O Lord, when the inner speech (*paśyantī*) conceals itself within you as if out of shame— characterized by the superimposition of objects well-known from other scriptures— and when even the intermediate speech (*madhyamā*) falters due to the intensity of its desire to utter sweet sounds; how then could the outer speech (*bāhyā*), which is merely the restlessness of those who practice flattery, exist there during the firm embrace of the Goddess in secret play with You?
In this context, there is the superimposition of worldly linguistic conventions upon a subject well-established in scripture.

It was stated previously that worldly linguistic conventions have many varieties due to the distinctions between *rasa* and so forth. Regarding the superimposition of a pure effect (*kārya*), the definition formulated in accordance with earlier treatises—namely, "based on the figurative nature of the effect's status as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) due to the similarity of qualifiers"—should be applied in whatever way is appropriate.

Having thus explained *samāsokti* (synecdoche) along with its elaborations, the author once again applies this definition to actual examples through a detailed analysis in order to make it accessible to the hearts of connoisseurs, beginning with the words "In this case, however" (*iha tu*).
Here:
"The autumn, bearing a rainbow upon her pale cloud-breast, resembling a fresh nail-mark..."
While making the spotted moon appear bright, she increased the heat of the sun even further.
In this case, there is indeed the perception of the sun and the moon as the hero and heroine;
yet, since there is no equality of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*) here, from where does that [perception] arise?
It arises because, through the equality of the qualifier "making the spotted moon serene," autumn is perceived as the heroine, and [the other elements] act in accordance with that.

If it is argued that the status of the two as lovers (nāyaka) is understood through the use of *samāsokti* (condensed expression), then how is the qualifying attribute "bearing a rainbow resembling fresh nail-marks" indicated by way of similarity?
Furthermore, a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartinī upamā*) has not been mentioned here, by whose power the understanding of their being lovers might arise.
How, then, is it established here?
To this it is said: If the simile that occurs in a single part (*ekadeśavivartinī*) were not mentioned for every word, by whom would it be refuted?
For it is possible even here, since it arrives by way of its general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Now, in this case, the hero is not perceived in his own form as the object of comparison; rather, there is the perception of the sun and moon themselves as the heroes, since they are the heroes here. Therefore, although the status of being the object of comparison (*upamāna*) resides in the word "resembling a fresh nail-wound" (*ārdranakhakṣatābha*) by virtue of direct expression (*śruti*), it must, upon consideration of the actual matter, be transferred to the rainbow (*aindre dhanuṣi*).

Because of the cognition that "she bears a nail-mark with the luster of Indra’s bow," just as in the injunction "one offers oblation with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) the injunction is transferred to the curd,
so too this is indeed *samāsokti* (speech of compression) animated by simile (*upamā*).

Furthermore, in this case, the perception of the "glories of the lake" (*saraḥśriyaḥ*) as heroines does not arise through *samāsokti* (speech of condensed meaning), because there is an absence of similarity in the adjectives (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the heroine is perceived here as the object of comparison (*upamāna*), and the perception of her as a heroine does not occur by way of being an attribute of the glories of the lake; thus, one must accept that this is indeed a *upamā* (simile) that is partially manifest (*ekadeśavivartinī*).
Because no other alternative is possible.
As for those by whom [the term] has not been mentioned, it must indeed be added to their list.

However, in cases such as "by the mass of hair like a swarm of bees," where there is a simile expressed through a compound (*samāsokti*), and where it is possible to apply the identity of adjectives through another compound, there [the figure] is produced by adjectives containing a simile within them (*aupamyagarbhaviśeṣaṇaprabhāvitā*).
There is no contradiction whatsoever, as this is indeed *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
The word "tāvat" is used here to indicate the absence of disagreement.
[The question] "From where? [is asked].
The thought is: "What is the cause of this?
[The answer is: "Because it is conducive to that," meaning because it is conducive to the perception of Autumn as the heroine (nāyikā).
"Of those two" refers to the sun and the moon.
"How?
[is asked] because, since they do not conform to the subject at hand, an identity [between them and the objects described] is impossible.
How is this established here?

Because the identity of the qualifiers is impossible, the compound expression does not apply; and because the simile—which functions through the transformation of a single part—is not explicitly stated.
This refers to the general definition.

The meaning is as follows: *upamā* (simile) occurs when there is a similarity between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), characterized by an equality of difference and non-difference.
Thus, by the very nature of the *ekadeśavivartinī upamā* (partial simile), the singularity of the hero (*nāyaka*) is understood here.
The word "now" (*atha*) indicates an alternative view.

If, by the very reasoning previously stated, the perception of the sun and moon as the two lovers is achieved through the device of *samāsokti* (synecdoche), then one might ask: how can the qualifier "resembling fresh nail-marks" be joined with them by way of similarity?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this case... and so forth.
He makes this very point clear to the heart by means of an example well-known in other treatises, beginning with: "Just as... and so on.

For by the originative injunction "one should offer the Agnihotra," the oblation (homa) is indeed enjoined. Since it is accepted that a further injunction of that same act—according to the maxim of "burning what has not yet been burned"—is valid only so long as it has not already been established, [the injunction] is not applicable there [to the oblation]. Therefore, because it has already been stated [that the injunction does not apply], the meaning is that [the injunction] is transferred to the qualifying term *dadhi* (curd).
"Enlivened by simile" means that it is brought forth by a qualifying attribute containing a comparison. "It is indeed *samāsokti* (speech of compression)" [is the meaning].
Furthermore, the simile that transforms only one part [of the object] is not a distinct category or a separate ornament; this is what Udbhaṭa and others mean by the word "yair" (by whom).
The intended meaning of the passage beginning with "yatratu" has already been stated by us.

Furthermore, that metaphorical expression (*samārokti*) occurs sometimes as residing in the corroborative instance (*samarthya-gata*) and sometimes as residing in the corroborated subject (*samarthaka-gata*). Examples in order are as follows:
Then, when the moon was embraced by autumn, the rainy season departed with its lightning-glances stilled;
for what women did not lose the quality of their good fortune, their breasts having fallen away like scattered clouds?
"What concern for women can there be for a high-minded man who desires to conquer the unconquered?
The sun does not enter its twilight rest until it has traversed the entire world."

Here, through the concealment [of the literal sense] and by means of the glances of the lightning appearing as a woman, the metaphorical treatment (*nāyakavyavahāra*) of the moon and the autumn is perceived; thus, the specific meaning embraced by *samāsokti* (condensed metaphor) is supported by *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), upon which the former depends.
And in this case, the emergence of that general principle occurs by virtue of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
The epithet "possessing glances like calm lightning," which contains a simile within it, is here identical [in structure] by virtue of its reliance on a different type of compound (*samāsa*).

However, in cases such as "asamāptetyādi" (beginning with "not completed"), because the word *strī* denotes merely the general quality of femininity, the general sense is brought forth through *samāsokti*— which is evoked by a connection to the function [of the words] and contains the indication of a specific gender— and thus the behavior of a hero (*nāyaka*) is superimposed [upon the woman].
The general theme is supported by the specific account of Ravi’s encounter with the twilight:
"Because of the encircling coils of the serpent-king’s slough, which slipped off due to the force of his dragging,
the Mandākinī quickly wound itself around the base of his feet for a long time, as if to soothe the pain from the churning of the ocean."

Here, by the negation of the snake-skin (*nirmokapaṭṭa*), the Mandākinī is superposed; that which is her actual encircling at the base of the feet is apprehended through a *śleṣamūla-atiśayokti* (hyperbole based on paronomasia) as an encircling at the base of [Śiva’s] foot.
That apprehension thus gives rise to a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), imagining it to be "as if for the sake of allaying the pain of churning.
Even as it is being raised, this *utprekṣā* internalizes a *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) based on the metaphorical relationship of husband and wife between the ocean and the Mandākinī.
Thus, in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *samāsokti* (condensed expression), there is a single point in time.

Likewise, in the example "As if they were nail-marks upon the forest grounds," the treatment of the forest grounds as heroines is rooted precisely in a *samāsokti* that has entered into another *utprekṣā*.
In this manner, this *samāsokti* possesses an infinite range of manifestations; its varieties should be inferred by oneself along these lines.
Thus, the elaboration [of the argument] is as stated;
for the word *aṅganā*, which denotes the universal (*sāmānya*), expresses merely femininity (*strītva*). This is due to the power of the pun (*śleṣa*).
For there is a close connection between the breasts;
as for the "distinction of gender," it refers to the activity known as "devotion" (bhajanā) performed by the Sun and Twilight in the forms of male and female.
Thus, he will also demonstrate its mixture with other ornaments by means of the verse beginning with "ākṛṣṭi" and so forth.
"Sā" refers to the poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
"Ekaḥ kālaḥ" means one and the same time.
Because the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) arises precisely through the depth of the implied metaphor (*samāsokti*) in the case of the knower;

Its mention here is due to the context of the variety of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The quality of the qualifiers consists in their being intentional (*sābhiprāyatva*) and in their containing a suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*). For this very reason, because its words are clear yet profound, this is not the domain of *dhvani*.
And thus, because the implied portion is directed toward the expressed meaning, the name *parikara* (the "elaboration") is meaningful.
"In the presence of King Duryodhana, whose wealth is his honor and who bears the bow, while the Kuru kinsman looks on and even as Karṇa and Śalya witness it—
today I have drunk the warm blood from the chest of that very man who dragged the hair and garments of the Pāṇḍava women, as he was being torn by my sharp claws while still alive."
In this context, in the passage beginning with "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*), there is the quality of clarity and depth of expression (*prasannagambhīrapadatva*) intended to convey irony (*sotprāsa*).
Likewise:
"O son of Aṅga, general, favorite of the king, you who mock Droṇa, O Karṇa!"
This should be understood from such passages as, "Now protect Duḥśāsana from Bhīma.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇena*) and so forth:
"here" (*iha*) refers to immediately after the discussion of *samāsokti* (condensed expression).
Furthermore, it is precisely the plurality of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) that is intended here;
otherwise, since "insubstantiality of meaning" (*apuṣṭārtha*) is designated as a poetic defect, this [figure] would be the domain of its opposite, namely "substantiality of meaning" (*puṣṭārtha*).
Thus, by means of the presentation of such numerous qualifiers, an excellence of variety (*vaicitryātiśaya*) arises, which constitutes its status as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Because the suggested meaning lacks primacy due to its orientation toward the expressed meaning, its "submergence" consists in being contained within that [expressed meaning].
"For this very reason" means because the suggested meaning lacks primacy;
"occurrence" refers to the fact that only the expressed meaning is indicated as primary.
"Depth (*gambhīratva*) consists in the inclusion of the suggested meaning by subordinating it;
and where the word and its expressed meaning remain as subordinates toward the suggested meaning, that alone is the domain of *dhvani*.
In this case, however, since that is not so, it has been stated that "this is not the domain of *dhvani*."

For this very reason, he states that even his name is etymological (yaugika) with the words "And thus," and so forth. "Intent on mockery" means as follows: since the king must protect the entire world, whereas for him [the prince] the protection of even his younger brothers has not been accomplished, his status as a king is something entirely different—existing in name only; thus, the intent is one of derision.
In this same manner, others should also understand this for themselves. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the following is included]:

"Rudra stands at the gate of the prison of the gods, accompanied by his lineage, while even Śacī, the wife of the Lord of the Gods, has her hand occupied with a fly-whisk—[all this] because of the thousand arms of that one [hero] who conquers."
This is his only daughter, and he is the sole lord of the night-rangers; this boy enters her inner apartments without hesitation—salutations to you, O Vaiṣṇava!
In such cases as well, the clarity and profundity of the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇas) should be understood.
Sūtra 34:
When the object of qualification (viśeṣya) is also identical [in both senses], the employment of two words [for the same object] constitutes *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
The identity of attributes alone has been discussed in the context of *samāsokti* (speech of brevity).
However, this [present discussion] is stated with reference to the identity of attributes joined with the subjects (*viśeṣya*).

In that regard, when there is the composition of words with double meaning (*śliṣṭapada*), whether both subjects are contextual (*prākaraṇika*) or both are non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*), or one is contextual and the other non-contextual, it is *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Among these, the first two types occur only when there is similarity between both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), whereas the third type occurs only when there is similarity of the qualifier.

However, if there were similarity of the qualified, then—given that the primary meaning is restricted by context, subject matter, and so forth—this would become the domain of suggestion (*dhvani*) regarding another meaning.
In the first two types, however, both meanings are expressed (*vācya*).
Therefore, it is stated here that "or when both are taken" refers to the scope of the third type;
whereas "even when the qualifier is equal" refers to the scope of the remaining two types.
[Regarding the phrase] "even when the qualifier... and so forth:
"This" refers to the definition of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
"The first" [type] occurs both by residing in the contextual subject and by residing in the non-contextual subject.
And here the particle *eva* should be understood as displaced;
by it, one should explain that there are only two modes.
Consequently, the result of the exclusion is that a third mode exists only when there is similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*).
Otherwise, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because this two-fold [simile] is seen even in the absence of similarity between the two qualificands (*viśeṣya*).
For example: "The mountain passes are purified by the absence of movement," and so forth.
Here, there is an absence of similarity between the two intended qualificands, namely, light (*prabhā*) and a cow (*dhenu*).

"May that Jina protect you—he whose foremost warriors and the breasts of the wives of the gods, though possessing the brilliance of the tips of many crowns, with chests armored, full of heat, scarred, crushing the hearts of enemies, and harsh; and though bearing the weight of their forms revealed by cast-off garments, remained unperturbed."
In this case, there is an absence of similarity between the two breasts, which are the non-contextual (aprakṛta) subjects of comparison;
for it is only when there is similarity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) that [the figure arises], and not when there is similarity of the subjects (*viśeṣya*).
Having raised the doubt as to why this does not also occur when there is similarity of the subjects, he says: "But when there is similarity of the subjects," and so forth.
For example:

"O little son of those who dwell in Laṅkā! People fear the palāśa trees, which have gained full sway in the month of spring and are yellowish-red in hue."
Here, the substantive "of the *palāśa* trees" (*palāśānām*) is itself a pun (*śliṣṭa*).

Due to the context, it is restricted to being expressed as a qualification of the specific tree; consequently, the night-stalkers (*niśācarāḥ*), who are not the subject at hand, are suggested (*vyaṅgya*) by virtue of being the topic under discussion.

In this case, it is more appropriate that the simile (*upamā*) alone is what is suggested, rather than the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), because the latter would serve no purpose here; thus, it has not been mentioned.

Now, one might object: "Just as this [second] type of *dhvani* is an object [of suggestion], why should the first two types not also be so? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the first," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the state of being denotable" (*vācyatva*), for this very reason, they are not objects of *dhvani*.
Because that [object] has a nature distinct from the expressed [meaning],
it is stated [as such] by way of being the object of a third mode, due to its predominance;
for it is possible to include both [the first two modes] within the first mode as well.
For example, in sequence:

"May that Mādhava, who is ever-present, protect you—he by whom the body of Bali was formerly made into a woman by the Destroyer of Manobhava (Śiva); he who wears a serpent as a necklace and bracelet and bore the Gaṅgā;

"The sight of those lotuses, reared in the forest, was like seeing those who have been brought to a state of agitation by greedy hunters with many arrows."

In this instance, both Hari and Hara are contextual (prākaraṇika),
while the lotuses and the deer are non-contextual (aprākaraṇika) because they serve as points of comparison; thus,
Īśvara and Manobhava possess the status of being both contextual and non-contextual.
Thus, because it exists by virtue of residing in both word and meaning, it is threefold.

But *arthaśleṣa* (semantic pun) occurs where there is no difference in accent and so forth;

However, by combining both, there is *ubhayaśleṣa* (both kinds of pun).
